Bulgaria restricts operation of Kozloduy NPP due to low water level in Danube — ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
17:14:49 UTC
02:14:49 KST

SOFIA, August 20. /TASS/. Bulgaria has to restrict the operation of its Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) due to low water levels in the Danube River, the country’s Energy Ministry reported.
According to the ministry, the capacity of Unit 5 will be scaled down by 120 megawatts on August 21 to avert a potential emergency.
"The decision to reduce the reactor's output by 120 megawatts is part of measures to ensure the safe operation of the Kozloduy NPP, which has become necessary due to the ongoing, unprecedented, and critical drop in the Danube River's water levels. The downward trend in the Bulgarian section of the river persists," the ministry said in a statement.
This marks the first time a power unit's capacity has been reduced due to environmental factors in the plant's 52 years of operation. Water from the Danube is utilized to cool steam in the condensers located in the non-nuclear section of the power unit, supplied by a dedicated pumping station on the riverbank.
According to the Executive Agency for Exploration and Maintenance of the Danube River, the water level near the city of Ruse has remained at 124 centimeters below the zero mark over the past 24 hours.

Qusra families fear permanent displacement as siege drags on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
17:14:28 UTC
02:14:28 KST

Breadcrumb
'We will stand our ground until death': Qusra families fear permanent displacement as settler siege drags on
Palestinian families forced from their homes in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra remain displaced even after the Israeli military moved to remove terrorist settlers from the area, an intervention that one displaced resident told The New Arab was intended to “silence the media” rather than bring the siege to an end.
The intervention followed days in which Israeli forces had enabled settlers during the siege, restricting Palestinian residents while allowing settlers to move through the area. The military later dismantled illegal settler outposts after the siege drew international attention.
Yousef Hassan, whose family home was besieged by Israeli terrorists on Sunday, 9 August, said the change had brought little relief. Israeli soldiers now occupy his home, and his family remains displaced elsewhere in the village.
Hassan said residents fear the Israeli army operation could ultimately make their displacement permanent.
"I believe the army carried out this operation to silence the media," he told The New Arab, referring to broad international coverage of the siege that preceded Israeli forces dismantling illegal settler outposts around the village.
The coverage brought widespread condemnation, including from US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, an avid supporter of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, who finally labelled the settlers' actions as terrorism.
Yet the military action that followed has not returned Qusra's displaced families to their homes.
Since the Israeli military declared the village, south of Nablus, a closed military zone on 13 August, several Palestinian families have been displaced to other parts of Qusra. Hassan's home remains occupied by Israeli soldiers.
The consequences are increasingly pressing. Hassan's four-year-old daughter is due to begin school soon, he said, and could be deprived of an education if the siege continues.
He does not know how long the situation will last. The family has nowhere else to go and remains determined to return home.
"We will stand our ground here until death," he said.
Conditions across Qusra, meanwhile, continue to deteriorate.
On Wednesday, Qusra's mayor, Abdul Azim Wadi, warned that the town was running out of food and medical supplies, an account Hassan also affirmed.
Despite the Israeli military presence, settlers continue to roam the area.
"Sometimes there are five and sometimes as many as 15," are present in and around Qusra, Hassan told Medical Aid for Palestinians.
The siege has also seen the Israeli military close a factory for a week, while supplies have entered the village only once through a UNICEF convoy.
Settlers cut water and electricity to the town as part of the siege, though the municipality has since managed to restore the utilities.
Even those efforts faced interference, with Israeli forces positioned around the village and the Ras al-Ain area attacking an electrical team during an earlier attempt to reconnect the village, Wadi said.
"What is different now is that there is an intention for this presence to continue," he added, comparing the current siege with decades of previous settler attacks in which Palestinian homes were burned and livestock stolen.
The deteriorating conditions have also created an increasingly acute healthcare crisis.
Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) held a medical day in Qusra on Tuesday, treating 431 patients in a single day.
Milena Ansari, Director of the Occupied Palestinian Territory Department for PHRI, told The New Arab: "Residents told us that Qusra, despite having more than 7,000 people, has only a tiny clinic operating in a room beneath the mosque, with a doctor available for just two hours once a week."
"Almost all types of medicines are missing," she added.
Ansari said the shortages could not be separated from the conditions imposed on Qusra. Israeli checkpoints effectively prevent residents from accessing homes, services and healthcare, restrictions she described as existing "by design".
"A medical team should not have to enter a besieged village simply to provide people with basic care."
The siege is unfolding amid a wider surge in settler terrorism and Palestinian displacement across the occupied West Bank.
Five Palestinians were injured on Thursday after Israeli settlers attacked a vehicle, causing it to overturn between the villages of al-Mughayyir and Abu Falah, north of Ramallah, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Human Rights Watch said on Thursday that 107 Palestinian communities have been fully or partially displaced since January 2023 because of settler attacks, while Peace Now has said settler outposts control nearly one fifth of the occupied West Bank.
Amnesty International has labelled the mass displacement of Palestinians through settler attacks as state-sanctioned ethnic cleansing.
Ansari said what was happening in Qusra could not be understood solely as settler activity, describing it as part of "the Israeli government’s tools of de facto annexation".
"Settlers attack Palestinians, seize land, destroy homes and agricultural property, and prevent farmers from reaching their own land, while the Israeli state and military repeatedly fail to protect Palestinians or hold perpetrators accountable," she said.
"Palestinians are pushed out, and settlers take over."

Beirut accuses Tehran of interfering in Lebanon's internal affairs

Lina Altawell
20 August 2026•Update: 20 August 2026
Lebanese Foreign Minister Yousef Raggi said on Thursday that Iranian officials must stop interfering in Lebanon’s internal affairs, adding that normal relations with Tehran’s diplomatic mission in Beirut can only resume once Iran respects Lebanese state decisions.
“Iranian officials must stop interfering in Lebanon’s internal affairs, the latest example being the statements made by the Speaker of the Iranian Parliament,” Raggi told Lebanese daily An-Nahar.
“Respect for Lebanon’s sovereignty is the essential basis for normal diplomatic relations between the two countries,” he added.
“Normal relations with the Iranian mission in Lebanon can only resume once Tehran complies with the Lebanese state’s decision and respects Lebanon’s sovereignty and the decisions of its institutions,” Raggi asserted.
He added that any resumption of normal ties must be done in accordance “with established diplomatic rules and procedures.”
On Monday, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun stressed the need for “state-to-state relations” with Iran based on mutual respect and non-interference in internal affairs.
The remarks come amid months of tension between Beirut and Tehran over statements by Iranian officials that Lebanon views as interference in its domestic affairs.
In mid-March, Raggi summoned Iran’s chargé d’affaires to convey Beirut’s objection to statements that he said constituted a “clear violation of our national sovereignty and a breach of our government’s decisions.”
Soon afterward, Beirut declared Iranian Ambassador Mohammad Reza Shibani persona non grata, citing what it described as “violations of established diplomatic norms and protocols” by Tehran.

German state bans pro-Palestine group over 'antisemitism'
Unknown

Breadcrumb
German state bans pro-Palestine group over 'antisemitism', raids former members' homes
Pro-Palestine group Palästina e.V. was banned by the German state of Hesse on Tuesday over accusations of antisemitism and support for terrorism.
Authorities raided five properties linked to the group, which an administrative court had previously ruled was carrying out activities that contradict Germany's constitutional order.
“With the ban on the association Palästina e.V., Hesse is sending a clear signal in favor of decisive action by the rule of law and against the rise of antisemitism,” Hesse Interior Minister Roman Poseck said in a statement.
The Interior Ministry also accused the group of "spreading antisemitic stereotypes, deepening social tensions, and seriously undermining the principle of international understanding".
The ban comes after months of investigations against Palästina e.V., with authorities having raided homes of the group's leaders in January 2025.
Hesse's Interior Ministry said that the group “spread antisemitic positions, denied the right of the State of Israel to exist, and disseminated corresponding propaganda publicly", adding that its activities "fuel antisemitic resentment and spread anti-Israel narratives".
Palästina e.V. was founded in January 2022 in Frankfurt, with its statutes calling for support for "all forms of Palestinian resistance" and the "liberation of all of historical Palestine from Zionist occupation, from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean Sea" - a slogan banned by Germany's federal government in 2024.
Authorities also accused the group of supporting terror, highlighting remarks made by a prominent member who described the 7 October attacks on Israel as a "successful resistance action". It is unclear when the statements were made.
Palästina e.V. dissolved itself in 2024, however authorities continued their investigations into the group due to the continued pro-Palestine activism of its members.
In its last statement on social media, the group said: “If you thought we’d just sit here like rabbits frozen in fear, waiting for your next attack, you are mistaken! You wanted to ban our association? It no longer exists! We officially announce the dissolution of Palästina eV!"
The ban follows similar measures carried out against pro-Palestine groups in Germany, in what activists have described as a crackdown on criticism of Israel.
In late 2023, Germany's Federal Ministry of the Interior banned international pro-Palestine network Samidoun and its local chapter, Samidoun Deutschland, accusing it of supporting Hamas.
In May 2024, Palestine Solidarity Duisburg (PSDU) was banned by authorities in North Rhine-Westphalia state after raids on members' homes.
Germany has supported Israel through its war on Gaza, including through arms sales and political solidarity with Tel Aviv. This has been accompanied by a domestic crackdown on pro-Palestine activism, including blanket bans on protests.
Germany has long portrayed its support for Israel as part of its repaying a historical debt for the holocaust - a framing activists have said places a false equivalence between the state of Israel and the Jewish people.

Russian Drone Launch Sites Hit at Two Airfields as Ukraine Strikes Nebo-U and Niobium Radars
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) struck drone storage and launch sites at two airfields overnight on August 20, including facilities in temporarily occupied Donetsk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR on August 20, operators from its Active Operations Department and Unmanned Systems Department carried out the strikes as part of a deep-strike operation targeting Russian military facilities.
The agency said both airfields had been regularly used by Russian forces to launch attack drones against civilian targets in Ukraine. As a result of the strikes, ground-based components of the drone systems and UAV launchers were damaged, while fires broke out at the impact sites.
HUR operators also struck two Russian radar systems in the vicinity of the Primorsko-Akhtarsk airfield.
The systems were identified by Ukrainian intelligence as a 55Zh6U Nebo-U and a 55Zh6UM Niobium radar, both of which HUR described as high-value Russian assets.
The strikes in Russia’s Krasnodar region extended beyond the airfield. Ukrainian Defense Forces drones also targeted an oil and gas terminal and a key electrical substation linked to the power supply of temporarily occupied Crimea.
According to the outlet, satellite data from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System detected fires at both facilities, including the Tamanneftegaz oil and gas complex in the settlement of Volna.

Several hundred Ukrainian soldiers desert during training in Germany — newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
17:09:38 UTC
02:09:38 KST

BERLIN, August 20. /TASS/. Hundreds of Ukrainian soldiers undergoing training in Germany have reportedly not returned to their units after completing their instruction, according to Die Zeit. The newspaper reveals that since 2022, more than 80 Ukrainian troops have deserted a training facility in Saxony-Anhalt alone, with several hundred cases documented across the country.
Under Ukrainian law, these individuals are classified as deserters and could face up to 12 years in prison if they return home.
Many of these soldiers did not volunteer for military service; instead, they were forcibly conscripted. When sent for training at the Altengrabow military training ground in Saxony-Anhalt, they seized the opportunity to escape. Unlike civilians fleeing Ukraine to seek refuge in Germany, Ukrainian military personnel in Germany are not protected under Section 24 of the Residence Act, which offers asylum to those "forced out of Ukraine." This legal distinction means that military personnel sent to Germany do not benefit from the same protections.
Since the onset of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, approximately 29,000 Ukrainian service members have undergone training at around 60 military facilities across Germany. Their instruction included marksmanship, camouflage techniques, first aid, and other basic military skills. While the German Ministry of Defense acknowledged that some soldiers have escaped from training sites, there is no centralized system tracking these incidents nationwide.

What is Egypt's role in the new regional security order?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
17:09:00 UTC
02:09:00 KST

Breadcrumb
What is Egypt's role in the new regional security order?
Egypt's current absence from the collective security pact signed between Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia, dubbed the ‘Mecca Agreement’, has brought renewed attention to Egypt’s security strategy towards its regional allies and the wider region.
While speculation surrounding Egypt’s absence from the agreement abounds, understanding Cairo’s position requires looking beyond the Mecca Agreement.
Egypt’s regional security posture has historically been shaped by a preference for strategic flexibility, driven by the recognition that its interests often require maintaining relationships with competing regional and international actors.
Today, this approach is being tested by an increasingly volatile regional environment marked by state and non-state threats, from Israel’s expanding regional wars to the US-Israel-Iran war and its fallout.
The complexities of this geostrategic environment have compelled Cairo to emphasise diplomacy, mediation, and issue-based security cooperation over concrete, bloc-based alignments.
Its rapprochement with Turkey, expanding security ties with major regional players including Saudi Arabia, and maintenance of diplomatic backchannels with rival actors underscore Egypt’s efforts to diversify its security partnerships while preserving the flexibility to engage across regional fault lines.
Security through diplomacy
A 1955 telegram from the US Embassy in Cairo to the US Department of State documented a tense exchange between then Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser and then US Assistant Secretary of State George Allen over Egypt’s acquisition of Czechoslovak arms.
During the exchange, Nasser expressed doubts about Washington’s reliability as a security partner and raised concerns about Israel’s growing influence and territorial ambitions, particularly the influence of the Herut party, the predecessor to today’s Likud.
The exchange reflects a key feature of Egyptian strategic thinking. Cairo has long been sceptical of overreliance on a single external security umbrella, preferring instead to preserve room for manoeuvre.
That instinct remains salient in Cairo’s approach today. "Egypt has largely focused on managing and balancing its bilateral relationships with all major regional players to address growing instability and threats,” Liam Karr, Africa Team Lead at the Critical Threats Project, told The New Arab.
Egypt’s security is increasingly being tested by instability beyond its immediate borders, primarily driven by Israel’s expanding regional wars and now compounded by the US-Israel-Iran war. Previously assumed to be relatively shielded from these developments, Egypt has increasingly found itself directly exposed to their consequences.
Israel’s war on Gaza heightened Egyptian threat perceptions, particularly amid Israeli calls at the time for the displacement of Palestinians into Sinai, a scenario Cairo repeatedly identified as a red line.
The war also brought Israeli incursions closer to Egyptian territory. Throughout the war, Israel repeatedly asserted control over the Philadelphi Corridor, a narrow strip along the Egypt-Gaza border whose security arrangements have been shaped by the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty and subsequent agreements.
“Egypt’s threat perception has been shaped particularly by Israel’s unilateral security expansionism. This perception led to a greater emphasis on mediation across regional fault lines, while balancing against Cairo’s rivals, first and foremost Israel,” Ahmed Aboudouh, Associate Fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told The New Arab.
Egypt’s response focused heavily on diplomacy. Alongside Qatar, Cairo maintained a central role in efforts to mediate between Israel and Hamas, positioning itself as an intermediary capable of communicating with multiple sides.
Earlier this month, US special envoy Jared Kushner met a Hamas delegation led by Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt, in a rare direct high-level meeting, to discuss implementation of the Board of Peace’s roadmap, namely the question of Hamas’s disarmament.
A durable end to the war on Gaza is vital to Egypt’s economic and security stability, particularly as the conflict continues to generate pressure along its border and across the Red Sea. Egypt’s economic vulnerabilities have raised the stakes. The Suez Canal, one of the country’s main sources of foreign currency, saw revenues collapse by roughly two-thirds at the height of Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping.
The resumption of attacks on Red Sea shipping and rising regional tensions stemming from the US-Israel-Iran war further jeopardise Egypt’s economic security. Cairo also remains heavily reliant on Gulf investment and financial support, making stability across the Gulf and Red Sea increasingly inseparable from its own economic security.
The Egyptian economy has, however, shown some signs of recovery. In July, the IMF reinforced confidence in Egypt’s economic reform program, unlocking an additional $1.8 billion in funds after Cairo completed its latest review. That said, underlying vulnerabilities remain.
The widening geography of the US-Israel-Iran war was underscored in late July, when a drone struck Egypt’s Damietta port. The incident marked the first attack on Egyptian territory since the outbreak of the war, illustrating the interconnectedness of regional conflicts and directly exposing Egypt to new security threats. It also highlights the urgency of reaching a durable resolution.
Egypt’s diplomatic leverage derives in large part from its ability to maintain relationships across divides. Earlier this year, Egypt used its diplomatic backchannel with the IRGC, an increasingly prominent decision-making actor in Iran, to help preserve a line of contact during a moment of heightened tension. Given the trajectory of regional dynamics, these channels are likely to remain important.
Egypt has also demonstrated a willingness to extend military support to its regional partners. During Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi’s visit to Abu Dhabi in May, he visited an Egyptian fighter detachment stationed in the UAE comprising Rafale jets and Egyptian pilots, alongside reports of Egyptian defensive deployments in Saudi Arabia.
Gulf security is closely aligned with Egyptian interests, but Cairo’s current absence from the Mecca agreement may reflect a recognition of the risks that a more hardened posture could invite, as well as a preference for maintaining strategic balance.
Issue-based cooperation over bloc alignment
Egypt maintains robust security relationships with all three members of the Mecca Agreement. Its current absence from the pact should therefore not be interpreted as a rejection of closer regional security cooperation.
Egypt and Turkey have considerably expanded their security cooperation as part of their broader political rapprochement. In June, the two countries conducted joint F-16 drills, the first exercise of its kind in almost two decades, building on the momentum generated by their 2025 joint maritime exercise, “Sea of Friendship.”
Ankara and Cairo have also pledged greater coordination on regional files including Sudan, Libya, and Gaza. Additionally, defence-industrial cooperation has expanded. Ankara and Cairo signed agreements worth approximately $350 million earlier this year aimed primarily at expanding joint production efforts.
These initiatives serve Egypt’s immediate defence needs while simultaneously enhancing regional strategic autonomy.
Cairo’s relationship with Riyadh is similarly deep. Egypt was among the 14 founding members of the Saudi-led Red Sea security maritime force. Its participation also builds on extensive experience in collective maritime security initiatives, including its current command, for the second time, of the Combined Maritime Forces’ Combined Task Force-153, the Red Sea focused task force.
“Egypt wants to be a central leader to regional approaches in its backyard, as shown by its involvement in the Sudan Quad, various multilateral security initiatives in the Red Sea, and the Libya and Palestine peace processes,” Karr told The New Arab.
Diversified partnerships
Participation in a formal collective security pact could strengthen deterrence, but it could also narrow Egypt’s room for manoeuvre and constrain its ability to mediate across regional divides.
“Egypt will maintain its cautious, defensive and risk-averse approach to avoid antagonising any party with leverage to pressure its direct national interests,” said Aboudouh.
Egypt will likely continue diversifying its security partnerships rather than committing to formal blocs. In line with this posture, China and Egypt are currently hosting the second iteration of their joint aerial exercise, "Eagles of Civilisation," from mid-August to early September, following the inaugural exercise held in 2025.
Strategically, Cairo will also have to guard against military overstretch as it manages simultaneous pressure across two turbulent fronts, the Middle East and the Nile Basin. Ethiopia's plans for three additional dams on the Nile have already drawn strong opposition from Cairo.
Managing these competing pressures will reinforce Egypt’s preference for diversified partnerships and strategic flexibility, allowing it to deepen cooperation where its interests converge while avoiding overreliance on any single security partner.
Hana Elshehaby is a Research Assistant for the Middle East Council on Global Affairs’ Foreign Policy Program. Her research interests include GCC foreign policy, regional security frameworks, and the Asian powers' expanding political relations with the Middle East

Cameroon president returns home after 10-week absence

Cameroon president returns home after 10-week absence
YAOUNDE, Aug 20 - Cameroon's President Paul Biya returned home on Thursday after his longest recorded stay abroad since taking power more than four decades ago, ending months of speculation about his health and whereabouts.
The 93-year-old leader arrived at Yaounde's Nsimalen International Airport aboard a chartered flight from Geneva, Switzerland, after more than 10 weeks away.
Biya, the world's oldest head of state, left Cameroon on June 7 for what the civil cabinet described as "a brief private stay in Europe".
The president, accompanied by First Lady Chantal Biya, touched down around 4.45 p.m. local time (1545 pm GMT) before departing in a motorcade for the Etoudi Unity Palace.
He waved through a half-open window to hundreds of supporters of the ruling Cameroon People's Democratic Movement (CPDM) who lined the streets of the capital to welcome him home, waving party colours and banners praising the president.
Biya's prolonged absence had fuelled widespread speculation about his health and capacity to govern, despite repeated assurances from authorities that he would return soon. It also raised more questions about political succession in a country where power remains highly centralized around the presidency.
Opposition politicians had called on the Constitutional Council to examine whether someone should fill in as head of state during the president's absence. The council did not take any action.
Under Cameroon's constitution, in the absence of a vice president, the president of the Senate should assume interim duties if the presidency is declared vacant due to death, resignation or permanent incapacity.
Biya has not appointed a vice president despite the reintroduction of the role last April, and critics say the lack of a clear succession framework raises uncertainty about a potential transition in the event he becomes unable to govern. REUTERS

The UN on Thursday renewed its demand for the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Gaza Strip.

"Meanwhile, our humanitarian partners working on shelter reported today that 94% of Gaza's 2.1 million people need shelter and basic household assistance," he added.
More than four out of five families face "critical or catastrophic" levels of hunger in their shelters, which lack fuel, energy and essential household items, he said.

Parliament votes on new Bangladesh’s president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
17:06:39 UTC
02:06:39 KST

NEW DELHI, August 20. /TASS/. Politician Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has been elected the 23rd president of Bangladesh following a parliamentary vote, The Times of India reported.
According to the newspaper, 255 members of parliament voted for Alamgir, the candidate from the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), while 88 voted for his opponent, Oli Ahmad, who was nominated by the opposition alliance.
This is the first time in 35 years that two candidates have been nominated in a Bangladeshi presidential election. The country’s last parliamentary-led presidential election took place in 1991.
The previous president, Mohammed Shahabuddin, who was elected head of state in 2023, resigned on July 24 due to health reasons. In accordance with the constitution, a new president was elected within 90 days through a parliamentary vote.
The president of Bangladesh is the head of state, but his powers are largely ceremonial. Executive authority is concentrated in the hands of the prime minister and the government. Typically, the president acts on the prime minister's and government's advice and does not make independent political decisions.

Will Ukraine hold elections during wartime after Fedorov's call?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:58:31 UTC
01:58:31 KST

Fedorov broke Ukraine's wartime election taboo. What happens next?
L: President Volodymyr Zelensky in Brussels, Belgium, on June 18, 2026. (Daniel Gnap / NurPhoto / Getty Images) R: Mykhailo Fedorov, then-Defense Minister of Ukraine, on June 17, 2026. (Roman Pashkovskiy / Mykhailo Fedorov's team);(Collage: The Kyiv Independent)
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has broken one of Ukraine's most politically sensitive wartime taboos by publicly calling for elections, bringing into the mainstream a debate that Kyiv had largely rejected when raised by Russia and the United States.
Fedorov said Ukraine needs a "safe and realistic mechanism" to hold elections during wartime that protects the voting rights of soldiers, Ukrainians abroad, and people in front-line regions.
"We must not let Putin decide when Ukrainians can choose their government," Fedorov said in a video address, adding that democracy is "part of what we are fighting for today."
The timing matters. His appeal came after weeks of political turmoil that had shaken public confidence in President Volodymyr Zelensky's governance, including corruption scandals, a chaotic government reshuffle, and nationwide protests over Fedorov's dismissal as defense minister.
For years, Ukraine's answer to the proposal to hold wartime elections was simple: not now. The majority of Ukrainians have expressed no desire to hold elections before a ceasefire is reached, according to recent polls. That consensus, however, is becoming harder to maintain.
Zelensky's team already considered elections
Fedorov's call for wartime elections may have sounded like a break with the government's position. But the idea was not new inside the President's Office. Ukrainian officials had been quietly discussing the possibility of elections for months.
In mid-June, a government compound outside Kyiv became the setting for a rare high-level meeting, bringing together some of the most powerful figures in Ukraine's wartime leadership.
The meeting included Zelensky, his chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, his security adviser, Oleg Tatarov, and David Arakhamia, the leader of Zelensky's parliamentary faction. Fedorov represented the government, while then-National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov also attended.
"We need to hold elections in September, October," Fedorov told those gathered.
Zelensky's team seriously considered holding a presidential election as early as mid-fall.
The discussions were prompted in part by confidential opinion polling that had recently reached Zelensky's team. The results showed stronger support for the president than expected, according to people familiar with the discussions.
That appears to have encouraged the idea. The logic was straightforward: Zelensky's approval was rising, so the administration could try to capitalize on the moment before the political situation changed again.
Ultimately, Zelensky opted against holding elections, a position supported by his main political rival at that time, Ukraine's Ambassador to the U.K., Valerii Zaluzhnyi, former Commander-in-Chief of Ukraine's Armed Forces.
Zelensky's legitimacy during war
Zelensky's constitutionally designated five-year term ended in May 2024, raising questions about his legitimacy. Yet elections alone do not make a country democratic, just as Ukraine's inability to hold elections during wartime does not, by itself, indicate a drift toward autocracy.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, much of Ukrainian society has accepted what could be described as an informal public contract: voters, civil society, and opposition parties have broadly agreed to postpone elections in exchange for national survival and stability during an existential war.
Under martial law, imposed on the first day of the full-scale invasion, elections are suspended, while elected officials remain in office until new elections can be held. Surveys and civil society organizations have repeatedly found strong public support for prioritizing national defense and preserving national unity over holding elections during wartime.
That understanding also helped shield Zelensky from criticism when U.S. President Donald Trump called him "a dictator without elections" after Zelensky refused to sign the first draft of a minerals deal with Washington in 2025.
At the time, Trump appeared to be pushing an idea contrary to Ukrainian public sentiment. Now, that unspoken consensus is being challenged from within.
The change followed a series of events that gradually weakened trust in Zelensky and his administration.
In July last year, Zelensky signed a law placing the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) under the prosecutor general, an official appointed by the president, stripping them of their independence. Street protests and pressure from Brussels forced the government to restore the agencies' independence.
The controversy became more significant as it emerged that Ukrainian law enforcement agencies were investigating people close to Zelensky.
Timur Mindich, one of the president's closest associates, was among seven people charged in a major corruption probe announced by NABU on Nov. 11. According to NABU, the group "set up a major corruption scheme to control key state-owned enterprises," including Energoatom, Ukraine's state-owned nuclear energy agency.
Weeks later, Andriy Yermak, head of the President's Office, resigned after NABU searched his premises on Nov. 28. Yermak was investigated in a case involving Energoatom, which became the biggest corruption investigation of Zelensky's presidency. Mindich was allegedly identified as the ringleader.
The scandals weakened the argument that every controversial government decision could be justified by wartime survival. Still, Zelensky was able to weather the storm of public discontent by caving into popular demands and distancing himself from the most contentious topics.
read also
Fedorov, protests, and lost trust
Earlier this year, Ukraine appeared to be in a relatively strong position.
In May, Ukraine liberated more territory than Russia captured for the first time since 2023, according to the Ukrainian monitoring group DeepState. The battlefield developments coincided with an improvement in Zelensky's approval ratings: his approval rose from 53% in February to 62% in early March, according to the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology. In early July, 61% of Ukrainians said they trusted Zelensky, while 34% said they did not.
Then came the government reshuffle.
Fedorov's dismissal was particularly difficult for the public to understand. He had become one of the government's most popular officials, overseeing reforms aimed at strengthening Ukraine's military and helping modernize the Armed Forces and expand the country's drone capabilities.
Zelensky never provided a detailed explanation for his dismissal, pointing instead to an alleged conflict between Fedorov and then-Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi. The explanation did little to calm public anger.
Protests erupted across Ukraine, with thousands gathering in Kyiv and other cities to demand Fedorov's return. The demands soon expanded to include Syrskyi's dismissal. Zelensky eventually removed him and appointed General Mykhailo Drapatyi, a widely respected commander, as his successor.
The move was welcomed by many Ukrainians, and some subsequent protests drew smaller crowds. But the central dispute remained unresolved: Fedorov was still out.
Thousands gathered in a Kyiv park on July 31 before marching through central Kyiv in what organizers called a "march for dialogue and reforms in defense." The protests continued, regularly drawing crowds in central Kyiv, showing that removing Syrskyi had not settled the anger surrounding Fedorov's dismissal.
With no way back into office, Fedorov recorded a video address alleging high-level corruption among people close to the president and demanding elections to reset the system, which the minister was part of for almost seven years.
Fedorov's election proposal went against the desires of those who took to the streets with their demands for the reinstatement of Fedorov as part of the existing power structure.
Dmytro Kozatynskyi, one of the protest organizers, wrote that "a street protest is definitely not the place for electoral discourse."
"I have a negative attitude towards elections during war — I cannot imagine how to technically provide the opportunity to vote and run for office to thousands of servicemen who are currently at the front," he added.
read also
What changed?
Fedorov's call was preceded by a gradual shift in the public discussion. Ukrainian public figures and some of the country's most widely read media outlets had begun breaking the taboo around discussing elections, as Zelensky faced growing criticism for ignoring protests outside his office and refusing to meet demonstrators' main demand: Fedorov's reinstatement.
The parliamentary opposition, however, remains more cautious.
Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, a lawmaker from the opposition Holos party, told the Kyiv Independent that he cannot imagine elections taking place until fundamental problems are resolved.
"Until we have an answer to the question of how to ensure that military personnel and Ukrainians abroad can vote, until the voter registry is verified, and — most importantly — until there have been no attacks for at least six months — I can't imagine how to hold elections," he said.
"That's why I don't understand how Fedorov can call on them to do so."
Volodymyr Ariev, a lawmaker from the opposition European Solidarity party, largely agreed but put the responsibility on Zelensky.
"Zelensky's selfishness, his detachment from reality, and his inability to take the steps that Ukraine — not his administration — needs are leading the country into disaster," he said.
"We've reached a point where we have to choose between elections and chaos — that is, between a bad option and a catastrophe. It's not an easy choice, but if Zelensky doesn't come to his senses, then elections will be the way out."
Mykyta Poturaiev and Oleksandr Merezhko from Zelensky's own Servant of the People told the Kyiv Independent that they cannot imagine holding elections at this stage of the war.
"Holding elections under martial law is legally and politically impossible," Merezhko said.
"The best way to lose the war is to start an election campaign which will inevitably lead to internal political divisions, fierce political struggle, enhanced vulnerability of the country, and, as a result, a starkly divided and dysfunctional parliament incapable of adopting unpopular but necessary laws."
Poturaiev was even more direct.
"I categorically do not support the idea — at least not at this stage of the war," he said.
"Mykhailo came out with a political manifesto in order to launch his own political project."
Poturaiev was among the most vocal public supporters of Fedorov before his recent address.
'Between Shahed drones and ballistic missiles'
People close to Zelensky told the Kyiv Independent that they cannot imagine holding elections at this stage of the war.
Winter is an especially serious concern, as Russia is expected to target Ukraine's energy infrastructure again.
"It's just strange to even think about a choice between Shahed (drones) and ballistic missiles," one senior official from Zelensky's office said. "(Fedorov) lives such a good life, completely detached from reality."
The official had held that view even before Fedorov called for elections.
Fedorov's team, meanwhile, points back to his own argument: democracy is not something Ukraine should postpone indefinitely because Russia attacked it.
"Democracy is not a peacetime luxury. Democracy is part of what we are fighting for today," Fedorov said.
He has not said whether he would run if elections were held. People around Fedorov say he currently has no intention of starting a political party or movement and plans to work in the miltech sector and with think tanks.
But his remarks about accountability quickly gained ground.
On Aug. 19, NABU searched the premises of Iryna Mudra, a deputy chief of staff in the President's Office, and lawmaker Vadym Stolar, according to a law enforcement source familiar with the investigation who spoke to the Kyiv Independent.
Zelensky fired Mudra shortly afterward. She had overseen the judiciary in the President's Office.
The timing showed the broader problem facing the Ukrainian government: the political argument over elections is no longer happening in the same environment as it was several years ago.
Before, whenever Russia or Trump raised the issue, Kyiv could respond with a straightforward argument: Ukraine was under martial law, elections were legally prohibited, and holding them could endanger the country's survival.
Now, the question is becoming more complicated.
Ukraine still faces a full-scale war. Its laws still prohibit elections under martial law. The security and logistical challenges remain enormous. But the political consensus that made the question almost untouchable has begun to crack.
Is an election even possible?
The legal obstacles remain substantial.
Ukraine's martial law, imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, explicitly bans presidential, parliamentary, and local elections.
The Constitution extends parliament's authority until martial law ends. It does not contain similar provisions for presidential or local elections.
That means a presidential election would require either lifting martial law or changing the legislation governing it.
Even if the legal barriers were removed, holding an election during or immediately after the war would require extensive preparations.
Ukraine would need to adopt special election legislation, amend existing laws, update the voter registry, allow time for voter registration and public information campaigns, and establish procedures for voting in areas affected by the war.
Authorities would also need to protect polling from political violence, cyberattacks, and foreign interference.
They would need arrangements for Ukrainians living abroad and for military personnel serving on the battlefield.
The country would also have to plan the transition from military to civilian governance, secure funding and personnel, and fill vacancies on the Central Election Commission.
None of this is simple.
That is why some Ukrainians see Fedorov's proposal as unrealistic, while others see it as the beginning of a necessary conversation.
And that is perhaps the most important change.
For years, the question of wartime elections was largely treated as settled before it was even debated.
Now it is being debated inside Ukraine — in parliament, among protesters, among political camps, and even within the President's Office.
Fedorov has not provided a ready-made mechanism for making elections happen.
He has done something potentially more consequential: he has made it politically acceptable to ask whether Ukraine should start figuring one out.

The EU has repeatedly stated that implementation of the E1 plan will undermine prospects for a two-state solution and the emergence of a viable Palestinian state.

Ousted Ukrainian defence minister's gamble against Zelenskiy backfires as protests end

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20

Ousted Ukrainian defence minister's gamble against Zelenskiy backfires as protests end
KYIV, Aug 20 - A bid by ousted Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov to broaden a political fight with President Volodymyr Zelenskiy by calling for wartime elections appears to have backfired, failing to win over protesters who had demanded his return.
Zelenskiy's decision to sack the tech-savvy and reform-minded minister in a government reshuffle in July triggered protests in Kyiv and other cities.
Many of the protesters said the dismissal of the popular young minister was poorly explained and could threaten Ukraine's war effort against Russia, and continued protests throughout the summer to demand Zelenskiy reinstate him.
Despite the protests, parliament on Wednesday approved a new defence minister chosen by Zelenskiy and later that day only a few dozen people remained in a central Kyiv square where thousands once joined rare wartime protests.
"When we came out to protest, we did not come with the idea that elections should be held," 22-year-old Iryna Vasyliaka told Reuters late on Wednesday. "That is not what we were here for."
Fedorov, who warned late on Tuesday that Ukraine was facing a crisis of governance, is widely seen as one of a handful of potential challengers to Zelenskiy's hold on power in the fifth year of the war triggered by Russia's 2022 invasion.
But opinion polls show little public appetite for elections in wartime, with Russian airstrikes ravaging towns and cities, hundreds of thousands of troops at the front and millions of compatriots living abroad or under occupation.
Olena Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund, said Fedorov had been poised to cast himself as "a statesman, a politician of a new generation" after the war, but miscalculated.
"With this statement, he pretty much played on Ukrainians' most sensitive pain points," Prokopenko said.
NO FEEL FOR THE PEOPLE?
A host of obstacles would need to be overcome for Ukraine to hold wartime elections.
An August 5 poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, conducted after the pro-Fedorov protests began, found 57% of Ukrainians want elections to be held only after fighting ends.
"Even amid these protests, people didn't want to hold elections," said executive director Anton Grushetskyi. "Why Fedorov didn't understand this remains an open question."
Appearing to announce the end of protests on Wednesday, chief organiser and veteran combat medic Dmytro Koziatynskyi said he "cannot imagine" how to hold polls with troops at the front.
It marked a stark reversal in fortune for Fedorov, who was credited with spearheading tough reforms and pursuing a innovation-driven approach to fighting Russia's bigger army.
Vasyliaka and others said they had joined the protests because they wanted authorities to respond to public concerns over Fedorov's sudden dismissal.
They had also rallied against unpopular military commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, accused by Fedorov of blocking his work. Zelenskiy later replaced Syrskyi with a younger military reformer.
Fedorov then ratcheted up pressure on Zelenskiy by refusing any other role than his old posting, turning down the offer of deputy prime minister.
Yet his call for elections, on the eve of parliament's confirmation of successor Yevhenii Khmara, appeared to be a clumsy misstep, one opposition lawmaker told Reuters.
"This demonstrates that (Fedorov) doesn't have a presidential-level feel for the country," said the lawmaker, who requested anonymity to discuss a sensitive political issue.
Prokopenko described Fedorov's move as a "false start" that could burn his political capital before elections can realistically be held.
ZELENSKIY THE SURVIVOR
The recent protests were the latest headache for Zelenskiy, whose wartime tenure has been marked by periodic scandals over alleged corruption or mismanagement.
Wednesday's confirmation vote for Khmara, a former top special forces commander, followed hours after anti-graft police unveiled an operation against a deputy chief of staff whom Zelenskiy promptly fired. She denied wrongdoing.
Still, Zelenskiy's approval rating has remained generally stable at around 60%. Public morale has also been buoyed by a recent successful Ukrainian campaign of strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and logistics.
"Mainly, people trust him because he's a wartime leader, and they say, 'We should rally around the flag to fight Russian aggression'," said sociologist Grushetskyi.
He said Ukrainians would like to see fresh faces including soldiers and military leaders in power, something that would be virtually impossible if voting were held in wartime.
"Elections without good candidates would be less legitimate in the eyes of the public," Grushetskyi said. REUTERS

Como mayor bans 'beasts' in city centre after being hit by bike
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
17:53:20 BST
01:53:20 KST

Como mayor bans 'beasts' in city centre after being hit by bike
- Published
The mayor of Como has banned riding bicycles in certain areas of the historic Italian city after he was hit by an electric one.
Alessandro Rapinese said the ban was necessary to improve public safety. It means from September, cyclists will have to dismount through an area of around 30 streets.
He told Italian news agency Ansa: "People act based on their own experiences and I know what it's like to be hit by one of these beasts."
Several other local authorities around Europe, including in the UK, have restricted where and how e-bikes and other single-person vehicles can be used.
The measure put forward by Rapinese is part of a package of new traffic regulations, establishing a Limited Traffic Zone (ZTL) to manage tourist growth, and which impose stricter rules on cars and vans in the city centre.
Many of the roads covered by the ban are the widest in the old town and are popular with delivery drivers.
The measure applies to both electric and push bikes, as the Italian highway code does not distinguish between models.
Rapinese explained his decision in a video as part of a series of online videos he produces himself, known as RapiNews24.
He recounted an incident in which he had been leaving city hall in July and collided with an e-bike shortly after his administration had discussed traffic restrictions in the city centre.
The cyclist involved in the collision has not been identified.
"In this case, I didn't even end up in the hospital," Rapinese said. "I was hit by a bike. I gathered information, and that's where the measure came from."
Como's Roman-walled centre is already covered by a limited-traffic zone, and bicycles have become a go-to method of transport for locals.
The new traffic regulations for the ZTL mean some vehicles will require an annual permit and, for each day of entry, a €3 (£2.60) permit.
Deliveries to shops and restaurants will only be allowed between 06:00 and 23:00, while tourists staying in hotels will only be able to drive into the centre if their accommodation has parking.
The ban has faced a backlash from locals and an online petition has been launched to block the resolution.
Civitas Como, a local citizens group, has challenged the legitimacy of ban, describing it as "questionable and erroneous".
The Nova Como association has organised a protest bike ride for 12 September.
Como is not the first Italian city to restrict bicycles in historic or busy parts. In Palermo, bikes have been restricted in some sections of the main streets since 2023.
Meanwhile, Paris recently clamped down on safety requirements for e-scooter users, having banned rental e-scooters outright in 2023.

IMF welcomes Lebanon bank law changes as 'major step'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:51:54 UTC
01:51:54 KST

Breadcrumb
IMF welcomes Lebanon bank law changes as 'major step'
The International Monetary Fund has welcomed the Lebanese parliament's passing of amendments to a bank resolution law as a major step, but challenges to implementing the law could further delay recovery for an economy battered by years of financial collapse and the conflict with Israel.
The reforms are among the IMF's requirements for Lebanon to access funding to bring government debt out of default after decades of profligate spending by the country's ruling elite, sending the economy into a tailspin in late 2019. Banks imposed sweeping capital controls, locking depositors out of their savings, and stopped issuing loans.
In January the IMF had demanded changes to the draft rescue law, Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam told Reuters at the time.
Now, the bank resolution law aims to address vast funding shortfalls in the financial system and is among a set of measures that ultimately aim to fix the banking sector and allow depositors who have been frozen out of their savings to gradually recover their money.
“We met 99% of what they wanted,” legislator Alain Aoun, who sits on Parliament’s Finance and Budget Committee, told Reuters.
The most notable amendments to the law include changes to the Central Bank’s governance procedures. The makeup of the Higher Banking Commission – a governing body within the Central Bank — will be altered, Aoun said. The amendments empower the body to “decide the fate of Lebanon’s banks,” and would determine if a bank requires restructuring or liquidation and any further steps to rehabilitate it.
Federico Lima, the IMF representative in Lebanon, said on Wednesday that the "effective implementation of this new bank resolution framework is critical."
"In addition, we are continuing discussions with the Lebanese authorities on the improvements needed to align the draft Financial Stabilization and Depositor Recovery (FSDR) law with international principles," he added.
In 2022, the government put losses from the financial crisis at about $70 billion, a figure that analysts and economists forecast is now likely to be higher.
Last week, the parliament passed amendments to the law, but it would still be pending approval by the Lebanese president.
The possibility of members challenging the law before the Constitutional Council — which has precedent for annulling provisions of earlier financial legislation — could also bring further delays.
The draft had already undergone several rewrites because of competing demands from different financial institutions; the IMF called on Lebanon to improve the law to bring it in line with international standards and consider tax reforms to spark public spending on reconstruction efforts.
The World Bank ranks the Lebanese economic crisis among the worst globally since the mid-19th century. Depositors were frozen out of dollar accounts, and the Lebanese pound fell by more than 90%. Additionally, the war with Israel was estimated to have caused $7 billion in damages.
"This is the only country in the world that has had a banking crises for seven years and has not tried to find a solution," a senior Lebanese official told Reuters. "Staying where we are shouldn't be an option."

Israeli settlers torch Palestinian homes amid record year of settler terror in West Bank
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank awoke on Thursday to homes in flames after Israeli terrorist settlers carried out fresh arson attacks, with rights groups telling The New Arab that escalating violence has left residents fearing Israel is seeking an excuse to unleash on the territory what it has done in Gaza.
Videos shared online showed flames tearing through a Palestinian home in Khirbet al-Fakheit, west of Yatta in the Hebron area, after settlers entered the community in the early hours of Thursday.
The attack comes amid a record year for settler violence against Palestinians, alongside unprecedented settlement expansion and the forced displacement of Palestinian communities across the occupied territory.
Settlers from Otniel, an illegal Israeli settlement built on occupied Palestinian land, entered the area before setting the house ablaze and leaving.
“These attacks might be today's news, but unfortunately, they are daily news for Palestinians in the West Bank,” Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch (HRW), told The New Arab.
“We've been seeing this escalating violence, whether it's taking the form of settler attacks like the arson attack in Hebron, or whether it's military raids and so-called ‘counterterrorism operations’.”
HRW has documented how the violence is increasingly driving the forced displacement of Palestinian communities, with dozens now at risk of erasure.
The rights group says settler attacks have fully or partially displaced 107 Palestinian communities since January 2023. Violence spiked further in March and April this year, with attacks including killings of adults and children, assaults, sexual violence, physical and mental abuse, arbitrary detention, arson, property destruction and theft.
But Sanbar said such attacks should not be viewed as isolated acts by rogue settlers, warning were being carried out by organised groups operating with the backing and protection of the Israeli state.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court, has previously described violent settlers as “juvenile delinquents”, a characterisation Sanbar rejected.
“It's the Israeli state that's providing [settlers] with the funding, with the arms, with the legal cover to commit attacks against Palestinians with complete impunity, and it's not a question of them failing to stop settler violence; it's a question of the Israeli government actively enabling it,” Sanbar said.

“There is a very real fear and concern amongst Palestinians in the West Bank that the Israeli government is just looking for any excuse to do in the West Bank what they did to Gaza,” Sanbar said.
That fear, she said, comes after years in which Palestinians in the West Bank have faced increasingly harsh treatment, a trend that intensified during Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
Sanbar said the events of October 2023 had further weakened what restraints remained on Israel's treatment of Palestinians, making previously understood limits increasingly unclear.

Mary Heilmann obituary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:50:35 UTC
01:50:35 KST

Visitors to Mary Heilmann’s show at the Whitechapel Gallery in 2016 were offered the novel experience of looking at art while scooting about on wheeled wooden chairs. These, too, turned out to be artworks. One, Sunny Chair for the Whitechapel, had been made by Heilmann for the occasion. Rough-hewn from plywood, backed in nylon webbing and painted bright yellow, it seemed happily untidy; as an object, but also as a type. This was true of all the works in Looking at Pictures, and was intentional.
Heilmann, who has died aged 86, had an untidy past as a maker. It was while doing a BA at the University of California, Santa Barbara (1959-62), that she discovered ceramics, which were to occupy her first decade as an artist. The untidiness of her artistic history, however, was to be shaped by more than her choice of materials.
Born in San Francisco, she was the daughter of John, a civil engineer, and Mary (nee Webb), a nurse. Her mother had insisted on continuing to work while raising her two children. She instilled the need for self-sufficiency into her daughter, who trained as a teacher before going to art school.
When Heilmann was seven, her family moved south to Los Angeles. The city’s surf culture attracted her, particularly diving. “I became a fledgling competitive diver at 11,” she told the Guardian in an interview for her Whitechapel show. “A little girl could get a lot of attention diving off the tower at the Coliseum.” As she would discover, though, attention was harder to come by as a female artist.
In 1965, she signed on to a ceramics and sculpture MA at Berkeley, taught by the celebrated ceramicist Peter Voulkos. “He was amazing,” Heilmann recalled. “A super-radical nut-job hippie.”
Voulkos’s huge, abstract expressionist ceramics were on the scale of sculpture, although he had initially trained as a painter. His student would now go the other way, exchanging ceramics for sculpture and then, by the late 1960s, painting.
For all that, Heilmann did not get the kind of attention she had had as a high-board diver, or that male friends such as Bruce Nauman and Richard Serra were now getting as students. “It was the case that girls were very not noticed as artists,” she told an Archives of American Art interviewer in 2022. “There were a lot of really good young women artists, but only a few got any attention.”
This, in part, is what drove her to untidiness. If teachers such as Voulkos overlooked her and her work, she would get their attention “not by being sexy and cute and flirty, but by being provocative and ornery, and then making art that was provocative and ornery”.
In 1968, Heilmann left California for New York, intent on meeting the minimalist artist Donald Judd. (Judd too had made chairs, although his “were not very comfortable”, Heilmann told Vogue magazine. “Mine are.”) Moving into Serra’s former loft in Manhattan’s Tribeca, she was visited by Holly Solomon, a dealer whose eponymous gallery specialised in the work of Californian artists. From 1976, Solomon gave Heilmann a series of shows. The third, in 1979, was a flop.
The problem was pink. In her desire to be ornery, Heilmann had made a series of paintings that defied the colour’s association with femininity – “fluffy dress pink”, as she called it. “Pink is a pretty colour,” Heilmann said, “but it was also a hip, culturally hip, naughty colour, or a rough, rough colour.”
The one she used for her paintings in the 1979 show was assertively naughty and rough – an acid, eye-popping pink offset in each canvas by black. The works, Heilmann said, may have been “playful and sarcastic”, but they were also “very, very serious, and formal, and colourist”, informed by the thinking of the Bauhaus colour theorist Josef Albers. This fact eluded the critic of the Village Voice, who sniffed that the canvases lacked “real muscle”, and that Heilmann “hadn’t been doing her push-ups”. What made this borderline misogynistic attack particularly painful was that the critic was a woman.
Leaving Holly Solomon soon after, Heilmann went to the gallerist Pat Hearn, who gave her a series of exhibitions throughout the late 80s and 90s.
Her life changed when, in 1997, she was taken up by the Swiss kingmakers, Hauser & Wirth. In that year, she had her first international one-woman exhibition in Zurich, at the Zürcher Stiftung für Konstruktive und Konkrete Kunst. A solo show at the Camden Art Centre in London followed in 2001, and at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne in 2010.
Through all of this, Heilmann and her art proved resistant to tidiness. The earliest pieces in her Whitechapel show, such as Little 9 x 9 (1973), were finger paintings, a method Heilmann had learned when teaching children. She would have a longer career teaching adults, at Stony Brook University on Long Island and then at the School of Visual Arts in Manhattan. “I made the work by squeezing through the paint with my fingers,” she said.
Black Cracky (1990) showed a fascination with breakage, a relic of her life as a ceramicist. That she saw the canvas as an object rather than just a surface – sides and stretcher bars were also painted – she ascribed to having been a sculptor. Her paintings were sculptures, as were her chairs. The blobs that seemed to fly up the gallery wall from the double canvas of Good Vibrations Diptych, Remembering David (2012) recalled “a time in the 60s, the hippy era, when people saw spots flying around due to certain substances that were also flying around,” Heilmann cryptically said.
That she had indulged in those substances herself was just one of her untidinesses. She had, she said, dried out in 1983, although titles of works such as Surfing on Acid (2005) suggested a lingering fascination with the beach and the counterculture it bred. Given all this, her attitude to Catholicism was perhaps even more surprising.
Brought up in a devoutly Catholic household – her brother trained as a priest – she had been sent to schools with names such as the St Rose academy and American Martyrs. The experience never left her. “I loved the whole Catholic culture as a kid, and that’s carried on into my life, the way I make things up now,” she told the documentary channel Art21 in 2009. Her 1983 painting Rosebud was a meditation on the martyrdom of St Sebastian. Another canvas was called Our Lady of the Flowers.
Heilmann spent her last years in Bridgehampton, Long Island. Her brother, John, predeceased her. She is survived by his three children.

Charity campaigner’s death from microlight crash injuries was accidental, coroner rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:49:04 UTC
01:49:04 KST

The death of a disability campaigner after a microlight crash while filming a TV programme for Apple was an accident, a coroner has concluded.
An inquest heard on Thursday that Claire Lomas, 44, died of severe traumatic injuries on 22 August 2024, five weeks after a light aircraft that she had been piloting while filming a promotional video for Apple’s Vision Pro headset “veered off the runway” and crashed into a rock in Amman, Jordan, on 15 July.
After she was paralysed from the waist down from a horse-riding accident in 2007, Lomas became a charity campaigner, raising more than £900,000 for the Nicholls Spinal Injury Foundation before her death and becoming the first person to finish a marathon with the aid of a “bionic” suit when she completed the London Marathon in 2012.
The inquest heard that the Royal Aero Sports Club of Jordan had concluded there was no violation of ground or air safety procedures, and that there was no evidence the 180-degree camera that was mounted to the aircraft had adversely affected the flight.
Concerns about Lomas’s confidence to fly the microlight were also explored during the hearing. Ben Ashman, a microlight designer whose company built an adapted version of the aircraft that allowed Lomas to fly without the use of her feet, said he believed Lomas may have been stressed before the flight because she posted on Facebook about putting her “brave pants” on, which he said was “unusual” for her.
Louise Pinder, the senior coroner for Rutland and North Leicestershire, recorded Lomas’s death as accidental, telling the hearing that she “was involved in the filming of an episode of Adventure which formed part of a series designed for a virtual reality headset”.
Pinder added: “During the final approach to the roadway, where she was to land, it became apparent to her and to those on the ground that the aircraft was not perfectly aligned.
“Claire made a split-second decision to abort the landing and go around but the aircraft touched down firmly, veered to the left, the left wheel leaving the road on to gravel causing her to further lose control. The aircraft collided with rocks approximately 10 metres from the metalled road surface, as a result of which she sustained multiple traumatic injuries.”
Pinder added: “I have heard no evidence establishing a causal link between any deficiencies in the risk assessment and Claire’s death. I am reassured, as I hope the family will be, that there have been thorough investigations as far as possible into the circumstances of Claire’s death and some lessons have been learnt.”
Pinder noted that Lomas’s family had raised concerns about the quality of care that she received while in hospital in Jordan, but said there was insufficient evidence to conclude whether there were any missed opportunities in her treatment.
In a statement, Katherine Allen, a lawyer speaking on behalf of the Lomas family, said the inquest’s conclusion marked “the end of a very difficult, emotional process” for them and that “the family continue to live with the devastating consequences of their loss”.
“Claire was deeply loved and her death has left a profound and enduring void in their lives,” Allen said. “They will never be the same again following what happened to her.”

Turkey says it will not fall into Israeli 'trap' in Syria, denies military presence in air base

"We are experienced enough not to fall into the trap of figures like (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu, who aim to undermine peace and stability in our region," said Burhanettin Duran, the Turkish presidency's director of communications.
After the site was struck, causing damage to its runways, reports said that a Turkish delegation had been at the site just hours earlier, but Turkey has denied a military visit to the location.
Israeli media said a Turkish military delegation had been at the site, and a Syrian monitor said the delegation was there as part of efforts to rehabilitate the base.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said Turkish forces had recently toured the base, warning that Israel would not tolerate a "threat" from a Turkish presence there.
"We will not tolerate a Turkish military entrenchment moving southward, because it threatens us," Netanyahu told an army radio podcast.
The premier's office also said on Tuesday evening that Israel had repeatedly warned Syria that deploying Turkish forces at an airbase near Aleppo would pose a threat to its national security, noting that Damascus had ignored the warnings.
The office stated that Israel and Syria had agreed to maintain the status quo on security matters, claiming that Damascus was on the verge of violating this understanding by allowing the Turkish military deployment.
But Turkish defence ministry spokesman Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk said the strikes were "unacceptable" and that Ankara would act "resolutely" to protect Syria's efforts to establish post-war stability.
"Israel's attack on the Abu al-Zuhur air base is aimed at harming Syria's stability, security, unity, integrity and infrastructure. Attacks violating Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity are unacceptable," he told journalists.
"In this context, our efforts and contributions to protect Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and help it establish a stable and secure environment, will continue resolutely."
Turkey’s presidency has also clarified that it is not considering retaliation.
Duran said that Netanyahu was "clinging to this irrational stance due to upcoming elections, internal political tensions, and fears. He views hostility toward Turkey as a political lifeline".
The development comes as Syria’s new transitional government has condemned the Israeli strikes, which marked the first time the location was targeted since the fall of the Assad regime.
The US has also rebuked the strikes, with US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack describing the attack as an "unnecessary escalation" that did not serve regional stability.
Barrack pointed to the approach taken by the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, saying Damascus "has not adopted a hostile posture nor maintained proxy forces, but has repeatedly demonstrated a preference for de-escalation with Israel".
He also emphasised Washington's efforts to reduce tensions between the two countries.
Barrack called on all sides to prioritise "reasoned dialogue" over further military incidents.
Since the fall of the Assad regime, Israel has stepped up its raids and incursions into Syria, while targeting much of the country's remaining military infrastructure.
Israeli attacks have struck Syrian air-defence systems, long- and medium-range missiles, weapons and missile depots, scientific research centres and other military facilities.
Israeli strikes have also hit several key Syrian airfields and military installations, including Hama airport, as well as Tiyas, Shayrat, Palmyra, Dumayr and Mezzeh airfields.

Lack of low-carbon power could deter investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
16:46:39 UTC
01:46:39 KST

Taiwan’s shortage of readily available low-carbon electricity could deter investment in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers despite the country’s technological strengths, a renewable energy executive said yesterday.
AI data centers require more than electricity: They need power that is available around the clock, scalable, affordable, low-carbon and deliverable within their development timelines, INA Energy Corp (寶晶能源) chairman Norman Tsai (蔡佳?) said at an energy transition forum in Taipei.
Large facilities can require between 50 megawatts and several hundred megawatts of power, with some reaching gigawatt scale, Tsai said.
Photo: CNA
The required power infrastructure must also be available quickly because data centers can be completed within 12 to 24 months, while new transmission lines or substations often take five to 10 years, he said.
“To achieve firm power, you need what I would call a combined approach,” Tsai said. “It involves not only power generation, but also the grid.”
“Taiwan is technologically strong, but it lacks sources of electricity, and that is why AI data centers are reluctant to establish operations here,” he said.
More specifically, Taiwan lacks green electricity, Tsai said, adding that identifying an adequate low-carbon power source would be the first challenge facing an AI date center operator seeking to establish a facility in the nation.
Citing the International Energy Agency, Tsai’s presentation said global data center electricity demand was projected to rise from 485 terawatt-hours (TWh) last year to 950TWh in 2030.
Corporate demand for green electricity is also spreading through the semiconductor supply chain because one company’s emissions from purchased energy, known as Scope 2 emissions, become part of its customers’ indirect Scope 3 emissions, Tsai said.
As a result, major Taiwanese semiconductor companies are helping their suppliers purchase or invest in green power, he added.
European Economic and Trade Office trade section head Christoph Saurenbach told the forum that Taiwan and the EU face similar difficulties reconciling decarbonization with industrial competitiveness.
Taiwan’s challenges are compounded by its geographic and geopolitical position and its heavy reliance on imported fossil fuels, he said.
The green transition is not only an economic and environmental necessity for Taiwan, but also “a strategic and political and security necessity,” Saurenbach said.
Rapidly expanding AI and semiconductor industries would make the transition more difficult and require greater investment and support from those sectors, he added.
European companies are major investors in Taiwan’s offshore wind sector, giving the EU and Taiwan a shared interest in the success of the nation’s renewable energy transition, Saurenbach said.
He also cited the Strait of Hormuz crisis as demonstrating the risks of long-term dependence on imported energy.
“Investment in renewables really is an obligation,” Saurenbach said. “There are absolutely no alternatives.”

Forcing drone procurement into the annual budget cycle could cripple Taiwan’s defense autonomy and deter the domestic drone industry from investing in crucial “non-red” supply chains, a national security official said yesterday, following a breakdown in negotiations over a special budget for uncrewed systems.
Earlier in the day, the Legislative Yuan’s Economics Committee failed to reconcile 14 versions of a special budget bill to fund the domestic development of surveillance and combat drones.
The opposition Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party disagreed with the Executive Yuan placing large uncrewed vehicle orders in a special budget and prioritizing military systems over those for civilian use.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
The national security official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that high-volume government orders, not empty platitudes, are needed for Taiwan to develop its drone-making industry.
Drone technology is rapidly advancing and a generation of uncrewed systems could become obsolete in a little more than a month, they said.
Maintaining the tempo of research and development to sustain battlefield relevance requires the industry to have confidence in government funding, which can only be provided through high-volume orders, rather than through annual budgets that fluctuate, the official said.
Under the circumstances, it comes as no surprise that big contracts and a focus on military applications have become the global paradigm for developing drone technology, they said.
Washington’s Replicator Initiative to obtain thousands of low-cost autonomous systems, which has counterparts in Japan, South Korea and the EU, exemplify that approach, the official said.
Orders for coastal surveillance drones, coastal attack drones and maritime loitering munitions are carefully designed to provide the military with mission-critical capabilities, they said.
Altering the number of systems in the orders or changing the delivery timetable would cause worrisome delays in the government’s force-building plans, they added.
The government designed the military contracts for drones to focus on stability and concentration of effort, which include acquiring weapon systems, maintenance and repair capabilities, as well as institutional knowledge, the official said.
The Cabinet’s plan to buy drones with a special budget is intended to establish the capability to mass-produce uncrewed systems without crowding out other essential government programs, they said.
High-volume manufacturing is a crucial aspect of drone warfare, given the scale needed in wartime, they said, adding that Taiwan especially needs self-sufficient drone-making capability to counter a potential naval blockade by China.
National security and economic interests are aligned on drones, instead of being in competition as the opposition party suggests, the official added.

Hyrox chases Olympic dream amid soaring popularity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
