Six UK pro-Palestine orgs demand end of arms trade to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:46:48 UTC
19:46:48 KST

Breadcrumb
On anniversary of 'symbolic' Palestine recognition, UK groups demand end to Israel arms trade
With the first anniversary of Britain's official recognition of the State of Palestine approaching, six British pro-Palestinian organisations have stepped up pressure on the government, calling for an end to the arms trade with Israel, the suspension of military and intelligence support, and comprehensive sanctions against it.
The demands come alongside calls for British action that goes beyond political recognition to practical measures.
In a comment to The New Arab on Wednesday, 19 August, Chris Nineham, vice-president of the Stop the War Coalition, said Britain's recognition of Palestine "was welcome, but, as we feared, it was symbolic", adding, "The people of Palestine need action, and we are calling on our government to end British support for Israel immediately.
"We are working to organise another mass demonstration on 10 October to pressure it to take action."
Nineham's comments come as the organisations prepare to organise a new national march in central London next October, in an attempt to pressure the British government to take tougher steps towards Israel.
In a joint statement on Wednesday, the organisations said that "Palestinians in the Gaza Strip continue to face killing, hunger and displacement, while British-funded humanitarian aid remains subject to Israeli restrictions".
They called on the British government to work to halt Israeli attacks and ensure aid reaches the Strip without restrictions.
The demand to lift restrictions on aid coincides with a position Britain announced at the UN Security Council on 11 August, when it called on the Israeli authorities to end what it described as "unacceptable restrictions" on aid and allow safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access to Gaza.
'Britain must act'
The statement is titled, "Three years of genocide... Britain must act".
The signatories said their next march will take place on Saturday, 10 October, at noon in central London, coinciding with three years since the ongoing genocide in Gaza.
The official website of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign confirms the date and location of the march.
The statement was signed by the Palestinian Forum in Britain, the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, the Stop the War Coalition, the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, Friends of Al-Aqsa, and the Muslim Association of Britain.
The United Kingdom officially recognised the State of Palestine on 21 September 2025.
At the time, the government said that the decision aimed to revive hope for peace and a two-state solution.
But the organisations that signed the statement believe the recognition was not followed by British action at the required level.
They say "real action" requires ending arms trade with Israel and suspending military and intelligence support that they consider to contribute to facilitating violations of international law.
They also called for British companies, banks, universities and charities to be prevented from supporting activities linked to the occupation or settlements, starting with a ban on trade connected to Israel's illegal occupation and extending to comprehensive sanctions against Israel.
Britain suspended 29 export licences to Israel in September 2024 after concluding that there was a clear risk that the equipment covered by them could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza.
The latest government data shows that six additional licences were subsequently suspended or amended as new information emerged.
The organisations expanded their demands to include the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, warning of continued settlement expansion, settler violence and restrictions on Al-Aqsa Mosque.
The British government, for its part, says Israeli settlements are illegal under international law.
It recently condemned the rise in settler violence and expressed concern about developments at the Noble Sanctuary in Jerusalem.
In June, London, in coordination with international partners, imposed sanctions on six entities and one individual, saying they were involved in financing, enabling or carrying out acts of settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Britain also strengthened its guidance for British companies and citizens in June, explicitly advising them against engaging in economic or financial activities in Israeli settlements, which it considers illegal, while reaffirming its continued support for trade with Israel within its pre-1967 borders.
In their statement, the organisations said Britain's commitment to international law "cannot be held hostage to the Israeli electoral timetable", arguing that the time had come to move from political recognition of the Palestinian state to practical measures.
The organisers are calling for widespread participation in the 10 October march, in an attempt to put pressure back on the streets of Britain.
They also want to place the issues of arms, sanctions, trade and military support at the forefront of the debate over what has actually changed in British policy since the recognition of Palestine.

In a comment to The New Arab on Wednesday, 19 August, Chris Nineham, vice-president of the Stop the War Coalition, said Britain's recognition of Palestine "was welcome, but, as we feared, it was symbolic", adding, "The people of Palestine need action, and we are calling on our government to end British support for Israel immediately.
"We are working to organise another mass demonstration on 10 October to pressure it to take action."
Nineham's comments come as the organisations prepare to organise a new national march in central London next October, in an attempt to pressure the British government to take tougher steps towards Israel.
In a joint statement on Wednesday, the organisations said that "Palestinians in the Gaza Strip continue to face killing, hunger and displacement, while British-funded humanitarian aid remains subject to Israeli restrictions".
They called on the British government to work to halt Israeli attacks and ensure aid reaches the Strip without restrictions.
The demand to lift restrictions on aid coincides with a position Britain announced at the UN Security Council on 11 August, when it called on the Israeli authorities to end what it described as "unacceptable restrictions" on aid and allow safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access to Gaza.
'Britain must act'
The statement is titled, "Three years of genocide... Britain must act".
The signatories said their next march will take place on Saturday, 10 October, at noon in central London, coinciding with three years since the ongoing genocide in Gaza.
The official website of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign confirms the date and location of the march.
The statement was signed by the Palestinian Forum in Britain, the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, the Stop the War Coalition, the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, Friends of Al-Aqsa, and the Muslim Association of Britain.
The United Kingdom officially recognised the State of Palestine on 21 September 2025.
At the time, the government said that the decision aimed to revive hope for peace and a two-state solution.
But the organisations that signed the statement believe the recognition was not followed by British action at the required level.
They say "real action" requires ending arms trade with Israel and suspending military and intelligence support that they consider to contribute to facilitating violations of international law.
They also called for British companies, banks, universities and charities to be prevented from supporting activities linked to the occupation or settlements, starting with a ban on trade connected to Israel's illegal occupation and extending to comprehensive sanctions against Israel.
Britain suspended 29 export licences to Israel in September 2024 after concluding that there was a clear risk that the equipment covered by them could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza.
The latest government data shows that six additional licences were subsequently suspended or amended as new information emerged.
The organisations expanded their demands to include the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, warning of continued settlement expansion, settler violence and restrictions on Al-Aqsa Mosque.
The British government, for its part, says Israeli settlements are illegal under international law.
It recently condemned the rise in settler violence and expressed concern about developments at the Noble Sanctuary in Jerusalem.
In June, London, in coordination with international partners, imposed sanctions on six entities and one individual, saying they were involved in financing, enabling or carrying out acts of settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Britain also strengthened its guidance for British companies and citizens in June, explicitly advising them against engaging in economic or financial activities in Israeli settlements, which it considers illegal, while reaffirming its continued support for trade with Israel within its pre-1967 borders.
In their statement, the organisations said Britain's commitment to international law "cannot be held hostage to the Israeli electoral timetable", arguing that the time had come to move from political recognition of the Palestinian state to practical measures.
The organisers are calling for widespread participation in the 10 October march, in an attempt to put pressure back on the streets of Britain.
They also want to place the issues of arms, sanctions, trade and military support at the forefront of the debate over what has actually changed in British policy since the recognition of Palestine.

25 turtle figurines dating back 16,500 years found in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:46:03 UTC
19:46:03 KST

Atahan Gezer and Muhsin Arslan
20 August 2026•Update: 20 August 2026
Archaeologists have discovered around 25 turtle figurines believed to be up to 16,500 years old at an excavation site in northwestern Türkiye.
The objects were uncovered at the Gedikkaya Hill and In Cave Archaeological Excavation Site in the Inhisar district of Bilecik province.
Excavations were conducted between May 18 and July 18 by a 14-member team led by Professor Deniz Sari of Bilecik Seyh Edebali University's Department of Archaeology, on behalf of the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
The figurines were made from limestone, with some covered in clay. The largest measures approximately 30 centimeters long and 20 centimeters wide.
Radiocarbon dating of the archaeological context placed the finds between 14,500 and 11,200 BC, during the Epipaleolithic period. Researchers believe the figurines were produced for ritual purposes and deliberately placed inside the cave.
 
'Important cult and ritual site'
Sari said archaeological material inside the cave was first identified during surface surveys in 2017.
Rescue excavations were subsequently conducted under the direction of the Bilecik Museum between 2019 and 2023, before the university began work at the site this year under a presidential decree.
"The artifacts show us that this was an important cult and ritual area," Sari said. "The turtle figurines we discovered this year have added a new dimension to the ritual context of the cave."
Most of the figurines were roughly shaped, which researchers believe supports the theory that they were produced specifically for rituals rather than as finely crafted decorative objects.
Sari compared their placement with practices associated with Hidirellez, a traditional spring festival during which people write down wishes before burying or leaving them at symbolic locations.
"There is a circular architectural arrangement here. Around it, we found turtle figurines made from limestone, many of them incomplete or quickly shaped, inserted upright into the soil," she said.
Researchers are also examining whether prehistoric communities may have believed that Gedikkaya Hill itself resembled a turtle, possibly contributing to the development of a form of mountain worship.
Sari cautioned that it might be too early to definitively describe the site as evidence of a mountain cult, but said many of the small figurines appeared to have been intentionally shaped in the form of Gedikkaya Hill.
She added that turtle symbolism was widespread in the Natufian culture of the Near East and in earlier Upper Paleolithic communities.
Turtles have represented longevity and endurance in many cultures, which could also explain their ritual significance at the site, she said.
The figurines have been transferred to the Bilecik Museum and Bilecik Seyh Edebali University for examination and restoration.

2026-08-20
10:43:50 UTC
19:43:50 KST

An overly fragmented single market cannot support Europe’s top priority of competing globally in the AI race, European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde warns.
Europe missed the first digital revolution and cannot afford to miss out again with AI, as it has the full potential to compete, Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank (ECB), said on Wednesday.
To win the AI race against giants such as the US and China, Lagarde told the International Business Council of the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Geneva, the EU needs to complete its single market and integrate capital markets that remain too fragmented.
"Europe largely missed out on the first digital revolution, as the commercial gains from the spread of information and communication technologies were captured disproportionately elsewhere. We cannot afford to repeat that experience with artificial intelligence (AI), the second digital revolution," she said in Geneva.
Lagarde's analysis largely echoes that of her predecessor, Mario Draghi, who in 2024 delivered a seminal report on relaunching the EU's economic competitiveness, which pointed to AI as the last chance for Europe to rejoin the international tech race.
Following Draghi's advice, the European Commission has put forward several initiatives to promote the uptake of AI in strategic sectors as well as the financing of massive data centres in an effort to develop new generations of the technology.
In her speech, Lagarde stressed that access to capital is limiting Europe's AI investments, notably because EU businesses get most of their funding through bank credit, while capital markets — the spaces where investors invest and firms raise capital — remain too limited at the national level.
Legal fragmentation creates practical barriers for firms in terms of costs, timings and their ability to operate across borders, she said. As a result, a company in Europe faces more hurdles to scale up than a US-based rival, and may end up turning to non-EU capital markets to solve the problem.
"Scale is particularly important as new technologies reshape the sources of productivity growth," Lagarde said.
The president added that Europe has the full potential to "make the most of new technologies", and that there are already "encouraging signs that European firms are investing in AI".
"The EU accounts for around 6% of the world's population but as many as 15% of its researchers. It also produces almost one-fifth of the world's most-cited scientific publications," the ECB president pointed out.
"Survey evidence suggests that firms in the euro area expect to allocate an average of around 9% of their total investment to AI this year," Lagarde said.
The challenge, she argued, is turning this knowledge into "commercial success" that spreads the technology across the economy. "Too often, the barriers that prevent firms from scaling also hold back that diffusion," she added.
The ECB president called for speeding up key reforms currently under negotiation in Brussels, namely the Savings and Investment Union (SIU) and single market integration reforms such as EU Inc.
The SIU is a package of legislation aimed at creating more integrated capital markets. Legislators hope to reach a deal by the end of the year, though significant divisions remain among EU member states, particularly over reform of the centralised supervision of capital markets.
EU Inc. is the Commission's proposal for an optional, EU-wide company structure designed to make it faster and cheaper for firms — especially startups — to incorporate and operate across borders and grow, sidestepping the current patchwork of 27 national systems. This file, too, falls under the single market integration umbrella and is expected to be approved by the end of the year.

Shanghai unveils measures to boost property sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
18:43:07 CST
19:43:07 KST

SHANGHAI, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Authorities in Shanghai rolled out a series of measures to further stimulate the property sector Thursday, including lowering the minimum down payment for second-home purchases in suburban areas.
The measures will take effect on Friday, according to a circular issued by six local government departments, including the Shanghai housing and urban-rural development commission.
For buyers purchasing a second home outside the city's outer ring road with a commercial mortgage, the minimum down payment is reduced from 20 percent to 15 percent.
The minimum down payment for second-home purchases within the outer ring road, or in the central city areas, remains at 25 percent. First-home buyers in Shanghai enjoy a minimum down payment of 15 percent when applying for commercial mortgages.
Homebuyers will also be allowed to withdraw their housing provident fund to purchase completed new commercial housing, expanding the policy beyond new homes sold on a pre-sale basis. The fund can also be used to pay home-purchase deed tax and buy parking spaces or garages, and storage rooms.
To support residents seeking to upgrade their homes through property replacement, Shanghai also rolled out a phased home-purchase subsidy program.
In the next seven months through March 31, 2027, buyers of new homes outside the outer ring road will be eligible for a subsidy equal to 1 percent of the mortgage amount, capped at 50,000 yuan (about 7,400 U.S. dollars), if they sell their existing home within one year before or after the online signing and filing of the purchase contract for the new home.
Buyers who sold homes located within the outer ring road will be eligible for an additional subsidy of 30,000 yuan.
The measures also call for greater government efforts to acquire more second-hand homes for use as government-subsidized rental housing.
At a meeting on economic work held by the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee at the end of last month, policymakers called for continued efforts to stabilize the property market.
In the four first-tier cities of Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen, new home prices fell 1.1 percent year on year last month, compared with a 1.3-percent drop in June, while the decline in second-hand home prices narrowed from 4.9 percent to 3.7 percent in July. ■

Estonia's population 13 percent smaller than it was when independence restored

Estonia's population 13 percent smaller than it was when independence restored
The population of Estonia has fallen by 13 percent compared with its figure in 1991, when independence was restored, Statistics Estonia reported.
Life expectancy, on the other hand, has risen by 10 years over that time, while wages have risen nearly 60-fold, the agency said.
Statistics Estonia has released figures on population, wages, employment sectors, births and marriages and more, to compare the situation today with that of the early 1990s.
The population of Estonia has fallen by 207,004 since 1991: Whereas Estonia's population stood at nearly 1.568 million in 1991, as of January 1 this year it was 1.361 million, Statistics Estonia noted.
Native Estonian speakers now make up 68.5 percent of the population compared with 61.6 percent on the eve of the restoration of independence.
Overall life expectancy in Estonia has risen from 69.6 to 79.8 years. The average age of first-time mothers, meanwhile, has risen from 22.6 in 1991 to 29.4 last year.
The birth rate has gone down too: in 1991, 19,413 children were born compared with 10,173 in 2025, a drop of over 50 percent.
The number of marriages has also declined at a similar rate. Last year, 5,998 marriages were registered, compared with 10,292 in 1991.
On the other hand, gross average wages have risen from just €35 in 1992, to €2,092 last year, a nearly 60-fold rise.
Another massive change compared with 35 years ago is the number of people employed in agriculture, including forestry and fishing. At the time, 152,000 people worked in these sectors, compared with 19,700 last year, or around 13 percent of the 1991 total.
The number of active companies of all sizes has risen from 24,000 in the mid-1990s to 160,000 in 2024.

Scientists say the human family tree may need a major rewrite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:42:59 UTC
19:42:59 KST

Scientists say the human family tree may need a major rewrite
- Date:
- August 20, 2026
- Source:
- Monash University
- Summary:
- The human family tree may be due for a major rewrite. Researchers argue that Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be folded into the genus Homo because new fossils have blurred many of the traits once used to separate them. The proposed shake-up could provide a simpler, more accurate picture of our surprisingly complicated evolutionary past.
- Share:
New research from Monash University suggests that recent discoveries about human evolution are challenging the traditional system scientists use to name and classify our ancestors.
The research, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, calls for a major reconsideration of human taxonomy. It proposes placing all human species and closely related fossil relatives from the past 4-5 million years within the genus Homo.
Human evolution is often depicted as a relatively simple sequence of distinct species, beginning with ape-like ancestors, continuing through Australopithecus and early members of Homo, and eventually leading to Homo Sapiens living today.
However, the fossil record reveals a much more complicated evolutionary history. As new fossils are discovered, many of the features once used to clearly separate humans from their close relatives have become increasingly difficult to define.
New Discoveries Blur Human Evolutionary Boundaries
Lead researcher Dr. Ian Towle, a Research Fellow at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute, said recent findings are making the existing classification system less useful and less accurate. That includes the way scientists categorize species within Homo as well as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, all of which lived during the past 5 million years.
"Recent fossil discoveries and advances in evolutionary and genetic analysis make this an ideal time to reconsider whether our traditional taxonomy still accurately reflects human evolution," Dr. Towle said.
"These groups do not necessarily represent distinct evolutionary branches, or 'clades', and differences in behavior and ecology once used to distinguish them have also become increasingly difficult to maintain.
"I propose expanding Homo to include these other groups to provide a more accurate and stable way to represent the complex evolutionary relationships revealed by the growing fossil record."
How Scientists Classify Evolutionary Relationships
Over the past 50 years, advances in the understanding of evolution have significantly changed the way scientists organize and classify life.
Modern taxonomy, the science of naming and classifying organisms, increasingly attempts to reflect actual evolutionary relationships by grouping species according to shared ancestry.
Human evolution, however, has been slower to adopt this approach.
In recent decades, scientists have increasingly sought to classify organisms according to genuine evolutionary groups, or clades, that contain a common ancestor and all of its descendants.
Traditionally, members of the Homo genus have been identified using traits such as large brains, advanced tool use, and certain anatomical and behavioral characteristics.
Those distinctions have become less clear. Scientists now know that some members of Homo had very small brains, while evidence suggests that Paranthropus and Australopithecus were also capable of complex behaviors.
A Proposal to Expand the Genus Homo
Dr. Towle argues that moving Australopithecus and Paranthropus species into Homo could create a more consistent picture of human evolutionary history. It could also reduce the need to repeatedly redefine groups as new fossils are uncovered and scientists gain a better understanding of our ancestors.
"The more we learn about our ancestors and close fossil relatives, the more we realize how complex and non-linear our family tree is," Dr. Towle said.
"Expanding the Homo genus to also include species of Australopithecus and Paranthropus will allow us to account for differences without regularly reclassifying particular groups."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Monash University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Ian Towle. Clades, Grades, and the Genus Problem: A Case for Revising Hominin Taxonomy. American Journal of Biological Anthropology, 2026; 190 (4) DOI: 10.1002/ajpa.70344

China adds Kyrgyzstan, Vietnam to 240-hour visa-free transit program
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
18:42:27 CST
19:42:27 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- China has added Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam to its 240-hour visa-free transit program, bringing the total number of countries eligible for this policy to 57, immigration authorities announced on Thursday.
Effective from Aug. 20, citizens of Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam holding ordinary passports and interline passenger tickets with confirmed dates and itineraries bound for a third country or region may enter China through any of the 65 ports across the country and stay up to 240 hours, or 10 days, without a visa, according to the National Immigration Administration (NIA).
Citizens of these two countries holding ordinary passports will also be eligible for the 30-day visa-free entry policy for Hainan Province in south China starting the same day, allowing them to enter the province through Hainan's open ports and stay visa-free for up to 30 days. With these additions, the number of countries covered by this Hainan visa-free policy has increased to 61.
During the visa-free period, travelers are permitted to engage in tourism, business, exchange visits and family visits. However, the two policies do not cover employment, study or journalistic activities, which still require appropriate visas, the NIA said.
These measures are part of China's broader efforts to boost international travel and exchanges following the COVID-19 pandemic.
In December 2024, authorities extended the visa-free transit window from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours. The country has also expanded its unilateral visa-free access program, allowing travelers from 50 countries to stay for up to 30 days.
These sweeping policy changes have facilitated increased travel to China, fueling a surge in online content and interest in "China Travel," particularly on platforms like YouTube.
China's border authorities handled a record 369 million inbound and outbound crossings in the first half of 2026, up 10.8 percent year-on-year, according to the National Immigration Administration.
Foreign arrivals in China rose, with visa-free entries surging 30.6 percent year on year to exceed 17.8 million during the same period, accounting for more than three-quarters of all foreign arrivals. ■

China Focus: Chinese-led team develops energy-efficient vision chip
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
18:42:20 CST
19:42:20 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese-led research team has developed a new type of vision chip that directly converts light into tokens, bypassing the multiple processing steps that typically consume power and slow down performance.
The study, jointly conducted by Nanjing University and the National University of Singapore, was published Wednesday in the journal Nature Sensors.
Unlike conventional sensors, which capture light and then digitize, buffer, and transfer data before token generation, the new device performs the conversion in the physical domain.
It features an array of specialized pixels, each capable of simultaneously sensing light, storing data locally, and performing computations. The chip's peripheral circuits can selectively activate pixel regions to divide an image into blocks.
For each selected block, a specific voltage sequence is applied, enabling the stored optical information to carry out mathematical operations directly in the analog domain, with the output current serving as the token.
"The chip physically eliminates data movement, which is the main source of energy waste," said Liang Shijun, a professor at Nanjing University. "Light comes in, tokens come out."
This approach, described as "physical tokenization," turns the chip from a passive image recorder into an active visual-semantic generator, Liang said.
In tests, a system using the chip achieved 87.3 percent accuracy in image recognition, close to conventional software baselines, while improving energy efficiency by more than 10 times during the tokenization stage, he said.
"This design overturns the traditional 'sense-buffer-compute' sequence and opens a new path to break the power and computing bottlenecks of edge AI in the post-Moore era," said Miao Feng, a professor at Nanjing University.
He added that the technology could provide a highly efficient, near-zero-latency vision foundation for embodied intelligence, drones and smart security, accelerating the large-scale deployment of physical AI. ■

The attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region lasted for almost nine hours, according to Ukrainian authorities.
At least 13 people were killed in Kyiv and another person died in the Kyiv region. More than 40 people were injured and are receiving medical assistance.
A school, a children’s hospital, and residential buildings were among the facilities severely damaged in Kyiv. Russia also attacked the Chernihiv and Odesa regions.
As of Thursday, Aug. 20, 462 State Emergency Service (DSNS) rescuers and 116 pieces of specialized equipment were working to clear the aftermath of the attack.
Sybiha said the barrage demonstrated the urgent need for stronger air defenses.
“Each Russian ballistic missile is an act of barbarism. And each interceptor delivered to Ukraine is an act of humanity and saved human lives,” he said.
The foreign minister called on Ukraine’s international partners to take three immediate steps: provide additional air-defense systems and interceptors, increase sanctions pressure to hinder Russia’s ability to produce weapons, and cooperate with Ukraine on developing anti-ballistic capabilities.

“We know partners who can deliver these interceptors, and we urge them once again to act without delay,” Sybiha said. “Every delay is measured in human lives.”
He also called on Ukrainians living abroad and Ukrainian organizations around the world to lobby governments in key capitals for additional support.
Russia publishes missile launch footage
Russia’s defense ministry published a photograph showing missile launches from Russian warships in the open sea.
The ministry accompanied the image with the caption: “Let’s fire a salvo.” It later added: “We give convincing arguments.”
The ministry also confirmed that its forces had used high-precision weapons launched from land, air and sea, as well as long-range attack drones.
The agency claimed to have struck military targets in Kyiv and the surrounding region but did not mention the civilian casualties reported by Ukrainian authorities.
Strikes hit warehouses and Red Cross facilities
In the Boryspil district of the Kyiv Oblast, Russian forces struck food warehouses and facilities belonging to the Red Cross during the overnight attack, according to Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
Fires were still burning at the sites, he said.
The scale of the attack also affected foreign officials visiting the Ukrainian capital.
Lithuanian Energy Minister Lukas Savickas and his delegation, who arrived in Kyiv on Wednesday, spent the night in a shelter as the Russian attack continued.
“We had to go through what a significant part of the people in Ukraine go through very often,” Savickas told Lithuanian outlet LRT. He said the delegation remained in a shelter as the air-raid alert continued throughout the night.
Russian strike leaves 13,000 without power in southern Odesa region
In addition, Russian forces launched another massive overnight attack on the southern Odesa region, damaging civilian infrastructure, according to Oleh Kiper, head of the Odesa Regional Military Administration (OVA).
The attack targeted civilian infrastructure in the southern part of the region, causing power outages in several settlements. As of the morning, 13,000 subscribers were without electricity, while power workers were working to restore supplies.
At another location, two food-truck trailers caught fire as a result of the attack. The fires have since been completely extinguished.
There were no reported injuries. Emergency and recovery crews are continuing to deal with the consequences of the strike.

Ben Gurion Airport to close: Chaos following shutdown of check-ins amid labor dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:37:28 UTC
19:37:28 KST

The Israel Airports Authority said that “following instructions from the workers’ committee” to disrupt operations at Ben Gurion Airport, air traffic would be reduced beginning at 2 p.m. Thursday until landings were halted entirely, while departures continued gradually according to an updated flight schedule. The authority later said operations would gradually resume from 3 p.m., in accordance with a revised flight schedule.
“Passengers are asked to remain in contact with their airlines and stay updated on their flight times and any possible schedule changes,” the authority said.
According to the Airports Authority, the workers’ committee was responsible for locking the entrances to the airport parking lots, leaving hundreds of vehicles stuck in traffic or parked in makeshift spaces along the sides of roads.
Passengers at Ben Gurion Airport whose flights were canceled described heavy crowding, compounded by the hot weather.
“We regret the conduct of the workers’ committee and apologize to passengers,” the authority said earlier.
According to the Israel Airports Authority, after airport employees halted operations, officials decided to stop check-in services and later to suspend airport activity altogether.
The suspension of check-in services caused chaos and heavy congestion at the airport on one of the busiest travel days of the year, with nearly 100,000 passengers and 600 flights. Pilots and airlines were issued a NOTAM stating that the airport would close to landings at 2 p.m. and departures would continue, but at a reduced pace.
“We are investigating the incident. We are at the peak of the travel season, alongside the presence of American refueling aircraft. If the investigation shows that this was indeed a work-to-rule action, we will act very harshly against those responsible. Heads will roll,” senior Transportation Ministry officials said.
The Histadrut labor federation, however, said no instruction to strike had been issued.
“The Histadrut’s Transportation Workers Union wishes to clarify that no directive was issued to stop work. The attempt to portray the chaos at Ben Gurion Airport as the result of a ‘surprise strike’ is untrue and diverts attention from the real failure: a severe and ongoing manpower shortage and inadequate preparation for the summer travel rush.”
"For many months, the Transportation Workers Union warned the Israel Airports Authority management and the transportation minister that the existing staffing system could not cope with the expected passenger volumes. The congestion at Ben Gurion Airport did not come as a surprise. The writing was on the wall, the warnings went unanswered — and now the public is paying the price.
“Ben Gurion Airport employees are going above and beyond to keep the system functioning, but the national airport cannot be run on the endless burnout of its workers. Employees cannot work hundreds of hours a month to make up for staffing shortages and inadequate preparation by the state.”
Workers’ committee chairman: ‘I warned there was a manpower shortage’
Pinchas Idan, chairman of the Israel Airports Authority workers’ committee, said: “They can’t just say ‘strike’ and make up stories because everyone wants to cover themselves. In June I sent a letter saying there was a manpower shortage, and then they said, ‘There’s no shortage, it’s the Americans, it’s Greece’ — fairy tales. A baggage handler cannot work 13 hours a day in this heat. What do you want? For people to collapse?”
He added: “Everyone says there’s no manpower shortage. Come, I’ll give you a tour and you tell me whether it’s normal for a baggage handler to start at 3 a.m. and finish at 3 p.m. We did not stop working. The morning shift started at 3 a.m. and finished at noon. At 1 p.m., the afternoon shift went back to work as usual. All the baggage handlers are working. They finished nine hours and went home. They deserve to.”
Idan also addressed a statement by Transportation Minister Miri Regev, who is currently in Morocco and said she had instructed Airports Authority management to petition the labor court against the workers’ committee “in order to force them to stop the thuggish and illegal strike.”
Idan responded: “I asked to go to the labor court. I asked for a judge to decide whether a baggage handler in this heat should have to work from 3 a.m.
“The CEO was abroad and asked me to wait until he returned, so I waited. The minister asked because she has elections, and I understood, but enough,” Idan said. “I spoke with her today. I don’t answer to anyone. They will not kill the workers, they will not abuse them. This is backbreaking labor in this heat. They have no shame.”
Airports Authority: ‘We are recruiting; halting operations is extreme’
The Israel Airports Authority said in response: “We regret that the workers’ committee chairman is choosing to divert the discussion from the main issue. In recent months, the Airports Authority has been working intensively to recruit new employees across all units, and as part of this effort dozens of additional workers have already been hired, with recruitment continuing even now.
“Shutting down Ben Gurion Airport at the height of the summer season is an extreme, difficult and unnecessary step that first and foremost harms the public,” the authority said. “Thousands of passengers, including children and families who planned their summer vacations for months, could find themselves today unable to travel abroad or return to Israel. Disputes between management and workers should be resolved responsibly and through dialogue, not at the expense of passengers.”
The shutdown also overwhelmed airline and travel agency service centers with calls from passengers. Some were stranded abroad and seeking information about return flights, while others were stuck in Israel unable to complete check-in.
“In the past half hour, I’ve been overwhelmed with calls from clients stranded at various airports who have no idea what is happening with their flights home or how many hours they may be delayed because of the chaos at Ben Gurion Airport,” veteran travel agent Yaki Lavi said.
Unusual congestion at Ben Gurion Airport this week
The Israeli aviation sector is already dealing with a series of disruptions, including long delays and unusually heavy congestion at Ben Gurion Airport. Recent problems have been attributed in part to refueling disruptions at the airport, air traffic congestion over Greece and staffing shortages.
Transport Minister Miri Regev is currently in Marrakesh for the renewal of Arkia’s route to Morocco.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Regev visited Ben Gurion Airport only a day earlier, where they were briefed on its operational activity during the summer season. At the time, operations appeared to be functioning normally. The situation on Thursday looked very different.
Staff shortages?
Current and former Ben Gurion Airport employees have argued that many of the recent delays stem from inadequate preparation for the summer season and a shortage of workers. They say the Airports Authority’s employment model leads to high staff turnover and means too few workers are sometimes recruited in time for peak travel periods.
“That’s how it always is,” one employee said. “There’s a huge amount of work and not enough staff. Every winter, veteran employees who are getting close to permanent status are let go, and then by summer there aren’t enough workers.”

NABU, SAP release Operation Themis video on illegal asset takeover by top OP officials, MPs
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:37:19 EEST
19:37:19 KST

(updated version)
Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) have released a new video exposing a corrupt organization led by a sitting and a former lawmaker along with senior officials from the Presidential Office: the "Themis" operation targets the illegal seizure of real estate and company assets through document forgery.
"As part of a special operation to dismantle high-level corruption, NABU and SAPO exposed a criminal organization led by a sitting and a former member of Ukraine’s parliament, which included senior officials of the Presidential Office and other individuals," the video, released on the anti-corruption agencies’ Telegram channels on Thursday, said.
According to the video released by NABU and SAPO, the criminal organization’s main goal was to seize valuable real estate and other company assets by illegally establishing control over business entities owned by other individuals.
According to the anti-corruption agencies, the suspects carried out raider takeovers of companies by forging ownership documents and court rulings.
The video states that the value of company assets illegally seized by the organization’s members in the fall of 2025 exceeded UAH 248 million.
"In May 2026, they attempted to seize properties in Kyiv worth more than UAH 207 million," the anti-corruption agencies said.
To carry out the scheme, the video says, the suspects recruited hackers who, posing as state registrars, accessed the register of legal entities and entered forged documents containing false information about the transfer of ownership from the legitimate owners to front men, who were in fact bodyguards of one of the scheme’s co-organizers.
"Aware that the owners of the seized companies might turn to law enforcement to reverse these illegal actions, the scheme’s organizers arranged for a criminal case to be opened based on a complaint from people under their control, and for the corporate rights of the seized companies to be placed under arrest in order to… make it impossible to carry out any registration actions," the anti-corruption agencies’ video says.
To retain control over the seized companies, NABU and SAPO say, the scheme’s participants "exerted influence on senior officials of the Justice Ministry."
According to the anti-corruption agencies, the aim of seizing one of the companies was to gain control over valuable real estate in downtown Kyiv by initiating bankruptcy proceedings in a commercial court with the help of controlled individuals.
In another case, fictitious debt was created for a company, making it possible to initiate bankruptcy proceedings.
Another episode involves the seizure of real estate in downtown Kyiv through the forgery of a court ruling, which was entered into the property register with the help of hackers.
"Justice Ministry officials, aware of the consequences of carrying out the illegal instructions of the deputy head of the Presidential Office, refused to take part in the crime," the video says. As a result, NABU and SAPO say, the intent was not carried through.
"The investigation established that the criminal organization’s activities were financed by a co-organizer and sitting member of Ukraine’s parliament, in an amount of at least $514,000. Scheme participants used these funds to pay hackers and to fund court proceedings as illegal benefits to law enforcement and judicial bodies," the anti-corruption agencies said.
The video released by NABU and SAPO contains fragments of audio recordings of the suspects’ conversations. One of the voices on these recordings resembles that of Iryna Mudra, who has since been dismissed as deputy head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office. In one fragment, that voice says, raising its tone, in Russian: "I’ve basically talked myself into a criminal charge, you understand?"
In the recorded conversations, the suspects complain about being unable to obtain information from NABU and SAPO and discuss how the anti-corruption system could be controlled.
"Corruption needs to be systematized and controlled… it shouldn’t be fought, it should be controlled," a voice resembling Mudra’s says in Russian.
The NABU and SAPO video notes that on Aug. 19, 2026, NABU detectives and SAPO prosecutors notified members of the criminal organization of suspicion under Articles 191, 206-2, 358 and 361 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code.

Anti-War NGO Reports Rise in Forced Enlistments Across Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:37:09 UTC
19:37:09 KST

Idite Lesom (“Get Lost”), a group that helps Russian men avoid military service, has reported receiving a growing number of complaints from individuals who were forcibly detained and coerced into signing contracts with Russia’s Defense Ministry.
Between Aug. 10 and 18, Idite Lesom recorded 14 separate cases from regions across Russia, including Krasnodar, Omsk, Arkhangelsk and the Jewish autonomous district, as well as the republics of Udmurtia and Buryatia.
According to the organization, police are detaining men on the street, at public venues and workplaces. Reported incidents include an individual detained after a high school class reunion, another stopped after leaving a supermarket and others picked up under the guise of routine identity or drug checks.
In multiple cases, men were heavily intoxicated when detained or were targeted specifically for public drinking before being pressured to enlist in the military.
Idite Lesom spokesperson Ivan Chuviliaev said the uptick was “significant” and part of a broader trend that began in July.
“The reason for it is likely another period of turbulence and uncertainty — hence the panic,” Chuviliaev told The Moscow Times, pointing to growing rumors of an upcoming wave of mobilization.
The Kremlin has denied any plans for a new draft campaign. President Vladimir Putin last called up 300,000 reservists in September 2022, Russia’s first mobilization since World War II, triggering rare public protests and prompting tens of thousands of Russians to flee the country.
Since then, Moscow has relied on generous signing bonuses and salaries to recruit contract soldiers rather than announcing another nationwide draft.
The renewed speculation over another wave of mobilization comes as Russia’s offensive has slowed to one of its lowest rates of advance and the country faces growing challenges in replenishing its forces.

How DW fact-checks fake news
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:37:00 UTC
19:37:00 KST

How DW fact-checks fake news
August 20, 2026
Not sure who to trust or where to find reliable, fact-based information?
False and misleading claims can spread around the world in a matter of minutes, making it increasingly difficult to separate fact from fiction.
At a time when false claims can spread faster than facts, independent verification is essential.
That's where DW Fact check comes in. Allow us to introduce ourselves and explain more about our work.
What topics we choose
DW fact-checkers investigate a wide range of claims and stories.
This can include statements made by politicians, government officials and political parties, as well as claims involving celebrities, athletes, business leaders and non-profit organizations.
We verify the authenticity of images, videos or audios that go viral on major social media platforms.
Increasingly, we also investigate whether widely shared content is authentic or has been generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence.
To decide which topics to fact-check, we assess claims based on four criteria:
- Virality: How quickly is a narrative spreading?
- Reach: Is the narrative being shared across multiple platforms and/or in multiple languages?
- Relevance: Why does the topic matter to our target audience? How important is it to the public debate?
- Impact: What consequences could the spread of the narrative have?
How we verify information
At DW Fact check, we investigate the origin of a claim, when and where it emerged, whether it has been manipulated, and who is behind it.
Whenever possible, we trace claims back to their original source and examine the evidence supporting them. We then compare the claim with reliable data, documents and expert assessments to determine its accuracy.
To fact-check information, we use a range of open-source intelligence (OSINT) tools and verification techniques.
DW has created a dedicated website where you can learn more about the verification workflows and tools we regularly use. There, you can explore methods for verifying images, videos, audio recordings, sources and text-based claims.
Transparency is an essential part of our work. Every fact check includes hyperlinks to the sources used in our reporting whenever possible, allowing readers to review the same evidence our journalists relied on.
Like all DW journalism, our fact checks are based on information that has been verified through reliable and independent sources.
Whenever possible, we follow the two-source principle and seek confirmation from more than one source.
While sourcing information from interview partners, we always select reliable and unbiased people. All interviews are recorded, with the consent of the interview partner, and archived.
We mention all sources by name and occupation and, where possible, link to their contact information so there is no lack of transparency.
Anonymity is only granted to sources in rare cases when their security is at stake or the topic is sensitive. In these cases, we are transparent about the reasons for granting anonymity.
How we rate claims
DW uses a collaborative process to evaluate claims and determine verdicts.
Before publication, the lead reporter recommends a verdict to two editors.
The rating system has eight categories:
- True: The statement is accurate.
- False: The statement is not accurate.
- Misleading: The statement is partially correct, but the information is portrayed in a way that creates a wrong impression.
- Unproven: The statement cannot be proven true or false.
- Fake: The image, video or audio is manipulated.
- Real: The image, video or audio is authentic.
- AI- generated: The image, video or audio was created using artificial intelligence.
- AI- manipulated: The image, video or audio was altered using artificial intelligence.
How we use artificial intelligence
DW has clear editorial guidelines when it comes to the use of artificial intelligence in journalism.
AI can help us improve workflows, accessibility, translation, data and content analysis and format adaptation. However, humans remain responsible for every journalistic decision and every item we publish.
You can read DW’s ten AI editorial guidelines here.
At DW Fact check we clearly label any content that we verify as having been generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence. We also explicitly disclose when we have used AI tools to help us verify content.
As part of our verification workflow we may use AI detectors to help assess whether content has been created or manipulated with AI. But because these detectors often produce inaccurate results, we use them with great caution. We use multiple tools to reduce the risk of error.
AI detectors do not determine our conclusions on their own. Any findings are reviewed and verified by our journalists using additional evidence.
How we correct mistakes
We do not manipulate images or videos we broadcast. When we correct or revise a text, or blur or zoom in on a video, we indicate which changes have been made and why.
We are committed to providing accurate and high-quality content free of errors.
However, despite numerous quality control measures, mistakes can happen.
At DW, it is important that we address these errors as soon as we become aware of them, and do so transparently. This means that when we publish an item that needs to be revised, we need to clearly indicate any changes that have been made.
This also applies to mistakes involving numbers, dates, names, locations, quotes and photos. These are corrected as soon as they have been verified, and the item is republished for online and social media.
A note added to the bottom of the article (or in a social media thread) informs the user of the revision and reason.
You can read DW's full guidelines on dealing with errors here.
How we work with other fact-checking organizations
The International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN) is an association of fact-checkers worldwide, with more than one hundred organizations as members.
DW Fact check has been a member since March 2024. Membership must be confirmed annually with an application process.
To be accepted into the network, members must prove that they guarantee a high level of credibility based on 31 criteria.

The 3 Best USB Phone Chargers (2026): Anker, DeWalt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:33:00 UTC
19:33:00 KST

A car charger is not a complicated device. The best USB car charger is the one that charges your phone quickly, does not overheat, allows multiple devices to charge, and remains compatible with whichever USB cable you (or your passengers) happen to have available. It is usually also a trusted brand, with certification to international standards—not a janky gas station charger that'll blow a fuse with an internal short or offer insufficient protection against dust and debris.
I put car chargers to the test with ammeters and phone apps, and on multi-hour road trips, to make sure each one lived up to its promises. The best car charger I've found is the three-port Anker 167.5W Nano ($38), which combines 100-watt fast-charging capability for auxiliary devices, plus dual-port USB-Cs, USB-A capability, and safety features that include overheat protection.
If you shun dangling cords, I offer the Anker 75W Fast Charger ($30) with slightly lower top amperage but a retractable cable. And for families whose kids can't live without constant tablets in the back seat, there's the DeWalt 72W Front and Back Seat Charger ($45).
For other power needs, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Portable Jump Starters, Best Power Banks, Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations.
The Best USB Car Charger
This three-port charger from Anker offers pretty much everything I want from a USB car charger while remaining hearteningly compact and affordable. The 100W fast-charging USB-C port kicks out nearly 7 amps at top speeds, enough juice to charge my Macbook Air to 50 percent in about 25 minutes, before fast-charging slows down, and does the same for my iPhone. But especially, Anker's PowerIQ technology smartly assesses the differing voltage needs of various phones to avoid over- or under-voltage. I've never actually seen this Anker on sale on Amazon above $40.
It also doesn't hurt that Anker makes some of WIRED's most trusted portable power technology—tech whose reliability we've verified over years of real-world testing. You don't overwhelmingly want a janky cheap charger that blows a fuse. Good insulation and a tiny built-in fan effectively lower overheating versus other fast-chargers, though you'll still notice some heat when charging at 100 watts or above. USB-A capability is welcome for versatility, though my testing showed somewhat lower power than advertised on that port.
Either way, I was able to charge both my top-pick portable jump starter, the 4000A Wolfbox ($120), in a little over an hour while also keeping my phone topped off on a road trip—which is pretty much as high-demand as I get while also blasting AC and the radio, and this caused no problems with the 15-amp circuit on my older car. But note that while most modern cars run on 20-amp fuses, the max capacity for this charger when drawing from all three ports does run pretty close to the max load for an older-model car charger. The charger is able to draw quite close to the maximum amperage on a 15-amp fuse.
A similar budget pick: The lower overheating on my top-pick Anker bodes well for longevity, which means it might still be a cheaper option in the long haul. But note that a similar three-port fast-charger from Chinese brand Ugreen ($21) performed comparably on charging speeds. But it also got significantly hotter within 10 minutes of fast-charging.
Best USB Car Charger With Retractable Cord
A retractable charging cable has the distinct merit of keeping your car tidy, without dangling charging cords to get tangled between your foot and the gas pedal. It also obviates the need to remember a cable at all. This Anker model offers a 2-foot cable that retracts quite easily back into its base after a quick tug on the cable, neat as you'd like. The cable's 45W fast-charging capability will max out the charging capability of most iPhones.
Anker is a brand I trust for charging technology. But it's worth noting that retractable cables introduce a couple failure points that could lower longevity. The cable can't be swapped out if it gets worn, and the retraction mechanism itself could wear out. Tidiness has a price, it seems. This said, the charger is not overly expensive, usually retailing closer to $20.
Best Front and Back Seat Car Charger
The modern car family involves a nest of devices—parents in the front seat charging phones, children in the back with tablets, somehow watching the same thing over and over. And nothing ends the peace of a road trip quite like a tablet running out of juice halfway through an episode of Bluey.
This DeWalt is a good solution, offering decent (but not great) 30-watt charging on the USB-C port for front-seat parents, and a couple of auxiliary USB-A ports to keep maintenance charge on backseat devices. DeWalt is a power tool brand, of course, and so these ports were likely designed for a tool or two resting in the back seat. But kids have tools, too, and this'll serve their needs.
It's perhaps frustrating that the back seat chargers are USB-A. But I haven't found a good USB charger with a back-seat USB-C charging setup, assuming your car doesn't have a back seat charger of its own. And so while this DeWalt is a compromise, it's the best compromise I've found so far.
Frequently Asked Questions
How I Selected and Tested USB Car Chargers
For this round of car-charger testing, I looked first for known quantities and trusted charging technology brands like Anker, Belkin, and Ugreen. I also ordered and tested devices that other credible sources had ranked as their favorite USB chargers, making sure that each charger is broadly available and easy to find. Needless to say, I only assessed and recommend UL-certified chargers, and avoided dodgy-looking brands: Short circuits in cars aren't fun, for me or for you.
I then set about testing the claims for each car charger, using ammeters for each port on each charger, testing with an ammeter while pulling max loads. I additionally used the Ampere phone app to test the peak draw for a Motorola Razr and an iPhone 13, and also tested to see whether the charger heated up while pulling max draw—both using the phone app and an infrared thermometer.
I tested with each charger's included cord, where relevant, but also with a fast-charging cable on USB-C devices that advertise this capability. For my top contenders among 100-watt fast chargers, I also tested to see how long it took to charge a Macbook Air M4 and my top-pick jump starter, the 4000A Wolfbox.
As with every device tested by the WIRED Reviews team, I subjected my top-pick chargers to real-world road tests. I went on multi-hour road trips with devices plugged in. I charged portable jump starters or laptops while also charging phones. I tested durability in real-world conditions that may also involve grubby fingers. I assessed each device not just for brute speed, but for versatility in different use cases. For now, I favor chargers that offer both USB-C and USB-A capability, so as not to leave any devices out in the cold.
I also checked up on customer reviews for each of these chargers. If I saw any customer complaints, I tried my darndest to replicate them. I jammed chargers in and out of the ports, and wobbled the chargers around in their sockets. I acted the way people act when they're fumbling for a device charger they're not looking at while driving.
Are Cheap USB Chargers Unsafe?
I've put a bit of emphasis on trusted brands while testing USB chargers, and this isn't by accident. The world is full of dodgy gas station or Amazon chargers, and bad cables, with insufficient electrical insulation and inconsistent current delivery.
Bad USB-C cables and electrical insulation are known fire hazards in the worst cases, but inconsistent voltage is also just bad for your phone or laptop battery over time. Poorly made chargers, connectors, and cables can have higher resistance (leading to overheating), bad or inconsistent connections, and poor protections against shorts and surges. All of these things are bad. At worst, they can fry your device or lower your battery longevity.
As a rule of thumb, look for language that a product is “UL-Listed” or "UL-Certified" not merely "UL-Classified" or “Recognized.” The latter two mean that a product has been tested only against specific hazards or under specific conditions. Listed and Certified products have fully passed all tests within a given standard. WIRED will only recommend chargers that are UL-listed or -certified.
Other USB Chargers I Recommend
Scosche PowerVolt 60W Dual-Port Charger for $20: This dual-port USB-C charger from California car brand Scosche is the simplest thing imaginable. Two USB-C ports, each separately rated at 30 watts. Each charges quickly and is reliable. Though this Scosche doesn't offer a fast-charging option for laptops, it's perfectly optimized for a pair of phones—and admirably low-cost. If you're mostly just going to charge a phone, this is a tight runner-up to my top-pick Anker—especially if you're pretty sure you'll never need a USB-A charger in your car.
Anker 40W Two-Port Charger for $20: Like the Scosche, this Anker is a purpose-driven phone charger with two USB-C ports. It's a little lower-powered than the Scosche, with a little less juice than the newest generation of phones can support. But the price is right if you're willing to accept lower charging speeds.
Belkin BoostCharge 42W Dual-Port Charger for $24: This compact, well-insulated dual-port charger from California tech accessory brand Belkin is great as a budget option, with decently fast USB-C and USB-A charging. Just note that the tiny device might be a bit shallow for some deeper car chargers, and that when plugged in, the charger has a nonnegotiable and oddly bright LED light that stays on even when no device is charging. This won't bother you unless it bothers you.
Nekteck 45W Two-Port Car Charger for $32: This basic, bare-bones Neckteck charger is a decent compromise for those who need fast charging on a QC 3.0-compatible USB-A device. While a 45-watt max speed for USB-C charging isn't fast by modern standards, it's still faster than most phones. And the QC 3.0 USB-A charger is significantly faster than most USB-A chargers, for those with older devices.
Lisen 90W Charger With Cord for $20: This charger from Chinese car-tech company Lisen performed reasonably well in testing, though true fast-charging isn't available and the listed charge speeds are a little confusing and don't add up. The coiled cord is not able to be retracted or removed, making this charger a bit ungainly for daily use, but the option on a 60- or 90-inch cord does make this Lisen the rare device suitable for charging a USB-C phone or tablet in the back seat. This said, I tested a shorter cable, and longer USB-C cables are notoriously finicky for high amperage.
Also Tested
The six-port Ai Aikenuo back seat charging kit is useful for keeping a large number of devices charged up for work use or larger families, but it disappeared from Amazon right before this guide's publication. I'll monitor to see if this is a momentary glitch or whether it's been discontinued.

A MAGA County’s Top Election Official Wants to Hire Election Denial Superstar Tina Peters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Last week, Clint Curtis, the top election official in Shasta County, California, publicly accused members of his own staff of bypassing security, which he later claimed was an attempt “to sabotage a federal election.”
Days later, Curtis announced plans to hire a new deputy: Tina Peters, the election denial superstar who was convicted of seven counts related to election interference in 2024 and sentenced to nine years in prison.
Peters, the former clerk of Mesa County, Colorado, has yet to publicly comment on the offer, but her lawyer Peter Ticktin tells WIRED she “is giving consideration to helping in the efforts in Shasta County, as there most definitely has been monkey business in the way the election was handled.”
Peters was convicted after she allowed Conan Hayes, a former pro surfer who later worked for pillow salesman turned election denier Mike Lindell, unauthorized access to election equipment in Mesa County as part of a scheme to prove that the 2020 presidential election had been stolen from Donald Trump. (Hayes was never charged for his role in the scheme). Colorado governor Jared Polis commuted Peters’ sentence in May after months of pressure from President Trump, who purported to have issued his own pardon even though Peters was convicted on state charges. Recently released court papers show how Trump and his advisers coordinated with federal agencies to cut federal funding and grants to Colorado as part of a pressure campaign to free Peters.
Curtis told The Guardian that Peters would not have access to the county’s voting system but refused to specify what her duties would include. Curtis did not respond to a request for comment.
Should Peters accept the role, she would likely feel right at home in Shasta County, a deep-red enclave in Northern California that has become ground zero for many of the election denial conspiracy theories promoted by Trump and his supporters over the past six years. And in Curtis, she would be working alongside a man who has a decades-long history of promoting many of the same election-related conspiracy theories she herself has championed.
“This should be stopped immediately: Shasta County Registrar Clint Curtis is trying to hire election-denier Tina Peters to collude with the Trump administration’s election mischief,” US senator Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, wrote on Facebook.
Curtis first came to national prominence more than two decades ago, when he claimed to have created a software program that could rig elections without election officials being able to notice anything amiss. Curtis, who testified before Congress about his program, said he did this at the behest of Florida state lawmaker Tom Feeney, who denied the claim.
In 2025, when the previous Registrar of Voters in Shasta County, Thomas Toller. retired midterm, Curtis put his name forward for the position, despite having no experience in running elections and spending most of his career working as a lawyer and a computer developer. He also lived in Florida at the time and had no ties to the area.
During the 2025 interview process for his current role, Curtis touted his associations with prominent figures in the election denial community, including Lindell, disgraced former national security adviser Mike Flynn, and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon.
Since his appointment, Curtis has faced a string of accusations about his behavior from members of his staff. An internal investigation concluded that he had physically threatened, verbally abused, and retaliated against staff at the Shasta County Elections Office, while an external investigation found he had retaliated against them. Among the specific allegations made by his colleagues were that Curtis threatened to have one employee dragged out by her hair and to “throat-punch” another. Curtis has consistently denied the allegations.
In June, Curtis lost his bid to keep his job past this year when Joanna Francescut, who worked in elections in Shasta County for 18 years, easily defeated him. Curtis had fired Francescut days after he took up his role.
The Board of Supervisors in Shasta County, having initially voted against censuring Curtis, last week voted 3-1 to censure him. However, Curtis responded to the public rebuke by making further allegations against his staff, including claims that they were bypassing security to tamper with elections. He subsequently invited the media back to his office to show them CCTV footage of one staff member opening a door without using a keycard.
When asked if he had asked the employee in question what he was doing, Curtis said he hadn’t.
"Shasta County has gone through a lot of controversy, division, and animosity related to elections, and based on the initial response from the public I’ve received already, recruiting Tina Peters would increase this and reduce trust in our elections," Matt Plummer, a member of the Shasta Board of Supervisors, tells WIRED, while acknowledging Curtis has the authority to make his own hiring decisions. The other members did not respond to a request for comment.
Plummer isn’t the only authority raising questions about the proposal. Stewart Buettell, the deputy CEO of the County of Shasta, tells WIRED, “There has been no formal process or application submitted to replace the current assistant registrar of voters,” adding that “any prospective employee would go through the same hiring process as anyone else seeking employment with the county.”
Brent Turner, the current assistant registrar of voters, told Shasta Scout on Tuesday that he was surprised to hear he may be replaced. “I believe I’m the assistant registrar. And if anything changes I will certainly let you know,” said Turner.
Curtis told the Redding Record Searchlight that he would be hiring Peters as a consultant as a way of circumventing what he predicted would be the county’s efforts to block the appointment. He said that as a consultant, she would be able to continue to work in Colorado and Washington, DC while also at times supervising onsite in Shasta County.
Buettell said that if Peters was hired as a consultant that would “typically require a contract for services, consistent with Shasta County policy, which has not been initiated.”
While there has been strong criticism of the effort to employ Peters, some election experts believe mechanisms are in place to prevent it from actually happening.
"This announcement seems to be nothing more than performance art by the current and outgoing clerk, who was rejected by voters in the primary,” David Becker, the head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research and a former Justice Department lawyer, tells WIRED. “It’s highly questionable that county officials could spend any taxpayer dollars on this or give any authority to a convicted and unrepentant felon like Ms. Peters.”
Despite her parole conditions barring her from travelling outside Colorado without permission, Peters has spent the months since her release appearing in-person at multiple MAGA events as well as numerous interviews with right-wing podcasters, continuing to promote election denial conspiracy theories. She has also met with Trump in the Oval Office and has claimed to have met the head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and presented her plan to secure elections.
If Peters does decide to take up the role in Shasta County, which Curtis told Action News Now would begin on September 4, it will allow her time to fulfil one more public engagement, when she is scheduled to speak at the Destroying the Whore of Babylon conference later this month.
