AI generated
TEHRAN – US President Donald Trump pledged “economic warfare” against Iran and threatened any country that trades with it, prompting Iran to dismiss the plan on Aug 20 as a continuation of failed policies.
The war between the two countries, started by the US and Israel in February, appears stalemated, with peace talks stalled, Tehran keeping the key Strait of Hormuz shut and Washington persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.
Under pressure at home over the economic impacts of this unpopular war and with midterm elections looming, Trump appeared to be searching for alternative ways to pressure Tehran.
In a post on his Truth Social, the US leader said he was announcing “the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY! This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale”.
“ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” he said.
The US has maintained punishing sanctions against Iran for decades, with Trump in his 2017-2021 first term ratcheting them up as part of a “maximum pressure” strategy in which he tore up a nuclear deal negotiated by his predecessor Barack Obama.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Aug 20 dismissed the plan as a continuation of “failed policies”, which he said would bring Washington “further defeat”.
“The so-called ‘Economic D-Day’ is a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs. Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat – and enmity of Iranians,” Araghchi said in a post on X.
“US economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide.”
‘Oil smuggling’
Despite the heavy international sanctions, Iran found ways to continue exporting its oil, with China the biggest buyer.
In his threat to those helping Iran, Trump did not mention any country by name, nor did he say what punishment third countries might face, although last August, the US slapped an additional 25 per cent tariff on India for buying Russian oil.
The US leader listed several activities that he said needed to stop immediately: “oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies”.
Like Russia, Tehran operates a so-called shadow fleet of tankers, all of which are under international sanctions, to continue its oil trade.
It is unclear what additional impact any fresh sanctions would have, given the US blockade of Iranian ports.
Tehran, though, continues to exert its own economic pressure campaign by keeping the strait of Hormuz largely closed. Before the war, around a fifth of global oil supplies travelled through the strait.
Attacks on shipping in Hormuz have continued, despite the lull in the wider war, while on Aug 19, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned Gulf countries against assisting the US.
That came after the United Arab Emirates said it was severing economic ties with Tehran over attacks on its shipping.
‘Diplomacy is doomed’
While it has been several weeks since the last round of tit-for-tat strikes, Iran has taken a more confrontational stance say analysts.
Ahmad Zeidabadi, a Tehran-based international relations expert, told AFP the shift reflected Iran’s assessment of Washington’s intentions.
“The Islamic republic believes the United States has likely ruled out war and now seeks to perpetuate the status quo including the US naval blockade and the economic pressure,” he said.
He said the “Iranians believe that diplomacy is doomed to fail in the current climate” and that “they may feel compelled to resort to offensive action to force the US to accept Iranian conditions”.
The tougher stance was also reflected in Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei appointing a number of hardliners to senior security positions in recent weeks.
“These appointments are demonstrative of Iran believing it will be in a wartime footing for the foreseeable future,” said Jason Brodsky, policy director of the US-based United Against Nuclear Iran think tank.
The war has also continued to spread, sucking in and reigniting Yemen’s smouldering civil war. On Aug 20, the Revolutionary Guards warned that Saudi Arabia would not be able to contain Tehran’s allies, the Houthi rebels.
The group, which controls swathes of Yemen and has been at war with Riyadh for over a decade, has declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and attacked ships in the Red Sea. AFP

Belgian car salesman becomes prince after royal parentage confirmed
- Published
Belgium's Prince Laurent has legally recognised 26-year-old former car salesman Clément Vandenkerckhove as his son and heir.
Vandenkerckhove, the result of a relationship between the royal and Belgian singer Wendy Van Wanten, was quietly brought into Prince Laurent's family at a town hall ceremony six months ago, although details have only just emerged.
While he formally becomes a prince, he will not receive a royal allowance.
The new prince has had several years to get used to the idea of having a royal father, and he said recently he was not yet sure he would begin using his father's name Saxe-Coburg.
"I might want to do that, but I am proud of the name Vandenkerckhove," he told Het Nieuwsblad.
"If I were to sacrifice that family name, it would be a betrayal of everything my mother has done for me."
He will not be part of Belgium's royal line of succession, unlike his half-sister Princess Louise and half-brothers Prince Aymeric and Prince Nicolas. Nor will he take part in public royal activities.
Vandenkerckhove is already well known to Belgians, having been the focus of a Flemish TV documentary last September, in which he described how he got to know his father.
His father had been in a relationship with Wendy Van Wanten, whose real name is Iris Vandenkerckhove, before he went on to marry Princess Claire in 2003.
During the VTM documentary, Clément described meeting the prince unexpectedly in a shopping centre in 2013, without realising who he was. It was only when he was 16 that his mother revealed his father's identity.
Four years later he plucked up the courage to ring him up, and after several more calls they met in person and eventually Prince Laurent suggested they take a DNA test.
"We went to the hospital together and I remember him saying 'I'll go first so you're feeling at ease'," he told VTM. Then he received an email from the laboratory which told him of a 99.5% DNA match.
Prince Laurent's DNA test is reminiscent of his father, former King Albert II, who had a test after a lengthy paternity battle. Albert admitted in 2020 that he had fathered a daughter during an affair and eventually recognised her as his own.
Albert II abdicated as king of the Belgians in 2013 as the paternity issue became a royal scandal.
Delphine Boël, a well-known artist, eventually won her court battle and gained the right to the title of princess, and now calls herself Delphine de Saxe-Coburg.
Under changes to Belgian law in 2013, only a few members of the royal family are entitled to public allowances - King Philippe, his father King Albert II, Prince Laurent and Princess Astrid.

Taliban secures pragmatic global alliances without formal recognition
Kabul expands trade and security partnerships across the region despite the ongoing lack of full international legitimacy.
The Taliban government in Afghanistan has successfully expanded its ties in security, trade, energy, and transport with various countries, five years after returning to power in Afghanistan almost as an international pariah.
While Russia became the first country to officially recognise the Afghan government in July 2025, the majority of the international community continues to withhold full political recognition, according to diplomatic sources and political experts.
Still, despite the lack of formal global recognition, the government in Kabul has actively integrated itself into the regional diplomatic landscape – and its relations with multiple countries are only growing.
Expanding diplomatic footprint
Afghan Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi told Al Jazeera that Kabul is “currently dealing with more than 40 diplomatic missions, including embassies and consulates in various countries, in addition to dozens of foreign missions and organisations working in Kabul”.
China has emerged as one of the Taliban’s most prominent partners, managing its embassy in Kabul and cooperating closely on security and investment.
The partnership is heavily anchored in mining, particularly the Logar copper mine project, which a Chinese company secured under a 2008 contract with a declared investment of nearly $3.4bn.
In January 2024, Chinese President Xi Jinping formally accepted the credentials of the Taliban’s ambassador to Beijing, even though China does not officially recognise the current government in Kabul.
Regional trade and tensions
Relations with neighbouring Pakistan represent the most complex dynamic for the Taliban. For decades, Pakistan was widely viewed as a key patron and ally of the Afghan Taliban, helping arm, finance and shelter leaders of the movement.
But relations have frayed dramatically since the Taliban returned to power, especially over Pakistan’s claims – which Kabul rejects – that Afghanistan is offering shelter and support to the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) armed group. The TTP is behind many of the deadliest attacks in Pakistan in recent years.
Kabul has increasingly used trade and border crossings as leverage, diversifying its trade routes through Iran and Central Asia to reduce reliance on Pakistani ports.
Meanwhile, Uzbekistan is actively building economic ties with the Taliban, signing trade agreements in 2026 worth approximately $520m.
A proposed railway project linking Uzbekistan to Pakistan via Afghanistan aims to give Central Asian countries access to the Arabian Sea.
Turkmenistan is similarly engaging with Kabul through the multibillion-dollar TAPI gas pipeline project, which includes a 735km (457-mile) stretch inside Afghanistan. The Turkmenistan- Afghanistan-Pakistan-India pipeline project is on the whole on hold, though, because of tensions between India and Pakistan, and now between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
Security expert Abdul Jalil Amini told Al Jazeera that anxiety over the ISIL (ISIS) group represents a “more pressing motive” for Russia and Central Asian states to cooperate with the Taliban.
Amini noted that these countries believe the Taliban is capable of controlling shared borders and has succeeded in maintaining a degree of security and stability.
Balancing regional powers
Iran and India are also carefully navigating their interests in the country. Tehran maintains extensive relations in trade and energy, offering the Chabahar port as an alternative route for Kabul, despite ongoing friction over the sharing of the Helmand River waters.
Meanwhile, New Delhi is gradually rebuilding its ties to counter Pakistani and Chinese influence. Farid Mamundzay, the former Afghan ambassador to India, told Al Jazeera that the Taliban operates a “pragmatic policy through which it seeks to maintain balanced relations with various powers to serve its interests”.
Gulf states like Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have maintained their diplomatic presence in Kabul, though their engagement remains limited compared with Central Asian nations.
Ahmed Karimi, a professor of international relations at Kabul University, told Al Jazeera that the stance of Saudi Arabia and the UAE is “more conservative” this time, settling for merely accepting diplomats from the movement.
Western security coordination
Western nations continue to communicate with the Kabul government primarily over security, counterterrorism, migration, and humanitarian aid, though issues surrounding women’s rights and governance remain major obstacles to formal recognition.
Strategic relations expert Najib al-Kuzi told Al Jazeera that the relationship between Washington and Kabul “did not stop since the American withdrawal, but they were largely confined to the security and intelligence fields”.
European countries also maintain working relations, with the European Union mission continuing its operations from Kabul.

“I wanna try it so bad”: How TikTok shapes what teenagers eat — and the role parents can play
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:14:10 UTC
19:14:10 KST

TikTok trends are influencing what teenagers eat, from viral restaurant dishes and fast food to recipes and influencer diets. But new research suggests parents may also have a role in limiting the platform’s influence.
TikTok is becoming a double-edged source of nutrition advice for teenagers: the platform can offer recipes, cooking ideas and healthier alternatives, while also exposing young people to dieting culture, unrealistic body ideals and potentially misleading health claims. That creates a complicated environment for adolescents still developing their relationship with food, health and their bodies.
A recent study of teenagers aged 15 to 16 found that food content on TikTok could trigger cravings, encourage young people to try new foods and, in some cases, influence how they eat in an attempt to emulate influencers.
"Adolescents described TikTok as a highly engaging environment where food content can quickly capture their attention and cue a desire to eat or try something new," said an author of the study, Adrianna N. Bell.
The findings come as policymakers and courts take a closer look at the impact of social media on children and young people.
Currently in the US, Meta is facing a legal challenge over allegations that it deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to be addictive for young users. In Europe, in the meantime, TikTok was accused of breaching the European Union's online content rules, exposing children to cyberbullying or contact from abusers, while some national governments are moving to impose bans on social media platforms, including TikTok, for children.
The TikTok research adds another dimension to that debate: what happens when social media does not just influence how teenagers feel, but what they want to eat?
“It makes me wanna try it”
The study examined how adolescents perceived TikTok’s influence on their eating and what role their parents played.
The teenagers described a food environment in which trends, adverts, recipes, restaurant reviews and influencer content could quickly turn curiosity into appetite.
Trending food was particularly powerful because it was new — and because everyone else appeared to be trying it.
“The reason why I want to [try the trending food] is because I’m like, ‘why do so many people want to do it, like what’s so good about it?’ so it makes me wanna try it,” one of the teenagers that participated in the research said.
Presentation mattered too. Attractive food, professionally produced videos and positive comments could encourage cravings. Teenagers also said they took comments into account when deciding whether to trust a recommendation.
Influencers were another important part of the equation.
One participant described changing their diet after watching an influencer with a muscular physique:
“So, sometimes I be changing the way I eat. Because I’ve seen some dudes that are so buff and they have a good body you know and I’m like damn and so I click on his account and see what they’d be eating. And then I sometimes change how I eat, like to try to match it. ”
The influencer, therefore, does not necessarily need to be explicitly selling a food product. The message can instead be about a lifestyle — with food presented as part of the route towards a particular body or appearance.
When fast food starts to look normal
The study also highlights the role of TikTok’s algorithm.
Teenagers said their food choices could depend on what appeared on their personalised For You page. Repeated exposure could even affect how they perceived certain foods.
“I see so much fast food that like I don’t see fast food as unhealthy even though it is pretty unhealthy,” another participant said.
That reflects broader concerns about social media food marketing. Research has found that adolescents are frequently exposed to food adverts online and can be more attracted to social media advertising than traditional television advertising.
A recent systematic review and meta-analysis also found that celebrities and influencers promoting foods high in fat, sugar and salt can increase adolescents’ consumption of those foods.
On TikTok, however, advertising can be harder to separate from entertainment.
Food content can be a brand advert, an influencer recommendation, a restaurant review, a viral recipe or a creator simply joining a trend. The commercial message may be embedded within a video that looks like ordinary user-generated content.
And then there are the parents
Perhaps the most striking finding concerns what happens away from the screen.
Most teenagers said their parents played little or no role in their day-to-day TikTok use. But when parents did intervene, “they also described times when parents played an important role by interrupting exposure to food-related content and encouraging critical conversations about that content,” Bell said
Sometimes the intervention was not about TikTok at all. Family meals, spending time with siblings or simply having parents around could interrupt long periods of scrolling and reduce exposure to food-related content.
Other teenagers described a more direct form of parental influence: learning to question what they see online.
One participant said their mother had explained that influencers have different bodies and lifestyles, meaning that copying their diet would not necessarily produce the same results after she followed a diet seen on TikTok.
“… cause TikTok told me at a young age that, “do this [diet] and you’ll be skinny in 22 days” and I followed that the hard way,” a participant said.
That points towards a form of parental involvement that is less about surveillance and more about media literacy.
While the study is small and exploratory, involving 25 teenagers, the message is clear: TikTok is not simply showing teenagers what food looks like. It can shape what looks desirable, popular and normal.
And sometimes, as one teenager put it, that is enough to make them think: “I wanna try it so bad.”

Ancient Egyptian tomb reveals 2,700 years of changing burials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:13:39 UTC
19:13:39 KST

Breadcrumb
What happened after the tomb was full? Unravelling 2,700 years of burial, reuse and ritual in ancient Egypt
Deep inside a burial chamber cut into the slope of Wadi Hatasun, a dry river valley on the Nile's west bank in Luxor, two mummified adults lie side by side, arms crossed over their chests in the sacred pose of Osiris, the ancient Egyptian god of the underworld. A mummified dog rests across their shins.
The scene is among the most striking to emerge from Theban Tomb 209 (TT 209) and the centrepiece of a new study published on 18 August 2026 by a joint Spanish-Egyptian team in the peer-reviewed journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.
The study examines how this single burial space was reused and reworked across roughly three centuries — from the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty (744 BC-656 BC), when Kushite kings from Nubia ruled Egypt, through the Persian and Ptolemaic periods — revealing that burial practices shifted from individually coffined bodies to the deceased being stacked directly on top of one another.
The excavation took four years, from 2018 to 2022, but the analysis has only now been made public.
The roughly 2,700-year-old tomb sits within the Theban Necropolis, part of a site UNESCO declared a World Heritage property in 1979.
Ancient Thebes and its Necropolis — one of the most concentrated archaeological landscapes on Earth — is a pillar of Egypt's tourism industry, with freshly unearthed tombs continuing to make headlines.
"There are always new things happening in Luxor," Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy said at the unveiling of the restored Colossi of Memnon last December.
The new TT 209 study is just the latest.
Of the many chambers inside TT 209, one in particular, known as Side Chamber 3 (SC3), holds the fullest, most intact sequence of bodies.
"This is the only one we have preserved like a good sequence of bodies," Dr Jared Carballo-Pérez, of Leiden University, told The New Arab.
Elsewhere in the tomb, remains have been looted or disturbed by later intrusions, leaving scattered bones rather than an intact sequence. Because of that, SC3 was the team's focus
The findings come from a joint Spanish-Egyptian project known as dos cero nueve, Spanish for "two zero nine," a nod to the tomb's number.
It was co-led by Carballo-Pérez and Dr Miguel Ángel Molinero Polo of the Universidad de La Laguna, under permits from Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities and the Supreme Council of Antiquities.
The challenge is to piece together a picture of the deep past from the smallest of traces, said Molinero Polo, the study's senior author and director of the mission.
"We have few details regarding how the people who entered tombs behaved, what their motivations were in each historical period, and how they conceptually reconfigured the pre-existing space," he told The New Arab.
TT 209 was built for Nisemro, a high official of Nubian origin active in Thebes in the early years of the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty.
The tomb sits on the slope of an active wadi. That makes it prone to flooding.
"The mummies were heavily affected by the fact that it was flooded," Carballo-Pérez said. It was also an opportunity for the team to compare ancient flood layers with recent ones, some from the 1990s and identifiable through datable plastic debris, helping them piece together a history of flooding in Luxor.
Inside SC3, researchers documented 16 human individuals in primary or partly primary positions, meaning their remains were found in the same location and arrangement as at burial.
They also found a mummified dog. A separate secondary deposit affected by burning and later disturbances contained 1,775 bone fragments from at least four more people.
Some fragments were later incorporated into a thick, reworked layer of sediment above it, and their original source is still unclear.
The study employed archaeothanatological techniques, which analyse the positioning of bodies and their decay in relation to surrounding earth layers, to understand how past groups treated the dead.
Similar studies have been done on predynastic sites in Egypt's western oases, but this is the first of its kind on the Theban burial sites of this period.
"I would say it is at least the first study we have with this approach," said Carballo-Pérez.
Previous studies looked at tomb reuse in Thebes, but from a different angle. Earlier work by Egyptologist Gianluca Miniaci "focused mainly on architectural restructuring or material culture," said Carballo-Pérez.
From individual burials to a shared, stacked space
The earliest burials in the chamber, likely from the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty, present the classic image of an ancient Egyptian burial: individual bodies in wooden coffins, each in its own space, surrounded by jars, amulets and beads.
"The earliest individuals buried here appear to have been of high social standing," Molinero Polo said, "as they were interred in coffins, with funerary nets and amulets, and with an assemblage containing costly items, such as the contents held in Phoenician amphorae."
Then, from the late Twenty-Fifth Dynasty onwards, burial practices began to change: the deceased were placed directly into spaces where others had already been buried.
By the Persian and Ptolemaic periods, bodies were routinely stacked on top of each other. Coffins, once a cornerstone of every burial, became rarer and then largely disappeared.
In the past, scholars have pointed to recycled tombs as a sign of economic decline, but Carballo-Pérez and his colleague push back on this narrative.
Both the earliest and latest burials included funerary items and offerings, he said. "I wouldn't say it's that they were poorer. I would say it's just a change in the funerary behaviours and the customs that this population had."
Tarek Sayed Tawfik, professor of Egyptology at Cairo University's Faculty of Archaeology and president of the International Association of Egyptologists, put it like this: "It could be called relative poverty," he told The New Arab.
"Owning a luxurious, decorated coffin points to a certain level of wealth, but relying on embalming wrappings alone doesn't mean a total absence of wealth – mummification itself was costly and shows that the person held a certain social standing."
An open question over arm position
The crossed-arm posture of some of the mummies in SC3 is known as the Osirian pose, named after Osiris – the god of the afterlife and resurrection, who was famously killed by his jealous brother Set and brought back to life by his wife, Isis.
A mummy with arms folded over the chest is one of ancient Egypt's most recognisable burial images. Though, as the researchers found, it was not a pose used at every point in time, or on every body.
Carballo-Pérez said the team found both the Osirian pose and straight, extended arms at every level of the chamber, with no statistically clear pattern by period, though the pose was somewhat more common in the Ptolemaic layers.
He said the sample was small, raising another possibility: that the pattern reflects a change in custom within the same population, rather than a change in who was buried there. "We can just say that there are some changes in the burial customs," he said.
The straight-arm position is understood as the older of the two, said Tawfik, "though it remains an observation needing more comparative study."
Both researchers agree that the evidence isn't yet strong enough to support a firm rule.
It is in one of the tomb’s later, denser phases – dated to the Persian period – that the mummified dog appears, placed across the lower legs of the man and woman in the Osirian pose.
Carballo-Pérez said this is, as far as the team could tell from a preliminary review of previously published finds, the first documented case of a mummified dog buried directly on top of a human body.
“There's maybe a closer relationship rather than an offering,” he said.
He also raised, then set aside, a tempting connection. Nisemro, the tomb's original owner, is shown in inscriptions with a dog named Hekenu, a detail Molinero Polo documented in earlier fieldwork on the tomb.
But Carballo-Pérez said the couple dated centuries later, too wide a gap to draw any direct link.
Molinero Polo offered another possibility: that the animal may have taken on the role of a psychopomp, a symbolic helper guiding the dead into the afterlife.
The most famous example from ancient Egypt is Anubis, the jackal-headed canine who leads the deceased to the underworld and oversees the weighing of the heart, or final judgment ceremony.
The paper's authors describe SC3 as a "mortuary environment," a term meant to capture how the chamber's organisation carried forward from one burial to the next, with the one-to-one relationship between an individual, their coffin and their funerary equipment gradually dissolving into a shared system.
As Carballo-Pérez put it, the wider Theban necropolis functions similarly: "the whole Theban necropolis is a funerary landscape – modified across time through the reuse of tombs."

He holds a Master's degree in science and technology policy from the University of Sussex

Lithuania’s election watchdog finds grave funding violations by Nemunas Dawn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:12:00 UTC
19:12:00 KST

Lithuania’s Central Electoral Commission on Thursday found that the Nemunas Dawn party and its leader, Remigijus Žemaitaitis, committed serious violations of election law in financing the 2024 parliamentary and presidential campaigns.
The decision was not unanimous.
The commission found that the party’s parliamentary campaign was financed with donations originating from companies and routed through third parties, while Žemaitaitis’ presidential campaign also received prohibited funding through intermediaries.
“The Central Electoral Commission has found that the Nemunas Dawn party and its chairman, Žemaitaitis, seriously violated the Election Code and the Law on Political Organisations,” commission chair Lina Petronienė told reporters.
The commission said 24,200 euros transferred to Nemunas Dawn by its member Robertas Puchovičius originated from two business companies, Tvari Statyba and Lajota. Another 4,500 euros from Tvari Statyba was transferred through Puchovičius to Žemaitaitis' presidential campaign.
Corporate donations are forbidden by Lithuania’s election law. It also puts a cap on donations by individuals.
The commission also found that Puchovičius had acted as an intermediary in channelling the companies’ funds to the campaigns.
In a separate case, Aleksandras Fursas provided funds through an intermediary, while Lina Šukytė-Korsakė transferred 5,000 euros she received from him to Žemaitaitis’ campaign as her own donation.
The commission also found violations involving party membership fees. Paulius Kazilionis paid 300 euros in membership fees using money received from Puchovičius, while Puchovičius’ father, Edvardas, and wife, Eva, paid 2,500 euros and 1,500 euros, respectively, from funds originating with Puchovičius.
The commission ordered Žemaitaitis to pay 9,500 euros in illegal campaign funding into the state budget within 20 working days. A decision requiring Nemunas Dawn to return 28,500 euros was postponed pending a separate decision on state funding for political parties.
The commission plans to notify the Special Investigation Service and the Prosecutor General’s Office of the violations.
Petronienė said the party could also lose state funding for up to two years. The issue is expected to be considered in the autumn.
Nemunas Dawn and Puchovičius have argued that the money transferred from the companies belonged to Puchovičius personally. The companies’ lawyer, Povilas Gruodis, said Puchovičius had previously transferred more than 50,000 euros of his own money to one of the companies and later withdrew about a third of it for personal and political purposes.
Puchovičius said he regularly placed spare personal funds in his companies rather than keeping them idle.
“All the money was working, and if I had spare money [...] it went back to the company,” he said at the commission hearing. He said he later decided to withdraw the money because it was his own, tax-paid funds and use part of it to finance his political campaign.
The commission said the explanations and documents submitted by the companies did not alter its findings, which were based on bank transactions, transfer amounts and timing, account balances, the movement of funds and the status of the individuals involved.
The latest finding is the second serious financial violation involving Nemunas Dawn.
In March, the commission found that the party had misused state funds by paying for the rental of cars from Žemaitaitis and another party member. As a result, Nemunas Dawn was denied 241,800 euros in state funding for the first half of this year.

Ukraine's New Vyrivnyuvach Guided Bomb Is Built With 90% Domestic and Western Parts
Ukraine’s newly developed Vyrivnyuvach guided aerial bomb relies on Ukrainian and Western parts for 90% of its components, as reported by The War Zone on August 18.
A representative from the Brave1 defense technology cluster revealed the detail, noting that the munition was developed by DG Industry with support from Brave1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian engineers engineered nearly all core elements locally—ranging from the wing structure to the flight controller software—with foreign dependencies limited primarily to specific chips and microcircuits.
Roughly 90% of the weapon’s component base originates from Ukraine, Europe, and the United States, allowing manufacturers to avoid critical reliance on foreign hardware.
The bomb features modern guidance algorithms, though specific operational metrics remain undisclosed. Representatives noted that the system's structural design differs from both Russian and Western equivalents.
Engineers spent approximately 17 months taking the project from initial concept to a functional prototype. Development began roughly two years ago amid concerns regarding future stability in foreign military deliveries.
Following a series of successful tests, the team confirmed the viability of the design by May 2025 and proceeded with project implementation.
Unlike France’s AASM Hammer, the current iteration of the Vyrivnyuvach lacks an engine, and officials have not specified whether future variants will incorporate propulsion.
While technical capabilities allow potential integration with Western platforms like the F-16 and Mirage 2000 subject to manufacturer certification, the munition was designed for immediate compatibility with Ukrainian aircraft.
It is currently integrated onto MiG-29, Su-24, and Su-27 airframes. The bomb has cleared operational testing and is officially being procured for service.
During the mid-May operations, Ukraine executed a record-scale drone attack targeting Moscow, which Russian media claimed involved between 500 and over 1,000 unmanned aerial vehicles.
While the Ukrainian side traditionally maintained silence regarding the specifics, multiple strikes successfully bypassed Moscow’s multi-layered defense network—which included over 100 launchers for S-300, S-400, and S-500 systems alongside more than 50 Pantsir-S1/S2 units—ultimately damaging key military and oil infrastructure across the region.

Germany’s half-empty gas stores spark winter supply warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:09:02 UTC
19:09:02 KST

Ayhan Simsek
20 August 2026•Update: 20 August 2026
Germany’s natural gas storage facilities are only about half full, the lowest level for this time of year in recent years, prompting opposition politicians to warn that Europe’s largest economy could face tighter supplies if winter turns severe.
Storage sites stood at roughly 50% capacity as of Wednesday, according to the energy regulator Bundesnetzagentur—about 26 percentage points below the average for recent years. German rules generally require facilities to reach 80% by Nov. 1, though limited exceptions exist.
“In such an uncertain world market situation, relying on a mild winter or functioning LNG markets so that half-empty storage facilities will be enough is a gamble,” Joerg Cezanne, energy policy spokesman for the opposition Left Party, told Rheinische Post daily.
Michael Kellner, a Green Party politician and former state secretary at the Energy Ministry, cautioned against assuming liquefied natural gas imports will always proceed without disruption.
“Last year we had the case that an LNG terminal was unable to operate because the Baltic Sea was frozen over,” he said. “Then they sent an icebreaker. The icebreaker broke down. The terminal was shut for several weeks, I think two or three weeks. And things like that can happen.”
Klaus Muller, president of the Bundesnetzagentur, called the current level unsatisfactory. “The gas storage facilities reached 50% filling 50 days later than last year,” he wrote on social media. “That means around 123.4 TWh is stored, but that cannot satisfy us. That’s why it is important that gas traders meet their responsibility toward their customers for the winter.”
Traders normally buy gas in summer, when prices are lower, and sell it in winter. This year, relatively high prices have reduced the incentive to stock up. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has also disrupted shipping, curtailing oil and gas cargoes through one of the world’s busiest energy corridors.
Despite the concerns, officials told public broadcaster ARD that Germany is not facing a crisis on the scale of the one that followed the start of the Ukraine war in February 2022. Before the war, Russia supplied nearly 55% of Germany’s natural gas. Berlin has since replaced most of that volume with supplies from Norway, Belgium, and France, along with LNG imports, largely from the United States.

Portrait of the Ukrainian Nation at 35 Years of Restored Independence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:09:00 UTC
19:09:00 KST

The first thing I consider extremely important is that Ukraine has overcome the fundamental regional differences we still observed before 2014.
The differences between East and West, South and Center have not disappeared. But they are no longer fundamental. We have become a united country in regional terms.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
For me, this is one of the most positive changes of the independence era. It greatly contributes to social solidarity. And without solidarity, it is impossible to have a viable future in the terrible war we are experiencing today.
In this sense, I would even say that we are now more integrated than many other democratic countries. Look at the US: regional and political divisions largely determine whom society elects and what direction the country takes. In Ukraine, these differences have lost their former sharpness.
There is another extremely important change. Sociology has a methodology for measuring social distance – how close we consider members of different groups to be and how willing we are to accept them, up to the point of being ready to see them as members of our own families.
Before 2014, Ukrainians had the smallest social distance between Russians and Belarusians. Traditionally, they were considered the “closest” to us. After the Euromaidan, the annexation of Crimea, and the beginning of Russian aggression, everything changed.
Today, citizens of Russia and Belarus are among the groups toward whom Ukrainians maintain the greatest social distance. And it is important to stress that we are talking specifically about citizens of these states, not about a person’s ethnic background.
EXPLAINER: 35 Years Ago Today, the World Held Its Breath
At the same time, we have moved significantly closer to Europeans. This is a very important change because there was a paradoxical situation in the past: we declared a European choice, but the average Ukrainian psychologically kept Europeans at a greater distance than Russians.
Now that distance is shrinking.
Ukrainians have always differed significantly from Russians in terms of political culture. We have a different history – not a monarchical-imperial tradition, but experience of living within the European political space, including the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Cossack state.
Ukrainians can be emotional, sometimes even inclined toward ochlocracy, but we are nevertheless democratic.
Our value system is changing as well. For a long time, we were relatively close to Russians in this respect – largely as a result of the Soviet legacy. But in recent years, we have been moving significantly away from it.
I see a shift from security and material well-being as the primary values toward self-realization, freedom, mutual assistance, and tolerance.
What is particularly important is that this shift accelerated after 2022. We have moved closer to the European value system and further away from the system we once shared with Russian society.
We still lack tolerance, of course. War intensifies emotions, and that is natural. But what matters is that Ukraine has vigorous public debates. That is part of a democratic political culture.
At the same time, I do not want to create an overly optimistic portrait.
The war has brought enormous losses. There are practically no people who have not been affected by it. Someone has lost loved ones; someone has lost their home, job, property or place of residence. This inevitably affects the psychological and moral state of society.
Our mood today is worse than it was in the autumn of 2022, when we experienced the highest level of optimism. At that time, around 70-80% of people viewed the future positively. Today, that figure is closer to 60%.
The number of people willing to accept significant concessions to Russia in exchange for ending the war is also growing. I estimate them at roughly 20% of the population.
But that is still a minority. The overwhelming majority of Ukrainians are not prepared to accept the aggressor’s terms. Given all our losses and psychological exhaustion, this is a very important indicator.
It seems to me that we have become more realistic. In 2022, many people were unrealistically optimistic. We thought the war would end within several months or half a year. Now we understand that it is a long process.
But there has been one fundamental psychological change: it is very difficult to live with a sense of being a victim. When Ukraine began systematically destroying Russia’s military potential, Ukrainians saw themselves not only as victims of aggression, but as actors capable of striking back.
We constantly need hope. Not an illusion, but hope – an awareness that we can influence our own future.
I am cautious about forecasts. To be honest, I have become disappointed in the predictive capabilities of sociology around the world.
Why? Because today the world is effectively being run by two old, sick, and deeply insecure politicians, whose decisions, ambitions, whims, resentments, and personal complexes affect the fate of billions of people. We have all become hostages to this situation.
And this is no longer only a problem of war.
The world is undergoing extraordinary changes driven by technological progress, demographic and climate challenges, and economic upheaval. Against this backdrop, people often choose leaders who offer simple solutions to complex problems. They lose their critical thinking and begin to believe in a messiah. Ukrainians, too, believe in their own messiah.
So I would not risk drawing a precise portrait of what a Ukrainian will look like in ten years.
But there is a scientifically grounded method – extrapolation, or projecting patterns of past development into the future. And I know what the trends are.
For us, the main thing is to withstand this war. We will not be abandoned. Otherwise, Europeans will have far more problems than simply helping Ukraine. We need to hold on ourselves and exhaust Russia, as we have been doing over the past six months.
The second important condition is that Europeans must remain consistent in supporting us, and that far-right forces seeking rapprochement with Putin’s Russia must not prevail.
Under these two conditions, I see a prospect for Ukraine’s value-based, normative, and institutional rapprochement with Europe. This means Ukraine will develop a real party system and a genuine system of local government. Then we will achieve our goal: we will become a normal European country. Perhaps a poor one. Perhaps not the most developed. But Eastern European. Not West Asian, but genuinely European.
Over 35 years of independence, we have become a more integrated country. We understand much more clearly how different we are from Russia. We have moved closer to Europe not only politically, but also psychologically and in terms of values.
And despite all the losses, we have preserved what matters most – the majority of Ukrainians remain ready to defend their right to determine their own future.
That is how I approach the 35th anniversary of restored independence: not without anxiety, not without fatigue, but with the understanding that Ukrainian society has become significantly stronger and more mature over these decades than we ourselves are sometimes inclined to believe.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

====================================================================================================

With climate change, areas of Europe hit by wildfire could nearly triple: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:07:40 UTC
19:07:40 KST

Zeynep Ozturhan
20 August 2026•Update: 20 August 2026
The area affected by wildfires in Europe could nearly triple by the end of the century under a high-emissions scenario as climate change brings hotter, drier, and windier conditions, according to a study led by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK).
Annual burned area could increase by around 39% under a low-emissions scenario and by about 192% under a high-emissions scenario during 2070-2100, compared with the 2000-2030 average.
The study, published in Global Change Biology with contributions from the Frankfurt-based Senckenberg Society for Nature Research, also highlights the importance of emissions cuts and stronger fire prevention, early detection, and firefighting measures.
"Climate change is driving up fire activity across Europe as hot, dry and windy conditions become more severe," said Maik Billing, a researcher at the institute and lead author of the study.
Billing said burned areas could increase widely even under warming of around 1.8C (3.24F), while a rise of roughly 3.6C (6.48F) could make fires much more prevalent, particularly around the Mediterranean and across Western and Central Europe, including areas that have historically experienced fewer fires.
 
Investment needed to manage rising fire risks
The study found improved fire prevention, early detection, and firefighting could reduce burned areas by 92% under 1.8C warming and by 72% under roughly 3.6C warming, although the authors cautioned that these estimates may be optimistic in a much warmer climate.
"We see fire conditions are increasing, so we need to invest more," said Thomas Hickler, a Senckenberg scientist and co-author of the study.
Hickler said greater investment in firefighter training, equipment, and coordination could make a significant difference, but warned that extremely severe fires could eventually exceed firefighting capacity.
"The recent record fires in France clearly show that we cannot simply extrapolate from the experiences of the past," he said.
 
Europe faces severe wildfire season
The findings come amid another severe wildfire season in Europe. Around 550,000 hectares had burned across the European Union as of Aug. 12, about 2.5 times the 20-year average for this point in the year, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS).
"The fires in France, Spain and Greece show how quickly hot, dry and windy weather conditions can stretch firefighters and their resources," said Kirsten Thonicke, a scientist at the Potsdam Institute and co-author of the study.
Thonicke said climate change could push fire conditions beyond the limits of existing prevention and firefighting capabilities, making emissions reductions essential alongside stronger local fire management.

MINSK, 20 August (BelTA) – On 20 August Belarus President Aleksandr Lukashenko signed decree No.277 “On the development of trade, public catering, and consumer services in rural areas and small urban settlements,” the press service of the head of state told BelTA.
 
The document aims to improve retail services, enhance their quality, and create additional conditions for the development of trade, public catering, and consumer services in rural areas.
 
To this end, a system or a set of standards is being established at the municipal level for the sectors of trade, public catering, and consumer services. On the one hand, it takes into account wishes of rural residents while, on the other hand, it bears in mind the economic interests of retail businesses.
 
The decree stipulates that retail, consumer services, and public catering in rural areas shall be conducted with due regard for local peculiarities. In particular, peculiarities concerning taxation, the organization of mobile shops (including mandatory route planning, frequency of service, and specified arrival times and locations), and the transfer of real estate for a price.
 
The decree establishes personal accountability for the heads of oblast and district administrations as well as the heads of retail entities for offering adequate retail services to rural residents.
 
The decree was drafted in accordance with the requirements and instructions given by the head of state at an offsite conference held in the town of Vileika on 7 August 2026 to discuss ways of ensuring that the rural population has access to a wide range of goods to fully meet their needs.
 
The legal acts that had previously regulated these areas are hereby repealed.

Archaeologists uncover human offering at ancient ceremonial site in Lima
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:05:54 UTC
19:05:54 KST

Archaeologists in Lima have uncovered the skeletal remains of an adult believed to have been placed as a ritual offering at Huaca Pucllana. The body was found inside a ceremonial canal dating to around 650 AD, when the Lima culture flourished on Peru's central coast.
Archaeologists in Peru have uncovered the skeletal remains of an adult believed to have been placed as a ritual offering more than 1,300 years ago.
The remains were discovered at Huaca Pucllana, a pre-Hispanic ceremonial and administrative centre in the heart of modern-day Lima.
The body was found inside an underground ceremonial canal, lying on its left side with its skull tilted westward towards the sea and a mud pyramid within the complex.
Archaeologist Gladys Paz, who is leading the excavation, says the position of the remains points to an intentional ritual placement.
"We are looking at the discovery of a human offering found inside a ceremonial canal belonging to the Lima culture," said Paz. "We are located at Huaca Pucllana, which corresponds to Sector B of Huaca Chica, at what would have been the main gate or entrance to the ceremonial center around 650 AD."
The discovery offers archaeologists an opportunity to learn more about how ceremonies were conducted at the site more than 1,300 years ago.
The excavation has also uncovered ceramic pieces, adding further evidence of activity at the ceremonial centre.
Huaca Pucllana is part of the modern landscape of Lima, where ancient archaeological sites can be found alongside the city's homes, businesses and public infrastructure.
Archaeologist Micaela Alvarez says this contrast is one of the features that makes the site particularly striking for visitors.
"It's a characteristic of Huaca Pucllana for quite a few decades now; in fact, it’s almost what attracts people who come to visit us, to find such an ancient archaeological site right in the middle of the city; it’s surprising, really."
The Lima culture flourished on Peru's central coast between 100 and 700 AD, before the rise of the Inca Empire.
Pucllana was one of its major ceremonial and administrative centres.
The discovery is not an isolated example of Lima's pre-Hispanic past. More than 400 sacred sites belonging to pre-Hispanic cultures are scattered throughout the capital, according to official data.
The remains are expected to be removed from the excavation site in the coming days.
For archaeologists, the find provides another glimpse into the rituals and beliefs of the people who lived in the area long before modern Lima was founded.

Hind Rajab family rejects Israeli probe after army admits firing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:05:24 UTC
19:05:24 KST

Breadcrumb
'We don't trust Israeli investigations': Hind Rajab's grandmother rejects probe after Israeli army finally admits firing
A leading pro-Palestine legal group and the family of Hind Rajab have rejected an Israeli military investigation into her killing, demanding an independent international probe after the army admitted for the first time that its soldiers had fired on the car carrying the Palestinian child.
Hind's grandmother said on Thursday that the family had no confidence in Israeli military investigations or the Israeli justice system, a day after the army announced a criminal investigation into the January 2024 killing.
"We are not demanding [an investigation] in the name of Hind alone as a child in Gaza, but in the name of all our child martyrs in Gaza," she told Anadolu, calling for those responsible for the killings to be held accountable.
The six-year-old was found dead inside a car riddled with hundreds of bullets in Gaza City alongside six members of her family, days after she desperately called for help during an hours-long phone call with the Palestinian Red Crescent.
Her cousin Layan, who was also in the vehicle, had earlier called relatives pleading for help before she was killed. Hind remained trapped alive inside the car among the bodies of her relatives and stayed in contact with rescuers for hours.
Two Palestinian Red Crescent paramedics sent to rescue her were also killed when their ambulance came under Israeli fire near the car. Their bodies were found almost two weeks later after Israeli forces withdrew from the area.
The Israeli military had repeatedly denied that its forces were present in the area when Hind, her relatives and the medics were killed. Those claims were contradicted by several independent investigations, which found evidence that Israeli tanks were operating at the scene.
On Wednesday, the army finally acknowledged that its soldiers had fired on the family's vehicle.
It said an internal review had identified alleged failures surrounding the coordination of the Palestinian Red Crescent ambulance and that the case would now be referred to the Military Police Criminal Investigation Division.
Hind's grandmother rejected the prospect of the Israeli military investigating its own forces, saying the family believed the civilian vehicle, which was carrying several children, had been deliberately targeted.
The Hind Rajab Foundation, a Brussels-based pro-Palestine legal group, also said it had "no confidence" in the Israeli military's investigation.
"These reported investigations, even if they do occur, should not be mistaken for a genuine step toward justice," the foundation said in a statement, describing Israel's internal probes as "fundamentally flawed".
The foundation, which pursues legal action against Israeli soldiers accused of war crimes committed during Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, said the military could not credibly investigate allegations involving its own forces.
Hind and her family have become one of the highest-profile cases of Palestinian civilians killed by Israeli forces during the war, generating international outrage.
Original audio recordings of her emergency call were later used in the Oscar-nominated film The Voice of Hind Rajab.
"Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division," the military said on Wednesday.
But Israel's internal military investigations have repeatedly been criticised by rights groups and legal organisations for shielding soldiers from accountability and rarely resulting in meaningful prosecutions or punishment.
In almost 90% of 52 publicly reported investigations, the military either closed the cases without finding wrongdoing or did not announce an outcome, according to Action on Armed Violence.
"Investigations into violations committed by Israeli forces overwhelmingly end without meaningful examination, prosecution, or punishment," the Hind Rajab Foundation said.
"In the small number of cases in which soldiers have been convicted of crimes, the punishments imposed have often been exceptionally lenient or administrative in nature."
The Israeli military on Wednesday also published findings into four other high-profile killings in Gaza and announced a criminal investigation into the massacre of 15 Palestinian aid workers in Rafah in 2025.
It declined, however, to launch criminal investigations into three other cases, including the killing of seven World Central Kitchen workers and four Médecins Sans Frontières staff.
World Central Kitchen described the decision as "deeply offensive" and said Israel could not credibly investigate its own conduct.
"We continue to demand an independent commission to investigate the airstrikes because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct," it said in a statement.
Australia's foreign minister said she was "outraged" by the decision and would summon Israeli ambassador Hillel Newman.
Australian aid worker Lalzawmi "Zomi" Frankcom was among the World Central Kitchen employees killed in the attack.
Since the start of Israel's war on Gaza, the military's internal fact-finding mechanism has examined around 150 incidents and referred them to military prosecutors, according to Israeli news site Ynet.
Dozens of those cases were subsequently closed by the military prosecution, reinforcing the long-standing belief that Israel's internal accountability system serves to protect its forces from independent international scrutiny.

Israeli occupier attacks displaced Palestinians from 107 West Bank communities since 2023: Human Rights Watch

Omar Alothmani and Ikram Kouachi

Escalating Israeli occupier attacks have fully or partially displaced 107 Palestinian communities since January 2023, Human Rights Watch said Thursday.
In a report, the rights organization said the figure was based on data from the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), which documented an average of 6.6 occupier attacks per day in 2026 resulting in casualties, property damage or both, the highest rate in its records.
The organization said occupier violence escalated in March and April, involving killings, including of children, assaults, sexual violence, arbitrary detention, arson, property destruction, and theft.
Human Rights Watch said it investigated attacks in April and May targeting seven Palestinian villages and towns in the governorates of Ramallah in the central West Bank, Nablus in the north, and the Jordan Valley in the east. It interviewed 20 witnesses and reviewed videos recorded by witnesses and surveillance camera footage.
“The Israeli government and the settlers share the same goal of maximum land and minimum Palestinians, with the authorities not only failing to stop settler violence, but actively enabling it,” said Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“Settlers shoot, attack, and expel Palestinians from their land, and the state provides the weapons, the legal cover, and the budget to do it,” she added.
The rights organization said that occupiers responsible for displacing Palestinians “operate with financial, material and legal support from the Israeli state.”
It added that “Israeli authorities are arming, funding, and granting impunity to the violent settlers responsible for these escalating deadly abuses.”
 
The organization cited a report by the Times of Israel saying that “the government had approved about 50 million shekels (about $16 million) for illegal settlement outposts, funding that has been used for all-terrain vehicles, night-vision goggles, and drones that settlers use to harass Palestinian communities.”
It said that “settlers responsible for displacing Palestinians operate with the financial, material, and legal backing of the Israeli state.”
 
“According to Amnesty International, the Ministry of Settlement and National Missions’ budget has increased 122 percent under the current government,” Human Rights Watch noted.
At least 15 Palestinians, including two children, were killed by occupiers as of July 24, compared to 16 such killings in 2023, according to OCHA.
Human Rights Watch said the escalation in occupier violence “has been clear since the current government took office in December 2022.”
In July 2024, the International Court of Justice concluded in an advisory opinion that Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territories is unlawful and that it had systematically failed to prevent or punish occupier attacks against Palestinians.
The occupied West Bank has witnessed continued escalation in occupier attacks and Israeli military operations since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza on Oct. 8, 2023, alongside the expansion of settlement outposts, the construction of roads, and increased restrictions on Palestinian movement.

Video: Bears in the crosshairs once again after lifting of years-long hunting ban
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:04:20 EEST
19:04:20 KST

The hunting of bears is permitted once again in certain parts of Finland after the lifting of a two-year ban, with the season beginning on Thursday 20 August and ending on 31 October.
The Supreme Administrative Court passed a ruling in June which allows for the culling of a total of 182 bears under specific regional quotas.
For the past two years, bear hunting was suspended outside reindeer herding areas due to legal appeals challenging the legality of culling permits. The court's ruling dismissed these appeals on the grounds that hunting is needed to prevent bears from causing damage to property or threatening people's safety.
The permits are concentrated in eastern and central Finland. North Karelia received the most permits with 118, followed by Southeast Finland with 24, South Savo with 14, and smaller quotas in Kainuu, Central Finland, and North Savo.
Hunting groups have welcomed the move, as Finland's bear population has grown to an estimated 2,400 individuals — according to figures provided by the Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) — and humans are encountering bears at a significantly increased rate, particularly near residential areas.
Sauli Härkönen, head of public administrative tasks at the Finnish Wildlife Agency, has urged hunters to prioritise bears that have caused documented problems, emphasising that the season runs until late October and there is no rush to meet quotas.
However, nature conservation groups have criticised the court's decision, arguing it violates European Union directives on the protection of native species.

Champagne harvest: why picking begins as early as mid-August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:04:03 UTC
19:04:03 KST

In Champagne, the grape harvest began as early as mid-August, unprecedented for some growers, after heat and drought sped up ripening and forced them to change their methods.
In Champagne, the calendar seems to have gone into overdrive. On the hillsides of Hautvillers, grape-pickers are already hard at work even though August is not yet over.
This year, the first picking officially started between 12 and 17 August, depending on the area and the grape variety. An exceptionally early start that speaks volumes about how the region's climate is changing.
For Alexandre Gobillard, production director at the Gobillard & Fils house, harvesting this early was once unthinkable.
"I've been working on the estate for 30 years, and when I started my father always used to say: 'On 15 August, go on holiday.' Today it's 18 August, and we're in the middle of the harvest. We've never seen anything like it," he explains.
The heat has dramatically sped up the ripening of the grapes. After a spell of frost at the end of March (another first), Champagne then endured several heatwaves and severe drought. Temperatures even reached 40°C in some parts of the region in June.
The drought has also increased the concentration of sugars in the grapes. Winegrowers therefore have to monitor ripeness extremely closely to strike the right balance and produce champagne that is sufficiently fresh and delicate.
A little further east, in Tours-sur-Marne, the situation is the same. The owner of these vines, Ophélie Lapie-Lamiable, can only observe that, for the past twenty years or so, especially since the 2003 heatwave, the harvest has been systematically brought forward, and that people will probably have to get used to it.
"2003 is still remembered as a landmark year. It was the first time we harvested in Champagne at the end of August. Since 2003, we've harvested at the end of August at least 10 times, so 2026 will probably also go down in history for its frost and its earliness. Perhaps in 20 years' time we'll be saying that in the end, harvesting on 15 August has more or less become normal," says Ophélie Lapie-Lamiable, manager of Champagne Lamiable.
Adapting to global warming at all costs
This shift is already forcing the industry to rethink its practices and consider grape varieties that can better withstand climate change. It also makes organising the harvest more complicated, as it is traditionally carried out by hand, with thousands of seasonal workers who need to be housed and transported in the height of summer, sometimes in sweltering heat.
Out in the vineyards, the first signs are still encouraging. The question now is what this lightning-quick harvest will produce once the wine is in the bottle.
In the cellars, the grapes are already being pressed. The first bubbles of this very early vintage are therefore beginning to take shape, and it will take a few years to know whether they have also lived up to all their promise and are considered a grand cru.

From technoparks to food and pharma: What Belarus offers Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:03:00 UTC
19:03:00 KST

MINSK, 20 August (BelTA) – Prime Minister Aleksandr Turchin outlined proposals to advance cooperation between Belarus and Myanmar during the Belarus-Myanmar Business Forum in Minsk on 20 August, BelTA has learned.
Promising areas of partnership include agriculture and food security initiatives. “Given today’s fierce global competition, we must place a special focus on the agricultural industry. Providing our citizens with high-quality, affordable food is a matter of national security. Belarus has a strong track record in this area and is eager to fully cover Myanmar’s market demand for high-quality powdered milk, baby food, rapeseed oil, and butter. For its part, the Belarusian market requires a broad spectrum of agricultural goods produced in Myanmar. Considering the current depth of our bilateral ties, we are keen on developing a more profound and substantive partnership regarding food security. In particular, we suggest that Myanmar leverage Belarusian technologies to set up its own domestic processing industry. You can fully rely on our active support in establishing highly efficient production facilities inside Myanmar,” Aleksandr Turchin said.
Another key priority is partnership in healthcare and pharmaceuticals. “Myanmar’s pharmaceutical industry can access high-quality, affordable medications made in Belarus. We are eager to boost our pharmaceutical exports and simultaneously suggest taking the next step: localizing production within Myanmar. A joint venture to package Belarusian bulk products at Myanmar facilities could serve as the initial phase. Furthermore, our businesses are currently developing a socially vital project to assemble mobile medical units. Launching this initiative will significantly improve healthcare accessibility in Myanmar’s remote regions,” the prime minister said.
Partnership in high-tech, science, and professional training is equally relevant. “We are glad that in this sector, Belarus and Myanmar are moving past mere declarations and taking concrete action, such as establishing a joint high-tech park in Naypyidaw. Specifically, it entails the joint development of technology solutions for the remote monitoring of natural resources. This is an ambitious yet fully achievable project. We completely share the Myanmar leadership’s commitment to securing digital sovereignty. Belarus is ready to offer relevant solutions powered by artificial intelligence and computer vision, which can be applied to both the digital economy and e-government systems,” he said.
A crucial component of high-tech cooperation is training a skilled workforce. “Without professionally trained personnel, any technology remains useless. Therefore, Belarus is ready to train Myanmar engineers and researchers at our leading scientific and academic centers. This will allow them to integrate seamlessly into all proposed projects, from tractor assembly to joint ventures in the space industry. Launching joint educational programs in Myanmar will help train specialists tailored to the economy’s needs, ensuring long-term technological continuity,” Aleksandr Turchin concluded.

A vocabulary for the future: touch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

A Vocabulary for the Future is a series by the Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona in which notable thinkers reflect on a word of their choosing and are paired with filmmakers who give their writing a visual interpretation. Together, they invite viewers to see familiar language anew, in the hope of laying the groundwork for a better tomorrow.
In this instalment, the American theoretical physicist and feminist theorist Karen Barad muses on the nature of touch. Drawing partly on their essay ‘On Touching—The Inhuman That Therefore I Am’ (2012), Barad begins with a puzzle from classical physics: touch, strictly speaking, never happens, since what we feel as contact is only electromagnetic repulsion between atoms that never actually meet. Turning to quantum field theory, they reframe the question entirely. If matter has no stable, self-contained identity – if it is entangled with other matter from the very start – then touch is not a failed meeting between separate bodies, but something already constitutive of what matter is. Paired with visuals by the Barcelona-based digital artist Blanca Rego, the result is a mesmerising set of images that, alongside Barad’s words, turn something as ordinary as touch into a doorway into the deepest questions in physics and philosophy.

====================================================================================================

Severe e-scooter crashes result in higher rates of traumatic brain injuries than motorcycle accidents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:00:52 UTC
19:00:52 KST

A fall from an electric scooter (e-scooter) can look deceptively minor. The rider is standing only a short distance above the road and, unlike a motorcycle, most e-scooters are limited to relatively modest speeds.
Yet trauma surgeons are seeing injuries that tell a different story. E-scooter crashes can cause serious head injuries, damage to internal organs, and complex fractures – sometimes after what appears to have been a simple fall.
This matters as e-scooters become an increasingly common form of transport in cities around the world. New research from England and Wales offers one of the clearest pictures yet of the injuries involved.
The study examined more than 15,000 people with moderate or severe injuries recorded in a national trauma database. This included 580 e-scooter riders, more than 7,000 motorcyclists, and more than 7,000 cyclists.
The clearest difference was what happened to riders’ heads.
Among seriously injured adults, traumatic brain injuries were around three and a half times as common among e-scooter riders as among motorcyclists, and around 1.7 times more common than in cyclists. More than a third of the injuries recorded among adult e-scooter riders involved traumatic brain injury.
Damage to internal organs and blood vessels was also proportionally more common. Fractures, however, were actually less common among e-scooter riders than among motorcyclists or cyclists.
There is an important qualification. These figures do not mean that taking an e-scooter journey makes someone three and a half times more likely to suffer a brain injury than riding a motorcycle. The researchers did not have comparable information on the number of journeys or distance travelled by motorcyclists and cyclists.
Instead, the results tell us that when people sustain moderate or severe injuries, the pattern of injuries sustained on an e-scooter is different. Head and internal injuries make up a much greater proportion of the resulting trauma.
That distinction matters when headlines describe e-scooters as “three times riskier” than motorcycles. The study cannot tell us whether an e-scooter journey is three times more likely to result in serious injury than a motorcycle journey, because the researchers did not have comparable data on how far people travelled on each.
Why e-scooters can cause serious injuries
One explanation for this injury pattern lies in how e-scooters are designed and ridden. Riders stand upright, giving them a relatively high centre of gravity. Their wheels are much smaller than those on most bicycles, while the handlebars provide a narrow point through which the rider controls the vehicle.
Hit a pothole, kerb or piece of debris and the small front wheel can stop suddenly. The rider keeps moving forwards and can be thrown over the handlebars towards the road, with very little protection between their head and the ground.
This makes helmet use particularly important. Among seriously injured e-scooter riders in the study, only about 6% were recorded as wearing helmets, compared with 45% of cyclists and 76% of motorcyclists.
Children also featured disproportionately. Around 16% of injured e-scooter riders in the trauma database were under 18 – substantially higher than the proportion among injured cyclists or motorcyclists.
A second part of the research examined more than 23,000 incidents involving rental e-scooters across more than 33 million journeys and almost 78 million kilometres. Collision rates varied considerably between cities, suggesting that where people ride may matter as well as what they ride.
Official figures give some indication of the wider burden. In Great Britain, police recorded 1,312 collisions involving e-scooters in 2024, resulting in 1,390 casualties: six people died and an estimated 444 were seriously injured.
How e-scooter injuries are treated
Treatment depends on what has been damaged. Minor fractures may need a cast or brace. More complicated fractures can require surgery involving plates, screws or metal rods. Serious head injuries may need intensive care, brain surgery, or prolonged rehabilitation, while internal bleeding may require emergency surgery.
The consequences can therefore extend far beyond the initial crash. A few seconds on an e-scooter can lead to months away from work, rehabilitation and, in the most severe cases, permanent disability.
Many of the factors contributing to these injuries can be reduced. A helmet cannot prevent a fall, but it can protect the part of the body that appears particularly vulnerable.
Riders should also become familiar with the acceleration, braking and steering before entering heavy traffic. Speed matters, particularly on wet or uneven roads. Using a phone, carrying another passenger or riding after drinking alcohol adds further risk to a vehicle that already demands balance and concentration.
E-scooters have clear advantages: they are convenient, relatively cheap and can replace short car journeys. Millions of rides take place without serious injury.
But their appearance can be misleading. An e-scooter may look more like a child’s scooter than a motorcycle, yet the injuries seen in trauma centres show that falling from one is not necessarily a trivial event.
