Press review: Ukraine crisis nears peak as Israel-Turkey tensions rise over Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, August 20. /TASS/. Ukraine’s political crisis could intensify by the fall amid new corruption investigations and mounting pressure on Zelensky; an Israeli strike on a Syrian airbase highlights the risk of an accidental military clash with Turkey; and Japan is expanding its long-range strike capabilities with hypersonic missiles and drones. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Ukraine's political crisis could peak as early as this fall
Ukraine is sinking deeper into a political crisis, which could reach its peak as early as this fall. A new investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) has once again involved people close to Vladimir Zelensky. At the same time, former Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov has returned to the public spotlight, calling for elections to be held even under martial law. Experts believe Washington could choose to back him amid the struggle for influence in Ukraine. Meanwhile, further confrontation could trigger a new wave of protests and public calls for a change of government.
Ukraine's political crisis is likely to develop fairly rapidly, former Verkhovna Rada member Spiridon Kilinkarov told Izvestia. In his assessment, the confrontation could peak in the fall of 2026, while the current developments are only the start of a broader domestic political struggle.
At the same time, the further politicization of street protests cannot be ruled out. According to Kilinkarov, even after a new defense minister is formally appointed, protesters could change their demands and focus not on Fedorov's return but on broader issues, above all the fight against corruption and the actions of the Ukrainian authorities.
The developments may be linked primarily to US interests, former Ukrainian lawmaker Igor Markov told Izvestia. In his assessment, Washington, having stepped back from directly supplying Kiev with weapons, is seeking to maintain its influence through NABU and SAPO, thereby limiting Zelensky and further escalation of the Ukrainian conflict. The ultimate objective of pressure from the anti-corruption agencies could be to remove Zelensky from power, Markov believes.
NABU and SAPO are not interested in a strong Zelensky, expert at the International Institute for Humanitarian and Political Studies Vladimir Bruter told Vedomosti. Zelensky needs to remain weak and controllable and must not try to dictate terms to the West, as he sometimes does, the expert said.
The scandal once again demonstrates that corruption is an integral part of Ukraine's political system and that the overwhelming majority of Ukrainian officials are involved in corruption-related crimes, expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government Denis Denisov told the newspaper. According to him, the published materials showed that Ukraine has a shadow government, a "deep state," that is more influential and powerful than the official authorities in Kiev.
For Russia, the destabilization of Ukraine's political system that could follow the scandal is undoubtedly beneficial, but it will not have any lasting consequences, the expert concluded.
Vedomosti: Israel’s strike on Syrian airbase highlights risk of tensions with Turkey
An Israeli air raid on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Syria’s Idlib province near the Turkish border on the morning of August 18 could have triggered a direct military confrontation between Israel and Turkey, US Special Envoy for Syria and Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack said in an interview with The Jerusalem Post the day after the attack. According to him, the Turkish military was unaware of the objectives of the Israeli operation and did not know that Israeli warplanes were heading specifically toward the Syrian base. As a result, Barrack continued, Ankara could theoretically have scrambled its own fighter jets, interpreting the Israeli Air Force’s actions as an attack on Turkish territory. Experts interviewed by Vedomosti consider a direct Turkish-Israeli military conflict over Syria unlikely, arguing that neither side is interested in an open confrontation.
Although Turkish officials have made no statements regarding efforts to restore the Abu al-Duhur airbase, Ankara is likely not opposed to the facility being used, Turkey expert Yashar Niyazbayev told the newspaper. In Turkey’s information space, the country’s presence in Syria is viewed as a necessary measure dictated by circumstances, the expert noted.
By carrying out the operation at the Abu al-Duhur base, Israel is seeking to hinder the revival of the Syrian Air Force, Kirill Semenov, expert at the Russian International Affairs Council, believes. According to him, the strike was carried out after Syrian Su-22 fighter-bombers began launching from the base. "The Israelis will continue to carry out periodic limited attacks on Syria in the future. Turkey’s actions, meanwhile, will be limited to statements," the expert said.
According to Niyazbayev, the prospect of a direct military conflict between Turkey and Israel is unrealistic for now.
Neither Turkey nor Israel is interested in a direct military confrontation over Syria, research fellow at the Center for Middle Eastern Studies at the Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO) Lyudmila Samarskaya said in agreement. Through its military operations in the neighboring country, Israel is signaling its unwillingness to accept an expansion of Turkey’s presence on Syrian territory, the expert continued. "The Israeli leadership fears the expansion of Turkey’s regional influence, while preemptive strikes against neighboring countries are consistent with Israel’s current military strategy, which also calls for proactively preventing potential threats," the expert said.
Izvestia: Japan expands strike capabilities as it moves beyond traditional defense posture
Japan, whose constitution has for 80 years prohibited the country from maintaining a military as an instrument of war, is beginning a program to develop weapons that, by definition, cannot be considered defensive. These include hypersonic missiles for submarines and long-range strike drones - a system designed to provide Tokyo with a "counterstrike capability" against enemy territory. While the ground-launched Type 25 could still formally be linked to the defense of Japan’s islands, submarine-launched hypersonic weapons and kamikaze drones are blurring the line between defense and offense. Experts told Izvestia Japan’s growing military capabilities are making the Pacific an increasingly significant zone of potential conflict for Russia.
According to the newspaper, these items have already been included in the Defense Ministry’s draft budget for 2027. Particular attention will also be given to technologies and weapons related to implementing the country’s "counterstrike capability." In particular, this includes equipping unmanned underwater vehicles with the capability to launch long-range missiles.
In addition, Tokyo plans to ease restrictions in the nuclear sphere. In 1971, the Japanese authorities adopted three non-nuclear principles: not to possess, not to produce, and not to permit the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japanese territory. However, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has now called for this taboo to be reconsidered.
"Obviously, the third non-nuclear principle could be revised in the coming years, with the next step being the deployment of air-delivered nuclear weapons at US bases in Japan," Junior Research Fellow at the Center for International Security at the Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO) Alexander Ermakov told Izvestia.
Russia is concerned about the militarization of its maritime neighbor, particularly after Tokyo identified Russia as one of the main sources of threats in its latest military doctrine documents.
"The Pacific Ocean is becoming an increasingly important zone of potential conflict for Russia, as much as the Baltic or Black Sea. Russia must not lose sight of these developments," the analyst said.
Vedomosti: Structural challenges widen Europe’s economic gap with United States
US nominal GDP is projected to reach $32.4 trillion in 2026, compared with just $23 trillion for the European Union, according to forecasts by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Thus, the combined economies of the EU’s 27 member states will equal just 71% of the US economy. Experts interviewed by Vedomosti attribute Europe’s widening economic gap with the United States primarily to lower labor productivity, structural and demographic challenges, greater dependence on foreign trade, exchange-rate effects, and a series of economic and geopolitical shocks.
Experts consider the current situation entirely predictable. A combination of serious structural problems and a series of shocks - the 2008 global financial crisis, the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the EU (Brexit), the COVID-19 pandemic, fuel crises, foreign trade tariffs, and the war in the Middle East - has significantly weakened the EU’s growth and the resilience of its economic system.
Around 70% of the gap between the EU and the United States in per capita GDP at purchasing power parity (PPP) can be attributed to lower labor productivity in the EU, stock market expert at Garda Capital Kirill Seleznev told the newspaper.
When comparing the size of economies, it is important to take exchange rates into account, Senior Analyst at BCS World of Investments Adam Abdulatipov believes. Currency fluctuations, such as a weakening of the euro, would lower the European Union’s nominal GDP in dollar terms even though the physical volume of production at European factories and farms would remain unchanged. It is also important to take into account the EU’s loss in 2008 of one of the world’s largest economies, the United Kingdom. More obvious factors, such as demographics, also contribute.
Europe needs access to foreign markets - this is precisely why tariffs, sanctions, standards, and the new industrial policies of major economies have a much more pronounced impact on the EU. The European economic model is considerably more dependent on foreign trade. The United States has an interest in maintaining a financially stable Europe, the BCS expert said.
Izvestia: Iran conflict drives up European household energy costs by at least €19 bln
Europeans have paid at least €19 bln (around 1.67 trillion rubles) more for energy because of the conflict in the Middle East, according to Izvestia. This is how much households had to spend extra between March and June, which represents only the direct impact of higher commodity prices, without taking into account how businesses subsequently passed their increased costs on to consumers through higher prices for food, transportation, and services. If the conflict continues, European families may need around €88.8 bln in additional spending on the entire consumer basket by the end of the year to maintain their previous standard of living.
The modern economy is closely interconnected through global supply chains, while a significant share of the world’s energy reserves and exports is concentrated in the Persian Gulf countries, stock market expert at BCS World of Investments Andrey Smirnov told the newspaper. As a result, conflicts in the region rapidly influence commodity markets. Countries are particularly vulnerable to disruptions in oil and gas supplies.
Rising energy costs are gradually squeezing other items in European household budgets: mandatory spending on heating and electricity is accounting for an increasingly large share of expenditures, leaving less money for non-food goods and services, Ahmed Yusupov, an economist and Partner at the Goldman and Po communications agency, explained. Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency forecasts that electricity prices in the EU could rise 1.5-fold by the end of 2026.
In Europe, the notable increase in gasoline prices stemming from the situation in the Middle East has directly affected household budgets. In Russia, however, the impact is limited. "When comparing the impact on households, Europeans face greater pressure: their economy is more dependent on energy imports and market prices, while the Russian fuel market is largely regulated by the state," economist Olga Gogaladze emphasized.
Nevertheless, the energy crisis in the EU also has an indirect impact on Russia. Despite sanctions and the deterioration in relations in 2022, Russia continues to trade with its eurozone partners. In the first half of 2026, trade turnover declined by 13% to €27 bln (around 2.4 trillion rubles). European countries’ exports to Russia fell by 1.3% to €14.8 bln (1.3 trillion rubles), while imports of Russian goods into the European Union dropped by 24% to €12.2 bln (1 trillion rubles).

Dolphins and other lovers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
41 minute listen
‘A nasty one, the dolphin,’ Derode grumbled when he returned home, trading the humid heat of an Amazonian afternoon for the cool, sheltered interior. Inside, his wife Rosa and I shot hungry looks at his empty hands. Once again, the Caquetá River surrendered no fish. I was only two weeks into my fieldwork with the Andoque people in southern Colombia, and my eyes zigzagged in confusion between the two septuagenarian spouses. What did a dolphin have to do with anything? Rosa explained: ‘Derode had left baits by the river, and it seems a dolphin had stolen the fish that had gotten hooked in them.’
Derode nodded.
The fishing had been poor ever since my arrival, and as Rosa cooked lunch from the rice and lentils I had brought from the city – the ‘White People’s Food’ – she reminisced with her husband about times when the river had been generous. She recalled how her grandfather had once hauled in an almost legendary catch by throwing poisonous plants into the shallow stream and asphyxiating the fish in great numbers. Among this enormous catch was a dolphin. Of course, she added, as if it needed no explanation, her grandfather did not eat it.
‘Why not eat the dolphin?’ I asked. The Andoque were accomplished hunters and fishermen, and there was almost no walking, swimming, crawling or flying creature that they wouldn’t relish, if they could catch it.
‘Because dolphins are people,’ Rosa said, matter-of-factly. ‘Besides, their meat smells terrible.’
Dolphins were not simply people, she went on, they were bad people, shapeshifters. Her father had once warned her never to accept the advances of unknown men while bathing at the river. As handsome as they may seem, he had said, they may be dolphins in disguise. Those reckless enough to fall for their charms would soon grow feverish, drift into madness and hallucinations, and ultimately die. No cure would save them.
Look what happened upriver, Rosa said. She then told a story about a strikingly handsome man and a stunning woman who walked into a riverside bar in some village one night. Both were impeccably dressed in white clothes, with fancy accessories, such as a belt, a watch and a hat. The man ordered drink after drink, while the woman remained quiet and abstained. The bar owner sensed something strange about them, though he couldn’t say what. The other clients were enchanted: the men drawn to the woman’s grace, the women to the man’s charm. Then, at some point late in the night, the couple disappeared. The last place they were seen was down by the riverbank. At dawn, villagers returned to the spot, and found the visitors’ elegant accessories scattered on the ground. Only now, those items had transformed: the belt had become an electric eel, the watch a crab. Gazing at the stingray that had previously been a hat, the villagers finally understood. It had been needed to cover a blowhole. The visitors were dolphins in human form, on the hunt for unwitting prey.
‘Such are dolphins,’ Rosa concluded.
I tried to lighten the mood. ‘Where I come from,’ I said, ‘dolphins perform tricks in aquatic circuses.’
Rosa was unimpressed.
‘You’re talking about sea dolphins. Those may be different. But river dolphins here are evil.’
When I laughed and, perhaps insensitively, mentioned a newspaper story I’d once read about a woman who had married a dolphin, Rosa’s face twisted in disgust, as if she might be sick. She changed the subject.
What initially drew me to Amazonia was the tendency of its Indigenous inhabitants to consider the forest and river where they lived as a delicate society populated by beings similar, in crucial respects, to humans. An ecology of persons. This is what led me to Andoque territory in 2018, and why I spent more than a year living with families like Rosa’s. I had set out as an anthropologist seeking to study their notions of power, and how this power is bound up with nonhuman persons – like dolphins. For the Andoque, these beings may wear the bodies of trees, plants, animals and insects, but they have wishes, thoughts, fears and cultural customs like humans do. What would power look like in such a world, I wondered. A deeper interest lay hidden within the word ‘power’ – hidden, back then, even from myself. I longed for a first-hand encounter with something truly powerful: the dangerous web of life and death that makes up the forest; the intricate wisdom of a people attuned to it. I wanted to bask in that power. I wanted to admire it, decipher it, crash against it.
But the world of the Andoque had been battered long before I arrived. Far from the postcard ‘isolated tribe’, they place relations with whites at the centre of their culture. ‘Whites’ is a term that, for them, refers not to skin colour but simply to anyone external to the forest and its ways. These outsiders are closely linked in Andoque mythology with the Caquetá river mouth, as it was from there, where the water meets the main Amazon River, that European merchants first arrived as early as the 17th century.
With almost no one speaking their native language, many Andoque sometimes doubt how Indigenous they still are
The Andoque, I was told, traded slaves with whites in exchange for coveted metal tools. By the turn of the 20th century, they began acquiring these tools in exchange for vegetal rubber. But that opportunity turned into a nightmare when the Peruvian Casa Arana company overtook the region. For the sake of a booming automobile industry thirsty for rubber, the Andoque were enslaved, suffering indescribable atrocities and massacres. From around 10,000 people in 1908, they dwindled to a few dozen survivors by the mid-1930s, when they rebuilt their maloca – a large residential and ceremonial house for hosting ritual dances – and healed the wounds of their ancestral territory. In their own words, they became human once more.
They also resumed rubber extraction under more humane conditions and, in the years that followed, took part in each economic boom that swept through the region. They hunted for animal pelts, worked in the commercial fishing industry, and tried gold-mining. Today, their world has become entangled with that of whites. The Andoque live alongside settlers and other outsiders, occasionally travel to Bogotá, and have become vulnerable to price fluctuations caused by wars in countries far, far away. They currently number around 260 individuals, and Colombia recognises their ancestral territory as an Indigenous reserve. However, with almost no one but the elders speaking their native language, many Andoque sometimes doubt how Indigenous they still are.
The word for ‘dolphin’ in the Andoque language – ama̰na̰ – is not Andoque at all. It is a loan from the Tupí-Guaraní language, whose speakers served as middlemen in the slave trade with whites (and, like the Andoque, were sometimes enslaved themselves). Ama̰na̰ appears virtually unchanged across the region’s several language families, which are otherwise markedly different from one another. It attests to the relative recency of the dolphins’ flirtation with the Andoque, who were originally inland hunters and ventured along the main rivers of the Amazon only when trade intensified during the 19th century. In the process, they borrowed a Tupí-Guaraní word to refer to the strange creature they encountered in those rivers: playful and intelligent, resurfacing for air like a human living underwater.
Known to biologists as Inia geoffrensis, these river dolphins have been around for at least 10 million years. They date back to a time when the sea that had once covered the northern part of South America receded and the saltwater dolphins who remained in the rivers adapted to freshwater environments. Today, the pink skin of river dolphins makes them an attraction to tourists. Their large bodies and high food intake, on the other hand, make them especially vulnerable during the increasingly frequent drought periods when fish become scarce as rivers dry out and water temperatures rise.
The men would sit with me for sessions of conversation called mambeadero that stretched from the afternoon deep into the night
I had known practically nothing about river dolphins before starting my research but, a few months into my fieldwork, dolphin talk kept popping up during conversations with the families I lived with. As in Rosa’s stories, they were always evil, but this wickedness was never explained.
My days of fieldwork found their rhythm in hunting, fishing and tending gardens. These were tasks I tried to assist with, though I was often more of a burden to my hosts. I found solace in the preparation of coca powder, a stimulant now referred to as mambe to distinguish it from the illicit version – the white one. You pick the leaves, toast them, pulverise them, add some ashes, and filter the mixture. This fine green powder is believed to carry the spirit of an ancestor and to open channels of communication with the dueños of the forest – the guardian spirits of animals, from whom permission to hunt must be sought to avoid retribution. This almost daily work earned me the trust of the men, who would sit with me for long sessions of conversation called mambeadero that stretched from the afternoon deep into the night, with lighter topics such as gossip and politics gradually giving way to mythology. But when I asked about the enigmatic dolphin during these gatherings, the man presiding the session would frown at me: ‘Dolphins do not enter my mambeadero!’
My curiosity grew stronger. If dolphins did not enter Andoque mambeaderos, I thought, perhaps I needed to enter their domain myself.
Nearly every week, I joined my hosts on boat trips to the nearby settler village to sell local produce. On one of these trips, four months into fieldwork, I was going back home with my friend Miller after his unsuccessful attempt to sell the meat of a wild boar. It was on that late afternoon that my dangerous liaison with the dolphin began.
As the sun sank slowly into the broad-armed Caquetá River, the rainforest alive and infinite on either side, I sensed a strange smell permeating the air. Sweet and sickly, entrancing yet nauseating – it was a scent so overpowering it could make you dizzy. It wasn’t the odour of the dismembered boar, which smelt like an armpit. This was something else entirely, closer to a piece of chocolate candy stashed away in a dirty sock. The odour, a euphoric scent that was at once uplifting and deeply unsettling, turned the sunset utterly foreign.
‘What is this smell?’ I asked Miller, and added – perhaps carelessly – ‘It’s nice.’
‘Nice?’ Miller shot me the most surprised of glances. ‘It’s the smell of dolphins. It’s disgusting!’
‘Right, right,’ I mumbled.
‘You don’t do that,’ his mother admonished me. ‘You don’t mess with dolphins!’
I had learned by then that a dolphin’s human victims were not entirely blameless. The dolphin would take any action that mimicked its behaviour as a sign of affection. Sniffling a runny nose would be frowned upon because it sounds like a dolphin breathing air. Splashing water by the river amounts to a frivolous invitation to play. And here I was, in the middle of the dolphin’s domain, foolishly babbling about how pleasant it smelled.
‘You won’t believe it,’ Miller told his parents as we shared the boar meat with them for dinner. ‘Eliran likes the dolphin’s smell! He said so on the way here.’ They shook their heads.
‘You don’t do that,’ his mother admonished me. ‘You don’t mess with dolphins!’
But Miller, a cheerful man in his mid-30s, only a little older than myself, couldn’t resist teasing me. ‘Tonight, you’ll dream of a pretty girl,’ he said with a grin, ‘and if you slip her your guama’ – the elongated ice-cream bean fruit growing on the tree outside the house – ‘that will be the end of you!’
Word of my taste for dolphins soon spread among Miller’s family. ‘That smell is the dolphin’s breath when it surfaces for air,’ his cousin explained, leaving me all the more unsettled by the unexpected intimacy I had shared with the animal.
That night, the dolphin visited me. While my body lay peacefully in a hammock within its mosquito-net cocoon, my mind was sweating with desire for a guy I knew in my 20s, who then morphed into a high-school classmate of the same name. Two dream lovers. Did that mean double the danger?
Normally, I would tell my hosts what I had dreamt the previous night, tossing one more convoluted narrative into the pot of dreams they would share with each other over breakfast. Every morning, I was amazed anew at how they deciphered dreams as messages from the forest. In their language, dreams are knei: ‘somebody said’. And what this mysterious ‘someone’ says is forever oblique. A person in a dream represents an animal or forest spirit, while an animal stands in for a human. So, if you dream of encountering a wise old man, you should be on guard for deadly anacondas crossing your path. Dreaming of besting someone in a fight or of resisting seduction means it’s time to pick up your rifle and head into the woods because an animal will become your prey. Eating with someone foretells disease – it means you’re joining the domain of animals by breaking bread with them. But dreaming of sex foreshadows a whole different magnitude of disaster.
Any animal, plant, pain or blessing has a mythical origin. But nobody would tell me the dolphin’s story
So, the next morning, I kept my mouth shut. I was embarrassed, but I also wanted to test the Andoque approach to dream interpretation. Would disaster really visit me? At first, this interpretation seemed off the mark: while everyone around me caught malaria during the following weeks, burning and shivering, I remained untouched.
And all the while, I kept cautiously asking for more information about the dolphins of the Caquetá. ‘Everything has its story,’ people would invariably say: any animal, plant, pain or blessing has a mythical origin outlining its essence and how to engage with it. But nobody would tell me the dolphin’s story.
Finally, during one of the late-night mambeadero sessions at the maloca of Dufi, an elder considered the wisest, he declared: ‘I can speak about dolphins without fear because I know their origin. By telling it, it’s as if I say to them – “I know who you are, I know your faults, so be ashamed to come here!”’ As crickets chirped through the dense, wet air outside the house and toads echoed the forest heartbeats with their deep croaks, I pulled out my voice recorder with broad movements. Dufi nodded and began his story.
Green Tapir was organising a ceremonial dance at his maloca when he caught his wife by the riverbank, having sex with her own brother. Enraged, he painted his spear in the red dye of annatto seeds and hurled it into the siblings, fusing their bodies together, and threw them into the river, where they transformed into dolphins. The splash of water from their bodies sent a shiver through him – the beginning of a vengeful illness sent by the dolphins. Bound together and still facing each other, the brother and sister swam downstream in the missionary position, which is endorsed by both human and dolphin lovers to this day.
After Dufi finished his story, we remained silent. The fire in the corner of the maloca died out and darkness suffused the house. But I was finally able to see the dolphin’s traits clearly. Its insatiable sexual appetite now appeared interwoven with its incestuous behaviour. In a society where men replace the exchange of hostilities with the reciprocation of marriageable women, as in Claude Lévi-Strauss’s classic alliance theory, coupling with one’s own sister signals a refusal of exchange – and thus a turning away from alliance toward hostility. Above all, the casting of the siblings downriver, the direction from which whites first approached the Andoque territory, marked an unmistakable connection to these outsiders. As the folklorist Candace Slater shows in her book Dance of the Dolphin (1994), this association is especially striking along Brazil’s Amazon River and its main tributaries, where dolphin tales abound among Indigenous groups and communities of mixed ancestry. The pink dolphin, or boto cor-de-rosa, is said to abduct his female victims into magnificent underwater cities, filled with palaces, gold paved streets and luxuries that, for humble Amazonians, must be the everyday fare of any common urbanite. In such riverine communities, whenever unfamiliar foreign men appear at traditional communal dances, women are cautioned to be wary, for the strangers could be dolphins in disguise.
By telling dolphin stories, Amazonians of Indigenous and mixed descent convey the dangers of ‘becoming white’
The stress on the dolphin’s pink hue is no coincidence: these are the adult males who turn pink, partly due to a low concentration of melanin across their larger bodies, and partly from the scars they earn in endless battles over females. The dolphin’s link to aggressive non-Indigenous sexuality then becomes clear: Europeans first entered the Amazon as bands of adventurous men with a taste for violence through the same major rivers where dolphins live. Like the dolphin brother in the Andoque myth, these outsiders showed little regard for reciprocity through marriage. In the Europeans’ case, this disregard was reflected in an imbalance: many more Indigenous women partnered with European men than Indigenous men found wives among European women.
In Indigenous thinking, and in Lévi-Strauss’s theory of reciprocity, a lack of matrimonial reciprocity is tied to violence. Consider that, in another version of the dolphin’s origin story, Dufi explained how the descendants of the incestuous couple returned upriver to avenge their parents’ disgrace and how they were pacified through offerings of coca and tobacco. The Andoque still commemorate this episode in a ceremonial dance to shield themselves from violence of non-Indigenous origin. During the past several decades, it has been celebrated to ensure that they are not caught in the crossfire between the guerrillas and the military.
As I began to connect the dots linking dolphins and whites, I wondered about the deeper meaning of such tales – a meaning that is often implicit for those sharing them. It slowly became evident that, by telling dolphin stories, Amazonians of Indigenous and mixed descent convey the dangers of ‘becoming white’. You leave your community, abandon tradition and cross into the parallel world of non-Indigenous people, forever lost to your family.
Upon hearing Dufi’s stories, I felt as if I, too, could tell the dolphin: ‘I know who you are, I know your faults, so be ashamed to come here!’
But the dolphin visited me again, finding its way one night into a dream – disguised this time as a guy from Bogotá I was dating.
Soon, I began to question my confidence.
A few days later, jaguar footprints appeared along the long path leading to a small harbour on the Caquetá River. For the next week, Dufi’s family expressed concerns about venturing down that path, especially alone, for fear of a jaguar attack. When I mentioned my plan to go there for a phone call, hoping for better reception by the river, one of Dufi’s sons again cautioned me about the jaguar. Dufi, however, quickly reassured me. I had nothing to fear because jaguars dislike the soapy, perfumed scent of white people, which, he added, is precisely the smell that attracts dolphins.
As I reached the Caquetá in the late afternoon, I sensed the dolphin smell again. Odours and attraction, I thought – at least it works both ways.
I called my Bogotá lover, but he didn’t answer.
By then, it was dusk. I stared at the broad river, its waters reddening, and realised that I was near the place where a boat Dufi had told me about had sunk. A ‘Dolphin Boat’ he called it.
What if the Andoque felt vulnerable to dolphin attacks precisely because this animal already sensed something ‘white’ in them?
The story took place at some indeterminate moment before the rubber genocide, in that murky zone where history and myth collapse into one another. Back then, Dufi explained, there existed a clan named after the Cacambra bird. Its members caught vast quantities of fish from the Caquetá River, salted them, and traded them with downriver merchants in exchange for manufactured goods. One day, a new trade boat approached their settlement and the Cacambra people eagerly climbed aboard to marvel at the exotic items. They tried on hats, admired themselves in mirrors, and doused themselves with perfume. Suddenly, the boat pulled away from shore, trapping the Cacambra people onboard. The goods, it turned out, were cursed. The hats brought on fierce headaches, the perfumes made them feverish, and those who gazed into the mirrors went mad. Farther downriver, the boat sank, taking all the Cacambra with it. The merchants, Dufi whispered, were actually dolphins in disguise, avenging the slaughter of fish.
Heading back to Dufi’s maloca, I saw the junk along the path differently. This motley cemetery of products beneath the voraciously fast-growing vegetation – used gasoline barrels, damaged solar panels, plastic shopping bags, empty shampoo bottles – now appeared ominous. What if the Andoque felt vulnerable to dolphin attacks precisely because this animal already sensed something ‘white’ in them – a budding preference for non-Indigenous goods and comforts? Perhaps, I thought, the more dolphin-like you become, the more vulnerable you are to a dolphin’s pull.
But the danger of dolphins goes beyond mere assimilation into non-Indigenous society. It also speaks to the traps of desire itself. The dolphin is in the bad company of other seductive creatures who have nothing to do with whites. My Andoque friends told me how the tapir deceives married women by taking the form of their husbands; how the earthworm climbs into hammocks at night, seeding its victims with slime and causing deadly pregnancies; and how the deer seduces young women in their gardens, appearing as a handsome man.
Men are not spared either. Lone hunters who venture deep into the forest, consumed by thoughts of their lovers, may encounter the fi’du spirit, called madremonte in Spanish. This ‘forest mother’ appears as a beautiful woman with long flowing hair, but to lie down with her is to lose your life. The elders often told of a young man who had met such a fate in the 1940s, while working in a rubber tapping group. Famous for his lewd jokes and boastful tales of the women awaiting him back home, his bravado met its end one afternoon when he was working alone, collecting latex from a rubber tree. A naked woman appeared and offered to help fill his buckets with the milky sap. He gave in to desire. The pleasure was immense, but the cost was, eventually, fatal. He turned ill, raving with fever and visions. Before long, he was dead.
When I jotted these stories into my field diary at night, I often found them hard to believe. How can you mistake a forest spirit for a human? How can you not tell a real person from a mere hallucination? And yet, the terror that registered in my friends’ faces as they shared these stories affected me.
After I left the forest territory of the Andoque in 2019, I spent two weeks in the Colombian city of Leticia with Rosa, who had moved there for her son’s medical treatment. In marathon-long interviews, I recorded her mind-bending stories of people turning into animals, of dolphins and fi’du spirits, of detached human heads that existed as parasites on their lovers’ shoulders, and detached tapir legs that roamed the forest. And then there was her own mother, who Rosa said had contracted the ‘deer disease’ – a kind of wasting sickness that had been slowly gnawing on her ever since she was a young girl who stopped her garden work when her eyes fell on a graceful, unknown man. Restless and without appetite, she grew emaciated and unable to work, wandering to her garden at dusk as if spending her life waiting for that man to return.
I began to fear that the power of the forest, of the Indigenous wisdom so generously shared, was turning against me
All these stories contained more of that thing I had been chasing since I arrived in Amazonia: a kind of power, difficult to define, that seemed bound to the forest and its rivers.
On our last day, I phoned Rosa and asked to cancel the session. We had enough material as it was, I said. But the truth was that I felt drained, my head pounding since the night before, my body slightly feverish, nausea overwhelming me.
I felt that something was wrong. I began to fear that the power of the forest, of the Indigenous wisdom so generously shared, was turning against me.
When I boarded the plane back home, I felt a huge relief. In Paris, where I did my doctoral studies, the power of the dolphin and its shapeshifting cronies waned. They became curiosities I would bring along to dinner parties, like a bottle of red wine. And things stayed that way until, about a year after leaving the Amazon, the power struck me again.
In March 2020, just as the pandemic was gathering force across the globe, I sank into my field diaries, coming across a long-forgotten piece of esoteric gossip, which had been shared with me playfully by several Andoque people. A renowned professor, a specialist of the region, they told me, had been visited by a fi’du spirit.
Once, on an expedition to visit sacred sites in Andoque territory, he spent the night deep in the forest with a small Andoque team. They urged him to hang his hammock near theirs, but he insisted, for reasons of his own, on sleeping a little farther away. In the dead of night, the Andoque leapt at the sound of his scream. The professor, pale and shaken, claimed that a pretty, fair-skinned girl had entered his hammock. His ‘We told you so’ companions shone a flashlight inside, and found a long, blonde hair – a silent memento from the spirit-turned-woman who had just sought intimacy with him. Amazed, the professor took the hair back with him, intending to show it to his students but, upon reaching the university, it had mysteriously vanished.
The world felt apocalyptic when I came across that anecdote. The number of people infected by the new virus was climbing globally. Lockdown was declared. Any stranger’s breath, any contact, was suspicious. You could be next – with as-yet unknown consequences. This story, about a scholar I knew personally, rendered the possibility of intimacy with a different kind of danger unsettlingly real.
Birds called in longing beyond the thin walls, monkeys courted in deep-throated howls, and insects buzzed their desire into the air
Like a magnet hauling metal, the story drew from the depths of my memory an incident from several years earlier. It was a trivial episode I had been ready to forget, but which now assumed ominous proportions. I remembered another seduction, one from long before I ever dreamed of dolphins from the Caquetá disguised as men.
In 2016, shortly before beginning my doctoral studies, I travelled to the Brazilian Amazon in search of an Indigenous community where I could carry out fieldwork. I approached the first community I visited with great excitement. The first day was exhilarating, but by the evening I was so exhausted from the scorching heat and my constant efforts to decipher people’s speech that I expected to collapse the moment I climbed into the hammock. Instead, sleep never came.
That night in a maloca, the chief and his family were all sleeping deeply in their hammocks under the vast, towering roof. In my own hammock, about 30 feet away from them, I listened to the forest alive around me: birds called in longing beyond the thin walls, monkeys courted in deep-throated howls, and insects buzzed their desire into the air. The forest was fertile, vibrant, sensual. I was overtaken by a strange cocktail of emotions – a mix of daytime adrenaline from finally immersing myself in the Indigenous village routine I had yearned to experience, and something more visceral, more banal: I was horny. Drifting into a restless sleep, I was startled awake by the unmistakable sensation of a hand moving down my body. It felt so real I could still sense its warmth on my thighs. Panicked, I grabbed my flashlight and scanned my hammock and its surroundings. There was no one there. And yet, I knew that a hand had touched me. Outside, the forest surged with a deafening uproar of life. I realised I would not sleep soundly until I gave in to my body. I did it discreetly, careful not to disturb the family sleeping nearby. By morning, shame kept me from meeting anyone’s eyes; I was convinced the entire village knew what I had done.
When I later came across my notes about the professor’s spirit encounter, my own incident suddenly crystallised in Andoque terms: the fi’du had touched me, and I had yielded. My memory of this experience became a dubious initiation into Andoque lore. The fi’du, the dolphin, the deer – an obscure bestiary suddenly made sense.
The mysterious and deceitful fi’du embodies the forest’s fertility, its raw vitality – the promise of that which has not been civilised or inhabited. It is the seduction of a million and one possibilities: everything and everyone that lies beyond us, all that is not us – life itself. In my arousal, I had succumbed to its pull, I had given it my semen, my body; I had helped it reproduce. But I realised the aftermath of that fi’du encounter only now, in retrospect. I recalled that the next morning, hitching a ride out of the village to a nearby Brazilian town in an open truck, I caught a cold that lingered for a month, worsened by heartbreak over a romantic relationship that had ended weeks earlier. Feverish in my forest hammock, and later in my city bed, I sank into months of depression, consumed by longing for an ex-boyfriend who had moved on with his life. Letting yourself be pulled outward, I realised, is the fi’du disease – it is the dolphin disease. It is the desire for an Other we yearn to possess, for a life force we can never truly claim as our own.
Amazonians know desire well: desire is what the rainforest is all about. Those who live far from the Amazon tend to see the food chain as its governing metaphor, but, for those who live inside the forest, the boundaries between eating and mating blur. It is no wonder that, for an Andoque hunter, dreaming of a beautiful woman signals an encounter with forest meat, while a dream about sex foretells illness. The Amazon rainforest is, at its core, a sexual space: 2.3 million square miles of desire, where survival depends on consuming others – culinarily or sexually – while living in constant fear of being consumed yourself. For Amazonians, the world is first and foremost a huge pool of potential partners and, by marrying them, an even larger pool of potential in-laws who would become allies. Even animals are drawn into this logic. For many Indigenous groups, sex and predation are two forms through which the same mode of relation materialises. The consummation of ‘marriage’ with animals may therefore take the form either of consuming their meat or of being consumed by them through fatal attacks. As anthropologists like Eduardo Viveiros de Castro and Aparecida Vilaça have shown, within this chaotic tangle of desire and survival, family – the people with whom the urge to consume or mate is deliberately restrained – must be actively created by sharing food, care and knowledge. In the Amazonian worldview, attraction is the rule, isolation the exception.
It was Miller, my companion on that dolphin-perfumed boat trip, who clarified for me why sexual seduction is the most potent weapon of dangerous forest creatures. One day, when I joined him on a hunting expedition, I asked about the sounds he used to attract prey. Many of these calls mimic an animal in heat. Seduction becomes a powerful weapon, drawing in a potential victim and holding them captive in a moment of confusion, just long enough for the fatal blow. In the relentlessly cruel and dangerous jungle, any distraction can be deadly. And sexual distraction, when one expects the highest of pleasures, is also the moment of greatest vulnerability. To be horny in the jungle is to be overtaken by a passion that pulls you toward countless potential connections, each one promising to lure you away from yourself.
Consuming the dazzle and convenience of non-Indigenous goods leads to being consumed by the forest
The Andoque have a word for people and things that do exactly that: yoóka, or ‘diverters’. Yoóka is whoever and whatever pulls you away from yourself – distracting you from your survival, wellbeing and prosperity, and instead turning you into raw material for the forest’s relentless cycle of life and death. It’s also the word they use for harmful goods from the non-Indigenous world – alcohol that stirs brawls, machetes that fall on your foot, rifles involved in shooting accidents and, in bygone days, goods whose arrival also brought epidemics.
Yoóka stand in contrast with bɨ’iá, ‘working tools’, which contribute to people’s prosperity and wellbeing: the very same alcohol can be bɨ’iá if it brings people together; the machete when it helps you open paths in the forest; the rifle when a successful hunt enables you to feed your family; and foreign goods when they sustain rather than undermine life. As the gruesome story of the enchanted boat that lured away the Cacambra clan recounts, deviation by yoóka is where the dolphin merges with the fi’du; where consuming the dazzle and convenience of non-Indigenous goods leads to being consumed by the forest. Living in the unforgiving Amazon, you constantly ward off blood-sucking mosquitoes, carry a machete just to bathe safely lest a venomous snake crosses your path, and witness vines strangling trees whose rotting corpses nourish new growth. Every time you see a shaman or elder ‘healing’ meat through chants before giving it to a child or a woman giving birth, you are reminded of the vengeful intentions of the guardian spirits of animals. In this zero-sum game between humans and nonhumans, it is little wonder that forest dwellers who become ‘white’ expose themselves to the jungle’s predatory forces.
While the Andoque and other Amazonians may seem removed from the global economy, it’s clear that most have been deeply entangled in it long enough to grasp its essence. One of the truths they hold, embodied in the dolphin, is that the vital yet perilous force animating the jungle is also the lifeblood of the commodity economy in which we all live. This economy thrives on our sense of lack. We restlessly yearn to resemble others in their beauty, wit or taste – even, paradoxically, in their uniqueness and authenticity. Beyond the familiar notions that ‘sex sells’, and that we consume goods and services to amplify our attraction, lies a deeper principle articulated by the thinker René Girard: desire is never truly our own. It comes from the outside world, as we yearn for the objects or lifestyles desired or possessed by others. These inevitable dynamics of human sociality – crucial to how we learn, mature and form our sense of self – are amplified exponentially in consumer society, with the reach of social media multiplying our social universe.
Far away from the poor internet connection of the Amazon, I scroll daily through the carefully curated lives of seemingly happy and successful acquaintances, celebrities and influencers, their auras beaming into my eyes just like the dolphin scent tickled my nose along the Caquetá. Uplifting yet unsettling. Their desire infects my own.
For the Andoque, giving into the desire of the dolphin, or of the fi’du, leads to illness. It begins with a restless, gloomy anticipation – eyes wide, scanning for something thrilling, beautiful or exotic from the outside. This yearning pulls its victims away from home, from their very humanity, undermining their groundedness in the immediate world. Stripped of this anchoring, they become vulnerable to whatever snares are lurking in their surroundings. The dolphin’s seductive lure is a recipe, in the long run, for losing ourselves or being consumed.
The Andoque perspective had taken root in my mind, reshaping the world around me
My interest in power had, ironically, resolved itself in the negative: a deep recognition of my own weakness. For the Andoque, oral tradition is a form of protection. It is a body of knowledge that keeps people safe from the forest’s dangers. I have come to appreciate the weapons that Andoque generations have crafted to protect themselves from such pitfalls: tales and rituals, spells and observances. To abandon them is to remain unguarded. Yet I also understand all too well why they fail to take up these weapons as resolutely as they say they should.
The words in the recordings of mythology that my Andoque friends shared with me during long mambeadero sessions, which likely originated decades or even centuries ago, are spoken now with languid and defeated voices. Listening to them is like swimming in an ocean of unfathomable wisdom. But we are swimming against the current.
And all at once, I am gasping for air, drowning. Little did I know when I left the forest, that the Andoque perspective had taken root in my mind, reshaping the world around me, recasting even my own life in its terms.
I check my phone: it’s already time. I stop the recording, silence the voices from the mambeadero, open the dating app, and send a message that I’m on my way. Before I leave, I put on my cap – just in case – to cover the blowhole.
Further reading
The understandings of reality espoused by many Amazonian societies, where nonhumans are endowed with souls and subjectivities comparable with those of humans, have been described by Philippe Descola as ‘animism’. A compelling analysis of animism, alongside its comparison with modern Western ways of relating to nonhumans, can be found in his book Beyond Nature and Culture (2005/2013).
For more about dolphins, Candace Slater’s Dance of the Dolphin: Transformation and Disenchantment in the Amazonian Imagination (1994) remains the most sustained study of Amazonian dolphin folklore, particularly in the Brazilian Amazon.
Eduardo Viveiros de Castro discusses common Amazonian notions regarding dangerous encounters with spirits capable of transforming humans into beings like themselves in his article ‘Immanence and Fear: Stranger-events and Subjects in Amazonia’ (2012). In an animist world, where animals and spirits are understood to possess souls, humans risk becoming overwhelmed by the subjectivity of nonhuman beings and accepting their framing of reality, in which humans may appear merely as prey.
In another text by Viveiros de Castro, Cannibal Metaphysics: For a Post-Structural Anthropology (2014), he discusses a conception widespread in Indigenous Amazonia, though potentially counterintuitive to many readers, in which relations of marital alliance and predation are primary and given, while blood ties must be actively constructed.
Aparecida Vilaça elaborates on this idea in her article ‘Making Kin Out of Others in Amazonia’ (2002), showing how the Wari’ of Brazil actively fashion the bodies of newborn children through feeding practices and dietary restrictions, differentiating them from the worlds of animals and spirits from which they are thought to emerge.

San Francisco Bay Area dethroned as largest 'tech talent' market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

San Francisco Bay Area dethroned as largest tech talent market
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The San Francisco Bay Area, epicenter of the artificial intelligence boom, is home to a massive amount of tech workers employed by some of the world’s most valuable companies, from Apple to Nvidia.
But for the first time, New York has eclipsed the Bay Area as the home of the largest “tech talent workforce,” a report by real estate and investment firm CBRE shows. The firm has published the annual report for 13 years.
Last year, the New York Metro Area’s tech talent workforce reached 394,300, surpassing the Bay Area’s 375,730, according to the report. Fueled by mass layoffs, the Bay Area’s tech talent workforce dropped by 6% from 2022 to 2025. New York’s tech talent workforce, on the other hand, grew by more than 8% during that period.
Tech talent workers include highly skilled workers in more than 20 technology-oriented jobs, employed in industries such as healthcare, financial services, government and more, according to CBRE.
The growth of New York’s tech talent highlights how tech workers are spilling into other industries and cities as Silicon Valley companies lay off workers. Companies including Meta, Block and Amazon continue to cut workers as they focus more on AI investments.
Tech giants such as Meta and Coinbase continue to lay off employees, citing the way AI is reshaping how people work. Tech workers are navigating a crossroads in their careers and a brutal job market.
“The Bay Area is likely to remain ... the central location for the AI industry and for innovation. But as we’ve seen during past cycles, as it tends to grow, that spreads out to all the key markets,” Colin Yasukochi, executive director of CBRE’s Tech Insights Center, said during a news conference Tuesday.
New York has gained tech workers in the financial services sector, which was an early adopter of artificial intelligence, said Lauren Crowley Corrinet, vice chairman of CBRE’s Consulting Group in New York. Meanwhile, AI startups have popped up in the Midtown South neighborhood and other areas.
New York has a transit-rich environment, making it an attractive place for companies to purchase new office space and workers to live in.
“The size of the market, just the sheer scale of it, really does support both the early stage growth, but also that ability to just scale fast,” she said.
In California, some cities grew their tech talent workforce. Sacramento’s tech talent workforce grew more than 8% from 2022 to 2025, reaching 42,970.
Los Angeles and Orange County’s tech workforce totaled 227,350 last year, up by less than 1% compared to 2022. Toronto, Washington, D.C. and Dallas-Forth Worth all had more tech talent.
CBRE looked at other factors beyond the size of a metro area’s tech talent workforce, such as average salary, rental prices and tech graduates, to rank the markets on a scorecard. The Bay Area still is at the top while New York is fourth. Los Angeles is ranked No. 18.
The drop in tech talent in the Bay Area comes as workers grow more worried that AI could lead to fewer jobs.
Roughly 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the United States over the next two decades, up from 64% in 2024, according to a survey released by the Pew Research Center on Tuesday.
While tech executives such as Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg have an optimistic outlook on the future of AI, they’ve also acknowledged that company sizes could shrink. But AI also could create new jobs.
The U.S. high-tech industry still is filling AI-related roles including data scientists and hardware engineers, according to CBRE. It remains to be seen whether hiring will outpace cuts, though CBRE executives also appeared optimistic.
“My expectation is that these jobs are going to continue to grow as companies, not only tech companies, start to figure out how they’re going to implement AI into their businesses,” Yasukochi said.

Latvian parliament gives “green light” to possible state involvement in airBaltic rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The Latvian parliament on Thursday gave its preliminary approval to possible state participation in the financial stabilisation of national airline airBaltic, including the potential purchase of up to thirty million euros in bridge-financing bonds and the conversion of fifty million euros in existing bonds into equity.
The bill has been designated as urgent.
The legislation would authorise the government to potentially participate in the purchase of up to thirty million euros in airBaltic bridge-financing bonds alongside private investors and on identical terms. The Cabinet of Ministers would be able to make a separate decision on purchasing the bonds if necessary.
The plan also provides for converting claims arising from a state loan and bonds already held by the state into the airline’s share capital. This means that fifty million euros in state-owned bonds and more than eighteen million euros remaining under the state loan could be converted into airBaltic shares.
The repayment deadline for the thirty-million-euro state loan is also expected to be extended from the end of August until the end of this year. By July 24, airBaltic had repaid a total of 12.9 million euros in principal and contractual interest payments on the state loan.
This week, airBaltic bondholders approved the capitalisation of the next two bond interest payments, as well as several other measures giving the airline additional flexibility in implementing its revised business plan.
Bondholders approved adding the interest payments due on August 14 and November 14 this year to the principal amount of the bonds instead of paying them in cash. They also approved a temporary waiver of minimum liquidity requirements until November 2026.
Meanwhile, airBaltic’s planned raising of 225 million euros in bridge financing was not considered at the bondholders’ meeting on Monday, August 17, because the issue was not included on the agenda.
The purpose of the bill is to establish measures for airBaltic’s financial stabilisation and ensure effective management of the state’s financial interests during the process. It would allow the state, as a shareholder, creditor and bondholder, to act in a timely and coordinated manner and on an equal footing with the airline’s other shareholders, bondholders and creditors.
One or more of the measures set out in the bill could be implemented to stabilise airBaltic’s finances. Decisions on individual measures would be taken by the Cabinet of Ministers, which would determine their scope, implementation conditions and other relevant terms.
Among the measures envisaged is an amendment to the agreement covering the thirty-million-euro state loan to the airline, extending the deadline for repayment of the outstanding principal, accrued interest and other obligations arising from the agreement.
The bill also provides for the full or partial conversion into equity of any claims arising from the thirty-million-euro state loan granted to airBaltic.
Another possible measure would allow claims arising from airBaltic bonds held by the state to be capitalised, converted or otherwise restructured up to the actual outstanding principal amount of those bonds, but not exceeding fifty million euros, plus the relevant accrued interest and other claims arising from the bonds.
The bill also states that the state could participate in providing bridge financing to airBaltic by purchasing up to thirty million euros in newly issued airBaltic bonds.
The newly issued bonds would be purchased in accordance with the bond issue documentation, including the prospectus and instructions from the issue arrangers. The Ministry of Transport would be responsible for preparing financial, legal, fiscal and state-aid assessments, as well as the terms of the bridge-financing transaction.
The Cabinet of Ministers would be required to report to the Saeima Budget and Finance Committee on the implementation of the financial stabilisation measures at least once every quarter.
As previously reported, airBaltic’s Supervisory Board has approved a business plan that includes raising 225 million euros in interim financing to improve liquidity, using the existing collateral package securing its 2029 senior bonds.
In the longer term, the plan envisages recapitalising the company through up to 225 million euros in new debt and 100 million euros in new equity. Part of the existing 2029 bonds would be converted into shares in the company, while the remainder would be replaced with new, smaller debt of up to 125 million euros.
The business plan also envisages airBaltic operating 36 Airbus A220-300 aircraft by the end of 2026, compared with 54 aircraft currently, with the fleet gradually increasing to around 40 aircraft by 2031.
The airBaltic Group generated revenue of 779.344 million euros last year, an increase of 4.2% compared with 2024. The group posted a loss of 44.337 million euros, which was 2.7 times lower than in 2024. In 2025, the airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers, an increase of 1% compared with 2024.
German flag carrier Lufthansa became an airBaltic shareholder last summer. The Latvian state currently owns 88.37% of airBaltic, Lufthansa holds 10%, Danish businessman Lars Thuesen’s Aircraft Leasing 1 owns 1.62%, and other shareholders hold the remaining 0.01%. The company’s share capital stands at 41.819 million euros.
In light of its 2025 financial results and current market conditions, airBaltic has suspended its potential initial public offering and does not currently consider an IPO a potential source of capital in 2026, according to the airline’s annual report.

Nearly 40,000 take shelter in Kyiv metro stations overnight
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
12:54:28 EEST
18:54:28 KST

Over 38,000 people, including more than 2,000 children, took shelter in Kyiv metro stations on the night leading into August 20, the press service of Kyiv City State Administration reported, citing Kyiv Metro utility company.
"On the night leading into August 20, during another massive shelling of the capital, over 38,000 people, including more than 2,000 children, were at Kyiv metro stations. Last night, the air raid alert lasted nearly 9 hours," Kyiv Metro reported, according to the administration’s website.
It is noted that 46 underground stations of the Kyiv metro operate around the clock as shelters during air raid alerts. All lobbies are opened for entry to make the route to safety as short as possible. Metro employees, together with police, ensure prompt and unhindered access to the stations.
The enterprise reminds that if there is a need to use the metro as a shelter in advance, people should arrive at the station before it finishes passenger transport operations. Operating schedules are posted at every station. Where possible, it is recommended to choose central stations, which typically offer more space to accommodate people.
Visitors are requested to bring only essential items and avoid using bulky items, particularly mattresses and tents. These occupy a significant portion of space needed by others during enemy shelling.
The enterprise also emphasizes the need to avoid sitting on escalators or leaving belongings on them. In the event of an emergency or the need for urgent evacuation, escalators must be brought into operation quickly. The presence of people or oversized items on them can slow down this process.
As reported, during the overnight attack on July 30, over 56,000 people took shelter in the metro system, and on July 2, 52,500 residents used it, including nearly 4,500 children.

On Syria, Yaalon argued that Israel had missed an opportunity following blows to Hezbollah and the Iranian presence.

On Lebanon, Yaalon claimed Trump was seeking to impose an arrangement on Netanyahu that "could be good for Israel," but that the Israeli premier was evading it.
On Iran, Yaalon claimed Netanyahu had sought to change the government to achieve a success that would make up for what he described as the premier's failures.
He described the outcome as a "farce" and claimed it had resulted in a crisis with Trump.
Yaalon further accused Netanyahu of trying to inflame tensions in the occupied West Bank through people he described as "pogromists," whom he accused of receiving support and encouragement from Israeli government ministers.
He said Netanyahu was disregarding what he called a "red card" from US Ambassador Mike Huckabee and claimed attacks were continuing.
Yaalon argued that the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem offered Netanyahu the best opportunity to ignite another war.
He called on Israeli opposition leaders to focus their efforts on removing Netanyahu from power to save the lives of civilians and soldiers and "prevent destruction."

Gangs suspected of stealing fire station equipment for ram-raids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
09:53:24 UTC
18:53:24 KST

Gangs suspected of stealing fire station equipment for ram-raids
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
More than 60 fire stations have been targeted in the last year by criminal gangs who steal hydraulic equipment to use in ram raids.
One fire station in Sassenheim, near Leiden in Zuid-Holland, was attacked three nights in a row in the last week, while 10 sites have been broken into across the country in the last fortnight.
Police told NRC the thieves were looking for equipment such as cutting gear and hydraulic jacks used to free people who are trapped beneath rubble.
The machines can be repurposed to break heavily fortified windows used by shops such as jewellers and electrical retailers. Last week thieves left behind a hydraulic spreader that they used to try to smash the window of a jewellery store in Den Bosch.
The number of break-ins has jumped in the last year, with just 18 thefts from fire stations recorded in 2025 and 17 the year before.
“We are trying to strengthen our response teams and making detecting these crimes a national priority,” police spokesman Dick Goijert said.
Safety boards would not say exactly what was taken in the most recent raids because the police investigation is ongoing and to avoid giving “unnecessary information to people with bad intentions”.
Accessibility issues
Fire station managers have tried to improve security, but locking away life-saving equipment means it takes longer to retrieve it in an emergency, when a few lost seconds can make the difference between life and death.
Evert Jansen, a former burglar who now works for the police to raise companies’ awareness of the need to improve security, said he suspected organised criminals were behind the thefts.
“Unless they know how the equipment works it’s difficult for them to use it,” Jansen told NRC. “Maybe the burglars are stealing it on the orders of experienced criminals.”

'RSS believes it knows the truth for everyone': Rahul Gandhi attacks Sangh over ideology

'RSS believes it knows the truth for everyone': Rahul Gandhi attacks Sangh over ideology
Edited by: Rajeev Singh / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 20, 2026, 15:44 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Rahul Gandhi drew a distinction between the RSS's worldview and Mahatma Gandhi's idea of 'Swaraj.
NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition (LoP) Rahul Gandhi Thursday accused the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) of trying to impose its idea of truth on people across India, arguing that every individual must have the freedom to find and define their own truth.Speaking at the "Hara Bhara Swaraj: A Tribute to Rajiv Gandhi's Vision" programme in New Delhi, the Gandhi Scion described the ideological contest in India as a deeper struggle over how people understand themselves, freedom and their place in society.
The Congress leader also drew a distinction between the RSS's worldview and Mahatma Gandhi's idea of 'Swaraj', saying no organisation or individual could claim to know what is true for another person."What Gandhiji was saying was that every living being is a unique entity with their own path towards the truth. I cannot tell you what your truth is. Today, the ideological battle in India is precisely that. It is not fundamentally about environment, politics, or free media--those are symptoms. The real fight is that a small group of people have decided, because they control the system, that they know the truth of everyone in this country.
That is my problem with the RSS: the RSS has decided that they know the truth of 1.5 billion people. And I say, no. Only 1.5 billion people can know their own truth," Rahul Gandhi asserted.He said even he could not claim to understand another person's truth because people's experiences, families and circumstances are different."And I say, no. Only 1.5 billion people can know their own truth. Even I cannot do that. If I begin to believe that I know your truth, I would be a madman. Because I am not you. I haven't faced what you've faced; I haven't seen what you've seen; I haven't dealt with what you've dealt with. I don't have the same parents, the same friends, or the same life. So how can I say that I know your truth?" he added.
‘My Experiments with Truth’ reflects individual journeys
Rahul Gandhi then referred to Mahatma Gandhi's autobiography, 'My Experiments with Truth', saying its title itself reflected the idea that truth is something each person explores through their own life."Please notice, Gandhiji's book was not called 'The Truth' or 'My Understanding of the Truth'. It was titled 'My Experiments with Truth'. I have experiments with my truth; you have experiments with your truth."
Rahul targets BJP-RSS over 'exclusion'
The Congress leader also criticised the BJP and RSS over what he described as the exclusion of sections of Indian society. He said people from different religious and social communities must feel that they have an equal place in the country."Imagine what the BJP and RSS have done. Imagine if I walked into this room and told 15-17 per cent of you--Muslims, Christians, Sikhs--'You do not exist, and if you speak up, see what happens to you.' Then telling 10 per cent Adivasis, 'We will take your land whenever we want, and if you resist, we will shoot you,' and Dalits, 'You are complaining for nothing; everything is fine with the caste system.' That is what is being done to our motherland. Every single person in this country--regardless of religion, community, or gender--must feel: 'I belong here. I can walk freely in this country. I am loved, respected, and appreciated here, and my search for truth matters to the nation,'" he said.
'Gandhi’s Swaraj is more than freedom'
Rahul Gandhi also explained why he believes 'Swaraj' should not simply be understood as the same thing as freedom or liberty in the Western sense.He used US President Donald Trump and Mahatma Gandhi to illustrate the difference, arguing that being legally free does not necessarily mean having control over one's own actions and desires."'Swaraj' is often confused with the Western word 'freedom.' People think that Swaraj means freedom; that it means liberty or independence. No--Swaraj means rule over oneself (Swa par raj / self-governance). If you go to America and ask, 'Is Trump a free man?', everyone will say, 'Absolutely.' But if you ask, 'Does Trump rule over himself?', the clear answer is, 'No, he does not.' Whereas Gandhiji in a prison 80 years ago would say, 'I am not free, but I rule over myself. It is Swaraj,'" he explained.The Congress leader said this understanding of Swaraj makes it a personal responsibility rather than something that can simply be granted by a government or another person."Swaraj is an Indian concept, and it carries deep responsibility. It is a way of thinking, and it is an individual project. I cannot give you Swaraj. Whatever I do... in a Western sense, I can grant you freedom by saying, 'You are not in prison; I have given you freedom.'
But I cannot give you Swaraj. Because Swaraj is your personal relationship with the universe. Swaraj is an individual path. And Gandhiji's conception of Swaraj was that every single person in this country should walk on this path."His remarks placed the idea of individual self-rule at the centre of his criticism of the RSS, while presenting Gandhi's philosophy of Swaraj as one based on personal responsibility and the freedom of each individual to pursue their own understanding of truth.
Rajeev Singh is a Digital Content Producer with The Times of India. He covers politics, policies, defence, and conflicts for readers curious to know their implications. He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

Taiwan to roll out NT$3.33 billion tourism subsidies in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
09:51:34 UTC
18:51:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Tourism Administration will launch an NT$3.33 billion (US$104 million) tourism promotion package Sept. 1, featuring accommodation subsidies, birthday vouchers, and incentives aimed at attracting both domestic and international travelers.
The domestic program includes five categories: weekday accommodation discounts, birthday accommodation vouchers, amusement park stay incentives, corporate employee travel incentives, and Taiwan PASS discounts, per UDN.
The international component includes four measures, including rewards for repeat visitors, support for MICE (meetings, incentives, conferences, and exhibitions) travel, additional incentives for group tours, and support for international flagship concerts.
Domestic travel incentives
Online registration for weekday accommodation and birthday vouchers begins Thursday, according to the Tourism Administration. The weekday accommodation program runs from Sept. 1 to Nov. 30. Weekdays are defined as Sunday through Thursday, excluding national holidays and consecutive holidays.
Travelers staying at participating legal accommodations can receive subsidies for up to two consecutive nights. In general areas, the maximum subsidy is NT$800 for the first night and NT$1,200 for the second night. On outlying islands, the maximum subsidy is NT$1,000 for the first night and NT$1,500 for the second night. The two nights may be spent at different accommodations or in different areas, but the stays must be on consecutive dates.
Completing the online registration only records an applicant's information and does not guarantee a subsidy. Travelers must present either their national identification card or National Health Insurance card at check-in so accommodation operators can verify their identity, per UDN.
The birthday voucher program runs from Sept. 10 to Dec. 31. Each month, 1,000 people celebrating their birthdays will be randomly selected to receive NT$1,200 in accommodation credit. Birthday vouchers can be combined with weekday accommodation subsidies.
The amusement park overnight stay program runs from Sept. 1 to Nov. 30. After registering, customers will receive amusement park points based on the amount of their accommodation discount. The points can be exchanged for admission tickets and related merchandise.
The Taiwan PASS double-savings program runs from Sept. 1 to Dec. 31. Travelers purchasing the Taiwan PASS Taiwan Railway Edition for NT$2,500 can choose between a 50% discount on the pass, saving NT$1,250, or an NT$1,500 weekday accommodation voucher. The accommodation voucher can be combined with weekday accommodation and birthday vouchers.
The corporate employee domestic travel incentive program runs from Sept. 1 to Dec. 15. Companies organizing two-day, one-night employee trips can receive NT$20,000 per group, with a maximum application limit of NT$60,000.
Incentives for international visitors
A special program designed to attract repeat international visitors will run from Oct. 10 through March 31, 2027. It applies to foreign travelers who have previously entered Taiwan since Jan. 1, 2023.
Individual repeat visitors will have a chance to receive NT$5,000 in prepaid credit. Those traveling with companions can receive up to NT$8,000, consisting of NT$5,000 for the repeat visitor and NT$3,000 for accompanying family members or friends.
For international group tours, groups of at least four people in which repeat visitors account for at least 10% of participants will be eligible for subsidies ranging from NT$10,000 to NT$30,000 per group, per UDN.
The program also targets overseas companies organizing incentive trips to Taiwan. In addition to existing subsidies, an additional NT$1,000 per person per night will be provided when travelers stay at legal accommodations south of Taichung, in Hualien or Taitung, or on outlying islands.
The additional subsidy is capped at NT$4,000 per trip. Applications must generally be submitted at least 15 days before arrival, or earlier when the application date falls before a national holiday. The incentive program for international travelers attending conferences and exhibitions in Taiwan will run from Sept. 1 through March 31, 2027.
Eligible visitors can receive a free half-day or full-day Taiwan sightseeing bus tour and a Taiwan PASS High-Speed Rail Edition. The Tourism Administration encouraged travelers to plan ahead and check participating accommodations, booking platforms, and available discounts before making reservations. A list of participating accommodations and booking platforms is available at TaiwanStay.
The Tourism Administration said each national ID number can be used only once in the weekday accommodation and birthday voucher programs. Only one incentive from each program can be used per room per night. For example, if two eligible travelers share a room, only one weekday accommodation subsidy and one birthday voucher can be redeemed for that room on a given night.
Consumers who believe a business has inflated room rates can submit evidence to their local municipal or county government. If the allegations are confirmed, the business may be removed from the program and lose its eligibility to participate.
