Deadly overnight storms batter Germany as Balkan countries fight wildfires
BERLIN (AP) — A woman died and at least two other people were injured as severe storms caused extensive damage overnight across parts of Germany. Further southeast, in the Balkans, firefighters continued to battle wildfires that have been raging across Europe all summer.
In Waldorf, in the southwestern state of Rhineland-Palatinate, a woman was struck by a falling tree and fatally injured, the German news agency dpa reported Thursday. Another woman suffered serious injuries in the accident, police said.
The women, 58 and 47, were walking together when a storm rolled in and they sought shelter under a covered seating area. Both women were struck when a tree was uprooted and fell onto the seating area. The 58-year-old died at the scene, a police spokesperson said. The 47-year-old was taken to a hospital.
A tornado struck the town of Fürstenwalde, 78 kilometers (49 miles) southeast of Berlin. Roofs were torn off and several cars were damaged by falling trees, and one person was injured, according to dpa.
In Höhr-Grenzhausen in the Westerwald district in western Germany, a storm tore walls from buildings. At least two homes were affected, according to dpa. Falling pieces of building facades and flying debris caused additional damage, and several trees were uprooted. A widespread power outage also hit the area, while strong gusts of wind overturned a truck on the A61 highway.
There were also numerous weather-related emergency calls overnight in Hesse, Thuringia and Bavaria.
A village festival in Kronach, Bavaria, was partially evacuated due to severe storms. About 3,500 guests had to leave the outdoor area of the festival grounds late Wednesday evening, local police said. They were able to continue celebrating inside the beer halls.
In Wetzlar, in Hesse, the storm damaged about 60 houses, according to the fire department. In some cases, pieces of roofing were blown as far as 100 meters (110 yards) away, dpa reported.
The German Weather Service warned that further severe storms could occur later in the day, particularly in Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria in southern Germany.
While the storms in Germany were accompanied by cooler temperatures, high temperatures continued to be recorded in southeastern Europe, and fires raged in some parts of the region.
Firefighters are battling wildfires in the Balkans
In Serbia, a Russian firefighting plane joined efforts in Serbia on Thursday to fight wildfires that devastated a nature reserve in the northeast as the Balkan country faces a fresh heat wave in the coming days.
The Il-76 plane landed in Serbia on Wednesday evening, also illustrating continued friendly relations between the two countries despite Belgrade’s proclaimed intention to join the European Union.
The fire in Deliblatska Pescara, or Deliblato Sands, first erupted a month ago, but was under control until early August when it started spreading swiftly, engulfing thousands of acres of pine forests and shrubbery.
Several other big fires also have been raging in other parts of the country, as well as throughout the region in the past weeks. An extremely hot and dry summer this year has fueled wildfires throughout Europe, from Belgium to Greece.
Croatian firefighters from the popular tourism hot spot of Dubrovnik on Thursday joined a struggle to contain a fire across the border in Bosnia to prevent it from spreading toward the medieval walled city that is a UNESCO protected heritage site.
“It was a hard night,” regional firefighting unit commander Stjepan Simović told the Hina news agency. “The fire is huge and in an inaccessible terrain, so we have to be vigilant.”

U.S. Air Force seeks proposals for Relentless Wolfpack weapons program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
08:52:45 UTC
17:52:45 KST

- The Air Force Research Laboratory opened proposals for Relentless Wolfpack, seeking weapons from different vendors that can coordinate against targets together.
- AFRL expects two to eight Other Transaction awards, with proposals due October 2 and work funded across fiscal years 2027 and 2028.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has opened a solicitation for Relentless Wolfpack, a program intended to demonstrate that weapons from different vendors can coordinate against targets in contested airspace, according to a call published under the PACER Broad Agency Announcement.
The call, issued by AFRL’s Air Warfare Directorate at Eglin Air Force Base, seeks proposals covering autonomy, swarming behavior and interoperability among what the lab calls an “affordable mass cruise missile.” AFRL said the program will demonstrate that multiple weapons from different vendors can work together to synergize effects and neutralize targets in a contested battlespace.
The Air Force expects to make two to eight awards through an Other Transaction agreement for prototype work, with the possibility of follow-on production contracts or agreements. Performers must request the full proposal package by August 26 to remain eligible, and completed proposals are due October 2. AFRL said it anticipates awarding contracts by December 10, with work incrementally funded across fiscal years 2027 and 2028.
The period of performance for the Other Transaction agreement is set at 20 months: 18 months of technical work followed by a two-month final reporting period. AFRL said no funding is currently available for the effort and will not reimburse companies for proposal preparation costs.
Proposals must demonstrate compliance with the Open Systems Architecture standard known as WOSA v3.8 and alignment with what AFRL calls M-Series requirements. Companies that have not achieved WOSA v3.8 compliance by the time of award must present a plan to do so within three months, and AFRL said failure to meet that standard within the window will be cause for dismissal from the project.
The solicitation places heavy emphasis on autonomy. Performers must describe whether their proposed swarm is homogeneous or heterogeneous, list previously demonstrated behaviors such as formation keeping, weapon-target assignment and coordinated time on target, and specify how those behaviors were demonstrated, whether through digital simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing or live cruise missile testing. AFRL also asked companies to address a scenario involving four homogeneous systems working together, followed by a heterogeneous swarm of four to six systems built by four to six different providers.
Performers with existing capability must supply a detailed technical description rather than citing a program name alone, according to the call. AFRL said proposals built primarily on general compliance statements or unsupported claims will be considered inadequate.
Technical merit carries more weight in AFRL’s evaluation than cost, with four subfactors weighted equally: the novelty of the proposed approach, the performer’s understanding of the technical scope, the soundness of the technical approach including risk mitigation, and the potential to transition results into future government programs.
Government-furnished property will be limited to radios provided to individual performers, according to the call. AFRL said it will not provide base support, network access, or additional government-furnished information or software.
The current call follows two earlier public postings on the Relentless Wolfpack effort: a request for information published April 1 and a Grand Challenge special notice published July 13. AFRL did not disclose the total program budget or the value of individual awards expected under this call.

Riigikogu speaker: Freedom should never be taken for granted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20

Riigikogu speaker: Freedom should never be taken for granted
Estonian-ness becomes visible when a person takes conscious responsibility for what belongs to them, Riigikogu Speaker Lauri Hussar (Eesti 200) said in a speech marking the 35th anniversary of Estonia's restoration of independence.
Hussar made his remarks at the flag‑raising ceremony on Toompea on Thursday, August 20, reflecting on the events of 1991 and drawing parallels with Ukraine's current fight for freedom. The speech follows.
Today exactly 35 years ago our national flag was not raised on Tall Hermann Tower in a safe and secure world but in Soviet-occupied Estonia. We remember well those unbearably anxious times when we all feared deep down in our hearts that the disintegrating empire would strike back in one last desperate attempt.
Back then, 35 years ago, members of the Defense League and Home Defense Guard, cadets from police schools, and volunteers had gathered here to defend Toompea, Pikk Hermann, and our flag. Exactly the same way thousands of people gathered across Estonia to defend our budding freedom.
That worry and fear in our hearts is also well familiar to us today when Ukraine is fighting the exhausting war of liberation against the same merciless Russian empire. And this fight is a clear reminder for us all that freedom is not to be taken for granted.
Since February 1989, our national flag was raised in this tower exactly 907 times still under the rule of the empire. Until that day in August when the flag was raised in a free Estonia that had just restored its independence. This was possible because we believed in our freedom, we were brave, and we worked together. Our biggest shield was our indelible faith in our independence, mother tongue, culture, and symbols.
One of the greatest luminaries of our era, reverend Toomas Paul, has put it well: 'We cannot separate ourselves from our era, our people, our kit and kin... I am linked to other people in a thousand ways.'
These words link us all to those who stood up for Estonia, but also those who made decisions for Estonia and in the name of independence, as well as to those who are defending freedom in Europe today.
The Estonian spirit is not just an emotion or a passive feeling of 'being Estonian'. It becomes visible when someone consciously takes responsibility for what belongs to them. Today, this means responsibility to safeguard our freedom and country, language and culture; support those who fight for their survival and freedom, and make sure that the flag in this tower would never again be submitted to a foreign rule. And today is the day when our national flag has been flying on this tower, in free Estonia, for 12,783 days — and this counter will never stop again.
Let us stay united and treasure one another; and most of all—let us have faith in Estonia.
I wish you all an excellent Day of the Restoration of Independence! Long live Estonia!

Prime minister: As a nation, we are now wealthier than ever before
Estonia is free, secure and rapidly developing, Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) said on Thursday, marking the 35th anniversary of the restoration of independence.
Michal made the speech which follows at the flag‑raising ceremony on Toompea on the morning of August 20, reflecting on Estonia's journey from occupation to a respected nation and highlighting the country's economic and social progress over three and a half decades.
Thirty-five years ago we managed to throw off the shackles of occupation all together. At that moment, we had little to lean on. We did not know whether the freedom would last. But we had a strong will and a clear sight—the ambition to live in freedom, decide our own future, and build Estonia into a better place for all of us.
We turned our gaze in awe to the free world. The world where we so ardently wished to return to. To freedom, rule of law, and human dignity — the world where people can shape their own lives and futures.
But today we can raise our eyes and see that the world is looking at Estonia with respect. We are seen as a country that also shows the way for others. Estonia is considered one of the best places to live in this world. Our economic freedom and freedom of speech, smart ideas, respect for human rights, pure nature, and nurturing attitude towards the environment are constantly highlighted.
With three decades, Estonia's GDP has increased 15-fold and wages 60 times. Our life expectancy has been extended by more than 12 years — this is the biggest rise among the European nations. We are high up in the global ranking of countries with a very high level of human development. Our economy has grown on 14 years out of the last 17. Over the last two years, our economy has been growing again, as the most recent figures show.
As a nation, we are richer today than ever before. We have reason to be proud of our country and of how far we have come. We have reason to be hopeful about the future. Estonia is free, protected, and developing fast.
All this is based on the will and determination of the Estonian people. Our ability to build our home and our country. Our courage to make decisions that look beyond today or tomorrow, decisions that look decades into the future.
We have not walked this path alone. We have had good friends — and we cherish them. But at a crucial moment, 35 years ago, it was the people of Iceland who took the first step to support us.
Iceland's brave decision to recognize Estonia, which had only very recently restored its independence, was followed by other countries. I am sincerely happy to see the President of Iceland Halla Tómasdóttir among us today. The courage to be the first counts at historical moments. Estonia remembers it with gratitude.
Our goal must be that the Estonian flag is raised every day, forever, on top of Pikk Hermann Tower. We cannot stop working for this end. Freedom does not stay on its own. A country can never be fully completed.
The world is unpredictable, but our focus is clear. We know what we are protecting, treasuring, and where we want to end up. Our strength is a united, wise, and brave Estonian nation.
We need to take care of Estonia. We need to continue building Estonia. We need to make sure Estonia stays free. Long live free Estonia!

17:49:51 KST

The Ukrainian company TAF Industries and the Danish Upteko have signed a memorandum that establishes a strategic framework for industrial cooperation between the two enterprises, focused on the development and production of drones.
The company announced this in a press release.
The agreement was signed on the sidelines of DALO Industry Days, Scandinavia’s largest defense exhibition, which is taking place in Denmark.
TAF Industries was represented at the ceremony by the company’s CEO, Volodymyr Zinovskyi. Upteko’s founder, Benjamin Meinertz, signed the document on behalf of the company.
The event was also attended by Chief of Defence of Denmark General Michael Wiggers Hyldgaard, Lieutenant General Per Pugholm Olsen, head of the Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation (DALO), as well as representatives of Denmark’s defense industry and international partners.
Under the agreement, the parties intend to expand their production capacity for FPV drones, jointly develop relevant technologies, and diversify their supply chains.
This should make them less dependent on individual suppliers and increase the overall production resilience.
Starting in early 2027, the joint production is expected to enable the manufacture of thousands of drones each month. The project will be implemented as part of the Ukrainian-Danish Build with Ukraine initiative.
“The Kingdom of Denmark is a reliable partner and one of Ukraine’s strongest allies in countering Russian aggression. Today’s agreement is yet another strategic step that will help further deepen cooperation both between our companies and between Ukraine and Denmark,” said Volodymyr Zinovskyi, CEO of TAF Industries.
Upteko is a Danish technology company founded in 2018 that develops unmanned solutions for the maritime and industrial sectors. Its activities include developing comprehensive drone systems using technologies in the fields of UAVs, electronics, software, and hardware development.
The company collaborates with representatives from industry, government agencies, and the maritime sector to develop technological solutions tailored to the needs of specific clients.
Upteko’s work focuses on innovation, engineering excellence, flexibility, and close cooperation with partners and customers.

Russia and Ukraine are sending assault groups deep behind enemy lines, blurring the front line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
08:49:13 UTC
17:49:13 KST

Russia and Ukraine are sending assault groups deep behind enemy lines, blurring the front line
The nature of the war has changed once again. Not only in the rear, where the intensity of mutual strikes has increased and warehouses belonging to online marketplaces and other businesses have often become targets. There have also been changes at the front, in tactics. Traditional infiltration by small groups has reached a new level. Now assault units try to slip through undetected not for hundreds of meters, but for kilometers. Sometimes the depth of these raids exceeds 10 kilometers. The idea is that such groups do not require large amounts of supplies and can therefore operate cut off from the main forces. The raids destabilize the enemy’s defenses and can also be dangerous for its drone operators. This has created a new picture at the front: in many sectors, the battle formations of the two armies have become intermixed; control over roads and towns is often unstable; villages change hands several times a week.
Kramatorsk agglomeration
- Russian forces are pressing their offensive on Kramatorsk and Sloviansk from several directions. Having captured most of Kostiantynivka — where video-documented resistance from Ukrainian troops has all but disappeared, suggesting most remaining Ukrainian forces there have withdrawn or been killed — Russian units are now trying to launch an assault on the next settlement along the road to Kramatorsk, the village of Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka. Fighting continues on the village’s southern outskirts, but Russian forces have failed to significantly improve their position there over the past two weeks. The main Russian force in the area is likely still busy clearing Kostiantynivka and nearby villages.
- East of Kostiantynivka, Russian forces have opened a path into the rear of Ukrainian troops that have held positions near Chasiv Yar for years, forcing a Ukrainian retreat in this sector along the Siverskyi Donets–Donbas Canal.
- Farther north along the canal, Russian forces are trying to expand a foothold just outside Kramatorsk, where assault units advanced several kilometers in quick succession and captured Vasyutynske, 5 to 7 kilometers (3 to 4 miles) from the city. Progress in this sector has slowed in recent weeks, since Ukrainian positions remain “intermixed” with Russian ones along the canal’s banks.
- Northwest of Kostiantynivka, Russian troops continue advancing along the Kazenyi Torets River toward Druzhkivka, pushing into the rear of the Ukrainian group defending the Kostiantynivka area. In recent weeks, they have captured Krasnyi Kut and reached Raiske, just 3 to 5 kilometers (2 to 3 miles) from Druzhkivka’s southwestern outskirts.
- Farther west, a Russian group fighting its way toward Dobropillia — the largest settlement in northwestern Donetsk region — has spent months battling to capture villages and towns on the city’s southern approaches, including Shevchenko, Chernihivske, and Krasnopodillia. That raises the threat that an assault on Dobropillia itself could begin soon. Russia’s Defense Ministry claims such an assault is already underway, carried out by troops it says infiltrated from the direction of Novyi Donbas, but that claim remains unconfirmed.
Where the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Dnipro regions meet
- Along the front stretching from Orikhiv, in central Zaporizhzhia region, to the point where the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Dnipro regions meet — where Ukrainian and Russian offensives are underway simultaneously — the trend toward deep raids is especially pronounced. The terrain helps explain why: steppe broken up by tree lines, rivers, ravines, and small, scattered settlements. In places, the fighting resembles maneuver warfare, with small groups of troops moving by vehicle and trying to “catch” similarly small enemy units, though more often assault troops move on foot through the steppe and tree lines.
- Drones are the main defense against these raids in areas thinly held by infantry. Fragmentary reports suggest drone operators themselves have sometimes become targets of enemy assault troops who infiltrated the area.
- Adding to the confusion, commanders on both sides are trying to demonstrate superiority through so-called “flag-planting” campaigns, ordering assault troops to prove their presence in various settlements by literally planting a flag there.
- Two large such campaigns played out on August 12 and 13. Ukrainian forces first raised flags in several villages across two sectors: in the Russian rear along the Haichur River (Rybne, Krasnohirske, Zlahoda, and Pryvilne), and farther east, where Ukrainian troops are trying to break through at the junction of the Russian Tsentr and Vostok groups in the Mokri Yaly valley (Yalta, Novokhatske, Tolstoi, Zelenyi Hai, and Piddubne). A day later, Russian forces raised their own flags in most of the same villages — sometimes no more than 100 meters (330 feet) from where the Ukrainian flags had gone up.
- The two sides’ explanations for the incidents naturally diverge, generally boiling down to accusations that the enemy published old footage, generated it with AI, or sent soldiers on one-way suicide missions purely for political effect. Russia’s version has an inherent advantage, since videos of Russian flags surfaced later — disproving it would require assuming Russian commanders knew in advance where Ukrainian forces planned to “plant their flags” and had prepared rebuttals ahead of time. Either way, it is currently impossible to reliably determine who controls specific settlements.
- The Ukrainian offensives on the northern flank, in the Haichur and Mokri Yaly valleys, were aimed at slowing the Russian advance eastward from Huliaipole toward Orikhiv — and largely succeeded. The main forces of the Russian Vostok group stalled for several months on their approach to Orikhiv, forcing Russian commanders to send reserves to counter Ukrainian brigades advancing from the north. Now the Russian advance has resumed thanks to a new tactic: assault units from the area of Vozdvyzhenka, a village that has changed hands several times, slipped through the steppe to reach the T0480 highway leading north from Orikhiv, near Liubytske and Novosoloshyne.
- At the same time, forces from Russia’s 58th Combined Arms Army, part of the Dnepr group, took advantage of the Vostok group’s advance to step up their own offensive on Orikhiv from the south. Russian assault units broke through what had once been an impenetrable Ukrainian defense at Novodanylivka, reached the southern outskirts of Orikhiv, and seized a stretch of the Orikhiv–Mala Tokmachka road.
- Russian wa bloggers reported that Russian forces had once again captured Mala Tokmachka — a town that has become something of a running joke — but it remains unconfirmed.
Kharkiv region
- Russian forces opened several new incursions of varying size along the entire Russia–Kharkiv region border in 2025 and 2026, but the two main fronts remain the older, interconnected footholds near Vovchansk and Kupiansk. Russian commanders had planned as early as 2024 to capture both district centers and push deeper into Kharkiv region toward Velykyi Burluk and Izyum, with the ultimate goal of cutting off the Ukrainian-controlled part of Donbas from the rest of the region.
- The Russian army did not capture the ruins of Vovchansk until early 2026 and still has not fully occupied Kupiansk. Ukrainian forces not only halted the Russian advance there but recaptured the southern part of the city and most of its center in a late-2025 offensive.
- After regrouping, Russian forces again went on the offensive against the city center, Zaoskillia — the half of Kupiansk on the Oskil River’s eastern bank — and neighboring industrial towns. By the end of summer, Russian forces had reached the river’s eastern bank in several places and once again seized central districts on the western bank, though Ukrainian forces continue to hold back the advance around the city.
- Near Vovchansk, however, the redeployment of Ukrainian troops to Kupiansk for the winter offensive weakened the defense there, allowing Russian forces to infiltrate the front line with relatively large units from two directions — from the north, out of occupied Vovchansk, and from the east, across the border at the village of Artelne.
- The groups that infiltrated from Vovchansk reached the outskirts of Bilyi Kolodiaz, but Ukrainian forces pushed them back. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its forces had captured the village, which is important for supplying the Ukrainian group, and videos later surfaced showing Russian assault units massing in tree lines to the north.
- Capturing Bilyi Kolodiaz and the surrounding area would open the way for Russian forces to break through to Velykyi Burluk, in the rear of the Ukrainian group defending Kupiansk.

14 killed as Russia unleashes massive overnight barrage on unprotected Kyiv, striking homes, hospital, school and railway infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
08:47:59 UTC
17:47:59 KST

Editor's note: This is a developing story.
Russia launched a massive overnight missile and drone attack targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing 14 people and injuring more than 40, Ukrainian authorities said on 20 August.
The attack involved ballistic and cruise missiles alongside hundreds of drones. Ukraine’s Air Force said the main direction of the attack was Kyiv Oblast, with strikes and debris recorded at multiple locations. Several explosions were heard in the capital around midnight on 20 August, according to Euromaidan Press reporters in the city.
Residential building hit in Kyiv
In Kyiv, strikes, damage, and fires were reported in the Sviatoshynskyi, Darnytskyi, and Solomianskyi districts.
In Solomianskyi district, the upper two floors of a nine-story residential building were destroyed, with a fire breaking out across the seventh through ninth floors.
People were trapped in two residential buildings and a school bomb shelter, prompting emergency crews to carry out rescue operations.
Thirteen people have now been confirmed killed in Kyiv, including a woman whose body was discovered by rescuers in Solomianskyi district, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a children's hospital and a school were also damaged in the capital.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city would observe 21 August as a day of mourning, with entertainment events banned and flags lowered.
Fires and damage across Kyiv
Around 20 residential buildings in Kyiv were significantly damaged, along with a school, children's hospital, and kindergarten, Vyhivskyi said.
In Sviatoshynskyi district, Russian strikes hit an industrial site and sparked fires at warehouses covering 500 and 1,000 square meters. Another warehouse also caught fire.
In Darnytskyi district, a non-residential site was hit, causing fires across warehouses and vehicles covering about 1,000 square meters. Rescuers saved one person and handed them over to medics.
Other locations saw damage to residential buildings, a medical facility, cars, garages, and stores.
More than 600 rescuers and police officers have been involved in clearing the aftermath since overnight. Emergency crews are currently working at two sites in Kyiv and three more in Boryspil and Brovary districts.
Rescuers are using specialized equipment and robotic systems to clear the rubble and check whether anyone remains trapped.
Police have set up assistance centers at the attack sites to register reports of damaged or destroyed property. More than 200 reports have already been processed in Kyiv, while psychologists are assisting people who lost relatives or their homes.
Kyiv Oblast casualties
The attack also hit Kyiv Oblast. One man was killed in Brovary district and another was injured.
In Boryspil district, six people were injured, four of whom were hospitalized. The attack damaged 14 private homes, four warehouses, a gas station, an apartment building, and eight vehicles.
Vyhivskyi said fires also engulfed warehouses storing household goods in Kyiv Oblast. Firefighters are working to contain the blaze, with aviation also deployed.
Zelenskyy calls for stronger ballistic missile defenses
Zelenskyy said Russia’s growing investment in ballistic missiles requires a stronger international response and more air defense for Ukraine.
He said Ukraine is working daily on its FREYJA interceptor program, but stressed that Patriot interceptors remain irreplaceable and are needed every day to protect Ukrainian cities from Russian ballistic missile attacks.
“Every additional missile saves the lives of our people,” Zelenskyy said, thanking those working to provide Ukraine with additional air defense capabilities.
Hundreds of aerial targets launched
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 168 Shahed-type attack drones, Gerbera decoy drones, and other drones, along with 36 Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kh-59 cruise missiles, eight Kalibr missiles, two Banderyl-type loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles including Oniks, Zircon, Iskander-M, and S-400 missiles.
As of 9:30 a.m., Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 31 cruise missiles, all eight Kalibr missiles, both loitering munitions, and 145 drones, according to the Air Force.
The Air Force reported impacts at 28 locations and debris from intercepted targets at two others.
The attack continued into the late morning, with air raid sirens still active and several Russian drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic and hypersonic missiles overnight, damaging a children’s hospital, with people trapped in a shelter
Rail traffic disrupted
Russia's strikes also disrupted rail traffic around Kyiv after railway infrastructure was damaged. Several suburban and regional trains between Kyiv and Nizhyn were rerouted or canceled.
Strikes reported in other regions
Zelenskyy said the attack also caused damage in Odesa and Chernihiv oblasts.
In Odesa Oblast, Russian drones targeted a border crossing with Moldova, while strikes in Chernihiv Oblast damaged gas infrastructure.

More permits issued for newbuilds but pipeline is filling up
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Turnover in the construction trade was up by 5.2% in the second quarter of 2026 while the number of newbuild permits was close to record levels, continuing the strong trend of the last 18 months.
Sales have grown by at least 5% in every three-month period but one since the end of 2024, although the market has cooled off from its peak of more than 7% aa year ago.
Newbuild permits issued in May, the latest month for which figures are available, stood at 10,824 for domestic houses and 2,637 commercial properties. The total figure is the highest since December 2024, when more than 13,600 permits were issued, statistics agency CBS said.
The number of buildings in the pipeline grew to nearly 234,000 houses and 48,000 commercial premises.
Permits are being issued faster than buildings are being completed, which has caused the pipeline figure to grow by around 33% for houses and 25% for business premises in the last two and a half years.
The CBS also recorded a steep growth in costs in the construction sector, with a 97% increase for domestic properties in the last year.
The agency said the spike was partly caused by congestion on the electricity network, which had prompted councils to speed up the planning process for newbuild projects before restrictions on new connections kicked in.
The labour market in the sector remains tight, with 28,600 unfilled vacancies recorded by the CBS. In the second quarter of the year 133 construction companies folded, five more than in the winter months.

3D printed banjo uses party balloon as its sound box to explore how air changes the tone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
08:45:22 UTC
17:45:22 KST

a party balloon becomes A hands-on lesson in sound
A 3D printedinstrument by Co:Creation Lab uses a replaceable party balloon as its sound box, turning the physics of resonance into something users can adjust and feel. Called the Balloon Banjo, the small playable object combines seven printed components with fishing line or nylon strings and a conventional round balloon, creating a DIY instrument that doubles as a simple experiment in acoustics.
Plucking a string sends the sound into the balloon, where the volume of air affects the resulting resonance. Inflate the balloon more or less and the character of the sound changes; alter the tension of the strings and it shifts again.
The way the instrument is made encourages users to modify the object. The balloon can be replaced with one of a different size, while the fishing line or nylon strings can be exchanged for different thicknesses. Each change becomes another small test.
all images courtesy of Co:Creation Lab
a printable instrument built for experimentation
The banjo consists of seven distinct printed parts and 19 pieces in total: a neck, left and right flanges, two bridge components, seven pegs and seven peg sockets. Once the sockets are fitted into the body, the instrument is assembled with plastic screws that can be turned by hand. There is no metal hardware, glue, or screwdriver, and the instrument can be taken apart again. The construction turns assembly itself into part of the design, while the absence of permanent fixings makes experimentation easier. The same object can be assembled, modified, disassembled, and rebuilt without committing to a single configuration.
The technical instructions reveal a similar attention to the behavior of the printed material. The model is designed around PLA, using a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer height, and 15 percent infill, with an estimated total print time of around 11 hours. The pegs and sockets use a finer 0.16 mm layer height because they carry the fit tolerance. The designer specifies a 0.15 mm clearance for PLA, with roughly another 0.05 mm allowed when printing in PETG.
Even the orientation of the parts is determined by how 3D printed layers behave under stress. The neck is printed flat because the direction of the layers affects its strength; printed upright, it can snap along a layer line once the strings are tensioned.
the playable instrument combines a printed body with colorful nylon strings and hand-turned plastic pegs
the 3D-printed Balloon Banjo uses an inflated party balloon as its sound box
the balloon sits inside the printed frame, where changes in inflation alter the instrument’s tone
with the balloon removed, the printed frame reveals the structure of the instrument’s sound box
its individual printed components and reassembled without glue or metal hardware
the design combines a 3D printed TPU sole, a leather inner boot inspired by traditional central asian makhsi and ichigi footwear, and a rope-based fastening system.

U.S. Army expands ultra-light vehicle buy 18-fold to 11,582
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
08:44:37 UTC
17:44:37 KST

- The U.S. Army raised its Infantry Squad Vehicle procurement objective to 11,582 vehicles, an 18-fold increase from the original 649-vehicle target.
- The Army is developing a heavy ISV variant with enhanced power generation to support next-generation command and control equipment.
The U.S. Army has increased its procurement objective for the Infantry Squad Vehicle to 11,582 vehicles, an 18-fold jump from the program’s original 649-vehicle target, according to Jacqueline Hames of the Army Acquisition Support Center.
The Infantry Squad Vehicle is an ultra-light tactical vehicle that carries nine passengers along with their equipment. The Army launched the program in 2019 to fill a gap it identified between the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle and the Humvee, both of which the service found too heavy for some battlefield tasks.
The procurement objective has climbed in stages since the program began. It rose to 900 vehicles in February 2021, then increased twice more to reach 2,593. In April 2025, the Army approved a utility variant of the vehicle and raised the combined objective to 5,733 across both variants. The Army set the current objective, 11,582 vehicles, in February 2026.
“This led to an explosive growth driven entirely by operational demand,” said Susan Fung, deputy project manager for the mobile brigade combat team within Portfolio Acquisition Executive Maneuver Ground.
“In February of 2026, the Army established the current position objective and procurement objective at 11,582 vehicles,” Fung said. “That shows you the increased objective based on soldier demand, and that’s really equivalent to about an 18-fold increase from the original requirement. Not because of requirements creep, but really because soldiers validated the capability in the combat training environments and demanded more.”
The Army built the growth on continuous soldier feedback gathered through its Transformation in Contact program, which tests emerging equipment with soldiers in operational settings. Fung said the team deliberately relied on commercial products and iterative testing rather than the Army’s traditional acquisition path.
“We are extremely proud of this program and what we’ve been able to achieve in a short period of time,” Fung said. “In this high-stakes environment of modern warfare, playing it completely safe is often the most dangerous thing a leader can do for decades.”
John Hufstedler, product director for ground mobility vehicles at Portfolio Acquisition Executive Maneuver Ground, said the team resisted adding capabilities beyond the vehicle’s core mission during development.
“Early on, the ISV succeeded by staying locked-in. A few key requirements were transportability, [but] mobility and payload and resisting requirements creep,” Hufstedler said.
“Anytime somebody wanted to add a radio with encrypted keys or hang another piece of encrypted equipment off the platform, leadership just didn’t buy into it. And that allowed the vehicle to stay focused and true to its mission, so we didn’t have to leave a soldier back with the vehicle. All nine could go execute the mission and objective,” he said.
Standard defense acquisition, which allows custom military specifications, extensive government testing and sequential milestone gates, typically takes four to 10 years and often results in cost overruns and technological obsolescence, according to Hufstedler. The Infantry Squad Vehicle program instead used commercial off-the-shelf components with minimal military modification, delivering the first equipped unit within 24 months, he said.
“With the ISV program, we prove[d] that calculated risk works,” Hufstedler said. “We keep going back to commerciality. I think that has helped us a lot: trusting our soldiers’ judgment and moving at the speed of relevance. I think we’ve delivered that capability.”
The Army is now developing a heavy variant of the Infantry Squad Vehicle, which will include enhanced onboard power generation and storage capacity to support next-generation command and control equipment, according to Fung.

Are Hormuz ships more willing to defy Iran or the US? What data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
08:43:17 UTC
17:43:17 KST

Are ships passing Hormuz more willing to defy Iran or US? What data shows
Most ships are trying to mask their identities while trying to cross the strait. But more seem scared of Iran than of defying the US.
United States President Donald Trump has insisted that his military remains in control of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, and suggested this past week that the US might even seek to take charge of the territory.
On Tuesday, he also claimed that the strait was open for vessels to pass through, despite Iranian insistence that the waterway was closed for all ships that don’t seek Tehran’s approval before transit, and even though the US itself has a naval blockade in place targeting all Iran-linked ships.
At the same time, Trump has threatened to bomb Oman, a US ally that sits across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran – the waterway lies in the maritime territories of Iran and Oman – in an apparent bid to dissuade Muscat from striking any deal with Tehran to jointly manage the strait.
So who really is in control of the Strait of Hormuz at the moment?
Amid the claims and counterclaims from both sides, actual data on the traffic passing through the waterway offers vital clues. We break it down.
What are the two main routes through the Strait of Hormuz?
Before the war started, the Strait of Hormuz was largely considered a single waterway, without distinctions between “Iranian” or “Omani” routes, and ships entered and exited along well‑established traffic separation schemes, mostly along the central part of the strait.
Decisions on how ships navigated the strait were determined by port calls, charter terms and safety rather than fear of military consequences.
Since the war has spiked tensions between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway has been fractured into two main routes. Tehran insists on the northern, Iranian route, hugging Iran’s coast near Larak Island and Qeshm Island, and feeding directly into Iranian ports and offshore terminals.
The other route is the southern, Omani route, closer to Oman and further from Iran’s shoreline. This is the route that Washington insists on, and is the one used by commercial carriers under US Naval protection.
What routes do ships carrying oil and gas use?
Data from maritime intelligence firm Kpler shows that 112 vessels carrying crude, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and liquefied natural gas (LNG) passed through the Strait of Hormuz – either entering the Gulf or leaving it – between August 1 and August 19.
Of those tankers and carriers, 21 openly used the Iranian route and only two formally used the Omani route.
The remaining 89 vessels, which make up more than 80 percent of the total oil and gas traffic through the strait in this period, went along dark or otherwise unclassified routes.
This happens when a vessel’s movements cannot be fully tracked or clearly linked to a declared route because the vessel either turns off its Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponder or the AIS data does not neatly fit into Kpler’s defined Iranian or Omani corridors. Hence, it is not clear which route these vessels took.
“While these transits can be observed once vessels reappear after crossing, the nature of dark routing makes it highly difficult to determine what proportion may also have used the Omani route or to confirm their precise routing from the available data,” Mohamed Rafik Halitim, a customer success manager for maritime and commodities at Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
What about cargo beyond just oil and gas?
Kpler’s data shows that 236 ships in all transited through Hormuz between August 1 and August 19. This includes not just oil and gas vessels, but others carrying dry cargo and chemicals.
Of these ships, 83 openly used the Iranian route, only three publicly used the Omani route and two used the old pre-war route that ran through the centre of the strait.
But the bulk of the ships, 148 of them, again went dark or used unknown routes while transiting through the strait. That’s more than six out of 10 ships that passed through Hormuz in this period.
By comparison, 35 percent of vessels openly used the Iranian route, and only a handful used the Omani or pre-war route publicly.
Why are so many vessels switching off their transponders?
Since the beginning of the war, both Iran and the US have not only threatened, but have actually bombed vessels that they each claim are violating their routes or rules for maritime navigation through the waterway.
Hence, several vessels are turning off their transponders to strip away the digital identifiers that military forces use to target them.
“Switching off transponders can reduce the visibility of a vessel’s precise location and movements, although it also creates concerns about maritime safety and transparency,” Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow at the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the UK-based think tank Chatham House, told Al Jazeera. “Some operators believe the commercial and security benefits outweigh those risks under current conditions.”
On August 8, the United Arab Emirates accused Iran of attacking a tanker owned by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) with a missile as it tried to pass through the strait.
In a statement, ADNOC said that since the beginning of the war, 15 of its vessels had been attacked by missiles and drones while transiting the strait, killing one crew member and injuring 20. The ADNOC statement did not blame either side.
Last month, the US fired on an oil tanker traversing through the strait towards Iran’s Kharg Island. The US said it fired Hellfire missiles at the ship after it ignored several warnings.
On August 11, the US said a Navy helicopter also fired two Hellfire missiles at the Panama-flagged Vela Nova cargo vessel, adding that the ship was attempting to break its blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf of Oman, which connects directly to the Strait of Hormuz.
Another reason to switch off transponders is to conduct ship-to-ship cargo transfers, mid-route, without being seen, experts say.
“According to sources and data over the past two weeks, some Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and Kuwait, have sent out some shipments through the Omani route by turning off their vessel tracking and by doing ship-to-ship transfers,” energy policy researcher and consultant Marc Ayoub told Al Jazeera.
In essence, a ship that wants to avoid the threat of Iranian missiles would travel through the Omani route with its transponder off, but then passes its cargo over to a ship outside the strait, which then ferries it to its final destination. The original “dark” ship then returns to its port of origin undetected.
Ayoub added that a number of Iranian vessels are also transiting through the Omani route – often including ship-to-ship transfers – to avoid sanctions against Iran and the US blockade.
“They send their shipment to Oman through the Omani route, they change the documents of those shipments so that they appear as if they are exported by Oman, and then they send it to the oil market.”
Are ships more scared of defying Iran or the US?
The fact that most ships passing through the strait are switching off their transponders or using unknown routes means that it is impossible to know, for now, exactly how many are actually using either the Iranian or the Omani route.
That in turn means it is difficult to conclusively say who “controls” the strait at the moment.
But the data does tell us which of the two powers vessels are more willing to defy and who they’re more scared of offending.
Despite a US naval blockade backed by the world’s most powerful navy, a fifth of all energy-carrying ships openly transited Hormuz through the Iranian route, defying Trump’s threats. And that number rose to 35 percent of all vessels when carriers ferrying cargo and chemicals are included.
By contrast, only two oil and gas ships, and four vessels in all, openly used a route other than the one prescribed by Iran.
The conclusion: The fear of offending Tehran appears to outweigh Trump’s threats.
Is Iran losing control of the Strait of Hormuz?
Experts say that Iran still retains significant capacity to control maritime traffic in the strategic waterway.
“Iran is not losing control in the current status quo,” Ayoub said.
However, he added that this scenario could ultimately become unsustainable for global oil markets.
“Iran still retains significant capacity to disrupt maritime traffic and threaten shipping in the Strait of Hormuz,” Quilliam said.
“However, the growing use of alternative logistics arrangements, ship-to-ship transfers, and enhanced regional maritime security measures suggest that Iran’s ability to exert pressure through the strait is not absolute,” he added.
Why is the Strait of Hormuz significant to the Iran war?
The Strait of Hormuz is a critical waterway through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and LNG supplies were shipped before the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28. Roughly 130 ships sailed through the strait each day, compared with the 236 in all that passed over 19 days in August 2026.
Iran closed the strait in early March, allowing only a few ships it deemed “friendly” to pass through the strait, until it signed the MoU with the US on June 17. Since then, it has become the key issue holding up talks for a lasting peace plan to end the war on Iran.
The US, meanwhile, has established its own blockade on Iranian ports in and around the strait. Last week, it fired on a Panama-flagged cargo vessel it accused of attempting to reach Iranian ports and which, it said, had failed to follow orders to change course.
The crisis has triggered global energy shortages, and the price of oil has soared. The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, was about $66 a barrel just before the Middle East conflict began. Over the course of the war, the price has surged past $100 on several occasions, most recently on July 23. In March, the price rose as high as $119.
The price of Brent crude fell significantly after the US and Iran agreed to a ceasefire in April, and then when they signed the MoU in June. But with tensions rising again, so too has the price of oil: Brent stood at $92.9 per barrel on Thursday morning.
“If Tehran’s influence over shipping flows is perceived to be diminishing, this could weaken one of its traditional sources of leverage in negotiations with the US,” Quilliam said.

Albanese wanted 'full accountability' from Israel. Instead, Australia is 'outraged'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
08:42:59 UTC
17:42:59 KST

In brief
- Australia says Israel's investigation into Zomi Frankcom's death leaves "many unanswered questions".
- Relations have deteriorated from close ties to sanctions and recognition of a Palestinian state.
Israel's decision not to pursue criminal proceedings over the killing of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom has sparked "outrage" from the federal government, signalling a new low for relations between the two countries.
The decision comes after almost three years of increasingly strained ties, with Australia moving from backing Israel after the October 7 attacks to imposing sanctions on Israeli government ministers and recognising a Palestinian state.
Despite previously conceding there had been "serious failures", the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) on Wednesday announced it would not prosecute those responsible for the death of Frankcom and six of her World Central Kitchen colleagues in an IDF strike in Gaza in April 2024.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the decision "falls far short of the accountability we expect" in some of her most critical comments against Israel since the Gaza war began.
Asked about Australia's relationship with Israel, Wong said it was facing a "difficult time".
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
She said the federal government only became aware of the decision moments before it was publicly announced, and it was "especially insulting" to Frankcom's family that it came on World Humanitarian Day, a point echoed by Zomi's brother Mal in a statement.
The Greens called for the Israeli ambassador, Hillel Newman, who was summoned by the government for an explanation on Thursday, to be expelled.
Opposition defence spokesperson James Paterson said the news was "incredibly concerning", but he needed to receive a full briefing before making further comment.
Frankcom and her colleagues were travelling in a marked aid convoy in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, when they were hit by three Israeli drone strikes on 1 April 2024.
The Israeli military initially said the convoy had been mistaken for a group of Hamas fighters before later acknowledging the vehicles had been misidentified and there had been serious failures in the decision-making leading to the attack.
A low point in relations
Australia and Israel have historically enjoyed warm relations, with Australia supporting Israel at international forums such as the United Nations.
The Australian government's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade states in a current country briefing on its website that "Australia and Israel share a close relationship with significant people-to-people links and broad commercial engagement."
There have been previous periods of tension, most notably in 2010, when then-prime minister Kevin Rudd expelled an Israeli diplomat after Israel's intelligence agency Mossad was accused of 'misusing' Australian passports for agents involved in the assassination of a senior Hamas operative in Dubai.
But Ian Parmeter, a research scholar in Middle Eastern affairs at the Australian National University and a former diplomat, said Israel's response to the Hamas October 7 attacks had seen the relationship sink to new depths.
"I think at this stage you can judge it to be the worst that it's been," he told SBS News.
"With the terrible pictures that we were seeing on the television screens of Palestinian civilians being killed by Israeli bombs, there was a substantial deterioration in the Australian public's attitude towards Israel, and the Australian government started to reflect that."
Hamas killed more than 1,200 people and took 251 hostages in its 7 October 2023 attack, according to Israeli authorities.
Israel subsequently launched a military campaign in Gaza, with 73,000 people killed in the territory, according to the Gaza health ministry.
A tentative ceasefire was reached in October last year, but both sides have accused each other of breaching it. More than 1,200 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed since it came into effect.
How did we get here?
Parmeter said Australia's position had progressively hardened as the war continued.
According to a study by the US-based Pew Research Center study published in June, 79 per cent of Australians held an unfavourable view of Israel, up five percentage points from a year earlier.
As Israel's military operations in Gaza expanded, the federal government increasingly emphasised the protection of civilians, allowing humanitarian access and the release of the hostages held by Hamas.
In December 2023, Australia voted at the United Nations in favour of a humanitarian ceasefire in Gaza, a move criticised by Israel and a shift from Australia's previous decision to abstain.
Throughout 2024, Australia increasingly backed calls for a ceasefire, Palestinian self-determination and a two-state solution.
Frankcom's killing in April 2024 became another major point of tension, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese calling for "full accountability" from Israel.
By July, Australia, Canada and New Zealand had issued a joint statement describing the humanitarian situation in Gaza as "catastrophic" and saying Israel needed to listen to international concerns about civilian protection.
In September 2024, Wong addressed the United Nations General Assembly about the deteriorating situation in Gaza, including the deaths of more than 11,000 children and the risk of food insecurity for two million people.
"Palestinian civilians cannot be made to pay the price of defeating Hamas," she said.
"All lives have equal value."
In June 2025, Australia announced, also in a joint statement with four other nations, financial sanctions and travel bans against Israeli ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, for inciting violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.
Recognition of Palestinian statehood
Parmeter said a turning point in relations came in September 2025, when Australia formally recognised the State of Palestine — a historic shift in Australia's policy towards Israel.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu personally criticised Albanese, describing him as a "weak politician" who had "betrayed Israel and abandoned Australia's Jews".
"This was pretty strong stuff," Parmeter said.
"I've not seen that sort of personal abuse come from the leader of a nominally friendly country towards an Australian leader in my time over the past 50 years."
Albanese did not directly respond to the criticism, but Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Netanyahu had "lashed out" at countries which had shown support for Palestinian statehood.
"Strength is not measured by how many people you can blow up or how many children you can leave hungry," he said.
The relationship was further strained after the Bondi Beach shooting, in which gunmen killed 15 people attending a Hanukkah event in an alleged terrorist attack last December.
Netanyahu accused Albanese of pouring "fuel on the antisemitism fire" by recognising a Palestinian state and failing to act against antisemitism.
"You took no action. You let the disease spread and the result is the horrific attacks on Jews we saw today," he said at the time.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog's visit to Australia in February was seen by some analysts as an opportunity to reset relations but was met with widespread protests, underscoring the depth of public opposition to Israel's conduct in Gaza.
The tensions between the two countries returned to the fore on Thursday following Wong's comments.
The federal government has so far stopped short of expelling the Israeli ambassador or other diplomats, but it could take further steps to pressure Israel, including imposing additional sanctions or reducing the level of diplomatic engagement between the two countries.
"We'll have to see if any of them are taken," Parmeter said.
How does Israel see Australia?
Dr Ran Porat, from the Australian Centre for Jewish Civilisation at Monash University and a research affiliate at the Australia Israel & Jewish Affairs Council, told SBS News that from Israel's perspective, Australia was "walking away from its support of Israel" and abandoning shared values around combating extremism.
"Over the last five years, and especially after October 7, we've seen a shift from the Australian government distancing itself from at least the current Israeli government in a series of decisions that started with the cancellation of the recognition of West Jerusalem as Israel's capital."
Despite the deterioration in relations, Porat said strong ties remained between Israel and Australia, with much of the current tension stemming from the relationship between the two governments.
Israel is due to hold elections in October, with Netanyahu's right-wing coalition trailing in the polls, raising the prospect of a reset in relations if a new government is elected.
"I'm hopeful that the countries can go back to the strong ties between themselves, because the platform for that exists," Porat said.
Parmeter noted that relations between Israel and Australia remained strong at the community level, with the Australian Jewish community playing a key role.
"There always is the opportunity for basically restoring a good sense of relationship between countries, and that well may happen," he said.
"In diplomacy you never say never."
Whatever happens after Israel's next election, the Frankcom case is likely to remain a sore point in the relationship.
On Thursday afternoon, Wong said the Australian government did not have confidence in the IDF's internal investigations, which had left "many unanswered questions".
"We will consult with Zomi Frankcom's family before we announce further steps," she said.
Wong also called on Israel to apologise to Frankcom's family.
Israel's ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, expressed sorrow over Frankcom's death on Thursday but stopped short of an apology, saying it could have "legal ramifications".

This refers to the Tamanneftegaz oil and gas complex in the settlement of Volna, which plays an important role in facilitating Russia’s oil exports.
As a result of the drone attack, oil and petroleum product storage tanks were likely set ablaze.
Tamanneftegaz is operated by the OTEKO group and is the largest privately owned oil terminal complex in southern Russia. The facility serves as a specialized transshipment hub for receiving, storing, and loading petroleum products.
The terminal has an annual throughput capacity of around 19.9 million tons. Prior to the start of the Ukrainian attacks, its storage tanks for petroleum products and liquefied gas had a total capacity exceeding 1 million cubic meters.
This is not the first attack on this facility. On July 30, at least three storage tanks and pipelines were hit. The disruption of this infrastructure directly interferes with the loading of oil tankers in the Black Sea.
In addition, a fire was reported at the Taman substation, which is a key hub of the Russian so-called energy bridge to the temporarily occupied Crimea.
A widespread blackout occurred on the peninsula last night. A complete power outage was reported in Simferopol, Sevastopol, Kerch, Feodosia, and Yalta. There are also internet disruptions.
The Taman power substation (Taman 500/220 kV substation) is a major 500 kV transmission substation that forms part of Russia’s Unified Power System.
It is one of the key elements of the power supply to occupied Crimea via the Kerch Strait. All four lines of the power bridge from Russia’s Krasnodar Krai to the invaded peninsula pass through the substation.
Taking such facilities out of commission creates a power shortage on the occupied peninsula and limits the operations of Russian industrial and military facilities.

Pakistan summons US diplomat after Trump envoy’s comments
Pakistan on Wednesday summoned the top US diplomat in Islamabad to lodge a “strong demarche” over remarks made by Washington’s ambassador in New Delhi that Jammu and Kashmir is an “important part of India.”
Sergio Gor, who is also the US special envoy to South and Central Asia, made the comments in Srinagar, the part of Kashmir administered by India, on Wednesday. Gor, a close confidant and former business partner of US President Donald Trump, is on a two-day trip to India’s Jammu and Kashmir state and the federally administered Ladakh region.
“Kashmir is an important part of India,” Gor told reporters after meeting Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah. “It is an incredibly beautiful place.”
India and Pakistan, which gained independence when Britain partitioned its colonial territories in South Asia in 1947, have competing claims on Kashmir.
Hours after the comments, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Charge d’Affaires Natalie Baker – the top US envoy in Islamabad – and lodged a protest over Gor’s “factually incorrect remarks” and “irresponsible statement.”
“It was underscored that Jammu and Kashmir is an internationally recognized disputed territory, awaiting final disposition in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people,” the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Nuclear-armed neighbors India and Pakistan clashed briefly with missiles and drones last year after 26 people were killed in a terror attack in Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi blamed on Pakistan-backed terror groups.
Gor’s comments have come despite a close rapport between Trump and Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir. Trump had claimed to have intervened to stop the India-Pakistan clash – an assertion that New Delhi dismissed. Islamabad, however, credited the US president with ending the short conflict and recommended him for the Nobel Peace Prize last year.
Trump has, in return, called Munir “my favorite field marshal.” Islamabad has also been acting as a mediator to end the Mideast war, which was triggered by US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
Indian authorities on Thursday used a bulldozer to remove temporary structures, traffic bollards, and barricades outside the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi, in an apparent retaliatory action after Pakistan carried out a similar drive outside the Indian mission in Islamabad on Monday.

Alarming study reveals that almost 40 per cent of music released globally in July 2026 used AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
08:40:30 UTC
17:40:30 KST

The use of AI in music creation continues to be a divisive topic and recent figures confirm that the onslaught of AI-generated tracks is not slowing down. Worse, certain artists are becoming more open about using the controversial technology.
“Just stop your crying, it's a sign of the times...”
What do you know about it, Harry Styles? Some signs are worth crying over.
Here’s one that is sure to provoke some sobbing: As AI-generated music continues to flood streaming platforms, a new study has revealed that almost 40 per cent of new music released globally in July 2026 used AI in its creation.
That alarming figure comes from a new survey by SubmitHub, an online platform that allows users to submit music to playlists and blogs. They analysed over a million pieces of music and using their own AI detector, SH Labs, found that 23.2 per cent of them were fully AI-generated.
In addition to that, 15.3 per cent were found to have used elements of AI-generated audio that had been "modified or processed" by humans. That totals to a whopping 38.5 per cent of all music released last month to have been made with the involvement of AI.
SubmitHub was launched SH Labs earlier this summer in order to highlight a “growing disclosure problem” with artificial intelligence in music. Their AI detection tool is being used by Bandcamp and Traxsource to uncover the use of AI in music, as well as GEMA, the performance rights organisation which recently won a landmark court case against AI music generator platform Suno.
In a statement, SubmitHub’s founder Jason Grishkoff said: "I think the path forward for AI music is disclosure. People should be able to decide for themselves whether they want to engage with AI-generated music.”
He added: “Our job is to give them enough information to make that choice."
These recent figures follow fresh stats from Deezer, who reported that AI tracks accounted for more than half of all new daily uploads in June. They also follow a 2025 study that found that 97 per cent of people “can’t tell the difference between real and AI music”.
Certain organisations are starting to finally wake up to the concerns of real artists and music lovers expressing concerns over the AI slop dished out on streaming platforms.
For instance, Bandcamp banned all AI-created music at the start of 2026, stating that they “reserve the right to remove any music on suspicion of being AI-generated", while streaming giant Spotify recently announced that it will begin adding an “AI Persona” badge to some artist profiles, helping listeners identify when an artist’s music may have been generated using artificial intelligence. That initiative starts in September.
While artists from Kate Bush to Queen’s Brian May have spoken out on the existential crisis AI represents to creatives, stating that “the unlicensed use of creative works for training generative AI is a major, unjust threat to the livelihoods of the people behind those works”, there are some creatives who have taken a more decomplexed approach to the use of the controversial technology.
Empire Of The Sun’s Luke Steele recently admitted that he uses AI to make music; Boy George said he used AI to help write his dire pro-Israel reggae track ‘We Will Dance Again’ (something which eventually led it to be removed from Bandcamp for violating its AI rules); and one recent artist who has provoked the ire of his peers is American rapper Tyga.
The latter admitted he used AI as a “tool” on his new (and critically panned) album, ‘$tarface’. Tyga used AI to generate the retro synths on his album, framing it the “tool” as being “no different than when Auto-Tune came out.”
Regardless, the album has been savaged by critics, with Pitchfork giving it the lowest possible rating of 0/10, describing ‘$tarface’ as “smug and complacent and depressing” and that “its very existence has made the world a worse place.”
Artists have called out Tyga – including Doja Cat, who spoke for many music lovers when she called him a “penis for making an AI album”.
A literal and figurative tool for some; a complete scam for others.
In a further sign that certain content creators are becoming more comfortable / shameless in embracing AI slop, American record prodcuer and rapper Timbaland has launched an “A-Pop” venture called Stage Zero and signed its first act, TaTa, which he describes as “a living, learning, autonomous music artist built with AI.”
These examples and recent figures, on top of the harrowing “music” by AI creations Tilly Norwood, Velvet Sundown and Breaking Rust - who compete with real artists for listening time as well as royalties - show that one thing is clear. We’re not out of the artificial woods yet.

When a former Swiss foreign minister turns her hand to acting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
08:40:27 UTC
17:40:27 KST

When a former Swiss foreign minister turns her hand to acting
Should Switzerland join an international democracy alliance? The fictional question behind a recent performance in Zurich questions the country’s global role and the links between politics and theatre.
In September 1946, in a famous speechExternal link at the University of Zurich, Winston Churchill called for a “United States of Europe” to follow the cataclysm of the Second World War. Almost 80 years later, on a balmy Friday evening in the same hall, his spirit is being invoked. This time, however, the talk is of an “International Democratic Alliance” (IDA): a group of 40-odd nations banding together against rampant authoritarianism. Can it save democracy – and should Switzerland be a member?
The scenario, as you may have guessed, is a theatrical one. But reality is never far away; from ex-Swiss Foreign Minister Micheline Calmy-Rey to ex-Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Löfven, most of the cast are real public figures, playing versions of themselves; the 200-strong audience also has a role as a “citizens’ delegation”, debating the arguments for and against the IDA before voting on Swiss membership. And while the fictional scenario is a future one – we are in August 2027 – but the global situation is plausibly turbulent.
“When such an evening is well constructed, a realness emerges that fosters political imagination,” says Eneas Prawdzic, the director of the Proberaum Zukunft show, which runs over four evenings in August as part of an annual festival. Within the space of two short hours – “condensed reality”, Prawdzic says – we are plunged into an alternate reality that not only asks us to consider the thorny question of Switzerland’s global role, but also aims to spur awareness of a real democratic emergency. Will it work?
‘Shattered’ rules-based order
The event goes to lengths to hammer home the stakes. In plugging the show beforehand, it highlighted dire threats to democracy in the real world of 2026. “The rules-based international order is currently shattered, with three big players [Russia, China, and the US] who don’t want to abide by it,” said Helen KellerExternal link, a University of Zurich professor and former European Court of Human Rights judge, who also performed on Friday. The fictional scenario of 2027 is also pressing: far-right politician Marine Le Pen is in power in France, the US has left the United Nations and NATO, cloud infrastructure has been weaponised, terrorism and “pogrom-like” riots abound (albeit not in Switzerland).
Orchestrated spontaneity also tries to create a sense of urgency. As the show goes on, speaking times get shorter; audience members have to wait to have their say. A US representative storms in to warn Switzerland against joining the alliance, levelling direct threats at the audience. It’s reminiscent of the chilling real-world remarks of Donald Trump, telling GreenlandersExternal link that “you can say ‘yes’ and we will be very appreciative, or you can say ‘no’ and we will remember”. But is it a heightening of reality or a pale imitation?
The public figures playing versions of themselves add to a sense of authenticity, if not always urgency. Many back the positions they would likely hold anyway. In such a context, “politicians are much better actors than actors themselves”, Prawdzic says.
As for the politicians, nothing concrete is at stake in the theatre, but a rhetorical goal remains. You still want to “pull listeners onto your side”, Nina Fehr Düsel from the right-wing Swiss People’s Party said before her performance on Friday. In the play, she is against joining the IDA – as is the official Swiss negotiating delegation, led by Social Democrat Calmy-Rey. Fehr Düsel says the performance felt like a “mix” between a theatrical and a political one.
>> The theatre also made use of a popular democratic form – the “citizens’ assembly”. What does this do?
More
Are citizens’ assemblies on the decline in an era of eroding democracy?
Politics or political attitude?
But blurring the boundary between reality and fiction, or theatre and politics, is naturally only the start. The larger goal of political theatre, as German critic Florian Malzacher described in 2023’s The Art of AssemblyExternal link, is to turn the performance itself into a public space that is “truly political and not just performing a political attitude” – to make it a “container for trying out, analysing, performing, representing, testing, pushing the limits of, and even reinventing social and political procedures”. Does the show in Zurich have such impact?
A few of those involved mention the effect it has of sparking discussions: about democracy, geopolitics, the future in general. Priska Seiler Graf, a Social Democratic parliamentarian who performed on Saturday, says debates really kicked off for her – including with her husband and son – after the show was over. Petra Holtrup, a University of Zurich political scientist who was part of an expert group which helped to design the evening, says the event fosters what is “perhaps what we most need for democracy right now: direct analogue exchange with others”.
Too much fun?
So far, so Swiss. But as the evening goes on, does a gap threaten to open between the sheer seriousness of the situation and the nature of the response? Before the event, the RepublikExternal link magazine worried it would be too “discussion-heavy” or theoretical. In the end, the danger seems to be a different one: of occasionally sliding into “cabaret”, as a reviewer wroteExternal link of another pre-enactment by the same theatre group. An audience wants to be entertained, but shouldn’t it also be jolted out of it comfort zone?
On Friday, despite the earnest efforts of figures like Keller, the evening often seems keen on providing enough fun to justify the entrance fee. It’s not all laughs, but there is banter among the cast, and some in-jokes about Swiss politics – “the government is always here for you”, says its fictional spokesman, to general amusement. But even when the US representative is threatening her worst, there is not much of the “unease and discomfort” which art historian Claire Bishop, writing two decades agoExternal link, identified as a component of art which explores “democracy as antagonism”.
Indeed, radical disagreement or antagonism is in much shorter supply than in the work of another Swiss director, Milo Rau. Whether this is due to topic, cast, or design is hard to say. Rau tends to use polarising figures; but Micheline Calmy-Rey is not Peter Thiel. A plot involving the mechanisms of Swiss democracy might also be less likely to really tap into the type of issues seen in Rau’s work or in re-enactment films such as Joshua Oppenheimer’s The Act of Killing: the far-right Alternative for Germany, Russian repression, or mass killings.
On a technical level, it’s also debatable whether Swiss democratic procedures – or the citizens’ assembly format – are best-suited to generate what Malzacher describes as a key goal of Rau’s: “experiences that are supposed to be cathartic and full of feeling”. In Zurich on Friday, there is occasional emotion. But it’s often most impressively realistic when most bureaucratic: midway into a long exposition of the budgetary set-up of the new international alliance (something of a UN-EU-NATO hybrid), you’d be forgiven for thinking you’ve been dragged into a parliamentary session in Bern.
>> Since 2024, Milo Rau has been the director – and disrupter-in-chief – of the Vienna Festival:
More
Swiss theatre director Milo Rau stages revolution in Vienna
The many forms of representation
Or does it come down to us – the audience? After all, just as citizens are not mere consumers of democracy, we are not only consumers of theatre this evening, but an integral part of it. Yet none of us, at least on Friday, manages to throw in the type of radical remark that could break the script. Not to mention that we are hardly a diverse bunch: urban, proficient in English, probably economically comfortable. This is not Rau’s “General Assembly”, a 2017 simulated world parliament which gave a voiceExternal link to “those who are underrepresented, who are not heard, the global Third Estate”.
As such, when the audience does vote, it’s not surprising that a majority opts for the rather “progressive” choice of IDA membership – despite opposition by the Swiss government. At least this sparks one of the more memorable speeches of the evening, when Calmy-Rey, a government minister until 2011, takes to the floor to remind us where we are. Such an outcome might be normal in Zurich, but Zurich is not Switzerland, she says. “Where are the farmers, the French-speakers, the Italian-speakers?” In a national vote or citizens’ assembly, whether at the theatre or the ballot box, the result would likely be a different one.
